I. Executive Summary
7. Overview
7.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
Patients with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) have decreased cortisol synthesis due
to an enzymatic defect in the adrenal gland that leads to increases in adrenocorticotropic
hormone (ACTH) and adrenal stimulation, causing excess androgen production. Patients
typically require supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages to reduce ACTH and control the
excess androgens. The excess glucocorticoid and uncontrolled androgens cause a variety of
adverse effects. Crinecerfont inhibits ACTH secretion by the pituitary. The Applicant,
Neurocrine Biosciences Inc., submitted this marketing application for crinecerfont (proposed
(b) (4)
trade name CRENESSITY)
Crinecerfont has fast track,
breakthrough therapy, and orphan designations and was granted priority review.
The application contains two adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations in classic
CAH—one in adults and the other in children 4 years of age and older. These trials clearly met
their efficacy objectives, demonstrating androgen control in the setting of reduced glucocorticoid
dosing, a clinical benefit given the known adverse effects of excess glucocorticoid use. The
review team did not identify any major efficacy issues.
The safety of crinecerfont is adequately characterized in the context of this rare disease. Risks
include hypersensitivity reactions, adrenal insufficiency/crisis (if an inadequate dose of
glucocorticoid is used, including during times of stress/illness), and tolerability issues (e.g.,
headache, fatigue). There is also a finding of mild reductions in neutrophil counts, which were
not associated with an increased risk of infection, may possibly be related to reductions in
glucocorticoid dosages, and are of unclear clinical significance. The trials had 2:1 randomization.
Three crinecerfont-treated subjects versus one placebo-treated subject in the adult trial and four
crinecerfont-treated subjects versus no placebo-treated subjects in the pediatric trial had an
increase in suicidal ideation assessed using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale. An
adult on crinecerfont also had a suicide attempt. The relationship of these findings to crinecerfont
is unclear given the very low event rates, remote history of suicidality in some of the subjects
who had an increase in their Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, lack of neuropsychiatric
findings in animals, and no increase in suicidality when crinecerfont was studied in a major
depressive disorder trial. All these risks and uncertainties will be mitigated with labeling, and we
will continue to monitor these risks in the postmarketing setting.
Existing human data regarding crinecerfont use during pregnancy and lactation are insufficient to
inform risks with these uses; therefore, we are requiring further assessment in these settings as
postmarketing requirements.
The entire review team and signatory authority agree that the application can be approved. There
were no areas of scientific or regulatory disagreement. The overall benefit-risk is favorable as
described in the benefit-risk framework below.

7.2. Conclusions on Substantial Evidence of
Effectiveness
Substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE) was established with two or more adequate and wellcontrolled clinical investigations.
Substantial evidence of effectiveness was established based on the two pivotal, phase 3, doubleblind, placebo-controlled efficacy trials, Trial NBI-74788-CAH3003 (Trial CAH3003, National
Clinical Trial [NCT] 04490915) conducted in adults with classic CAH, and NBI-74788CAH2006 (Trial CAH2006, NCT 04806451) conducted in pediatric subjects aged 4 to 17 years,
inclusive, with classic CAH. In both studies, crinecerfont had a statistically significant greater
effect than placebo on the primary efficacy endpoint, as described below. In Trial CAH3003,
crinecerfont also had a statistically significantly greater effect on the key secondary efficacy
endpoints of change from baseline in serum androstenedione level at Week 4 and the proportion
of subjects with a reduction to physiologic glucocorticoid dose while maintaining
androstenedione control at Week 24. In pediatric Trial CAH2006, crinecerfont was statistically
significantly better than placebo for both key secondary efficacy endpoints (i.e., change from
baseline in serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone at Week 4 and the percentage change in daily
glucocorticoid dose while maintaining androstenedione control at Week 28).
The order of the primary and key secondary efficacy endpoints differed in the two trials. Data are
presented as least-squares means with standard error of the mean or 95% confidence interval in
parentheses. In the adult trial, CAH3003, crinecerfont resulted in a significantly greater mean
percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24 while androstenedione
(A4) levels were controlled (i.e., A4≤120% of baseline or ≤upper limit of normal (ULN) for age
and sex), which was the primary efficacy endpoint. Crinecerfont allowed for lowering of the
glucocorticoid daily dose by 27% (2.4) compared to 10% (3.2) in the placebo group at Week 24
while androstenedione levels were controlled. The treatment difference was -17% (95%
confidence interval [CI]: -24, -10). Serum androstenedione at Week 4 was a key secondary
endpoint and significantly decreased by 299 (37.7) ng/dL compared to an increase of 46
(51.0) ng/dL in the placebo group. The treatment difference was -366 ng/dL (95% CI: -457,
-232). In addition, 63% of subjects receiving crinecerfont compared to 18% in the placebo group
were able to reduce their daily glucocorticoid dose to the physiologic range (i.e., dose
<11 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents) while maintaining androstenedione control at Week
24.
In the pediatric Trial CAH2006, the primary efficacy endpoint was change in serum
androstenedione at Week 4. Crinecerfont significantly lowered serum androstenedione levels
-197 (39.4) ng/dL, compared to an increase of 71 (56.2) ng/dL for the placebo group at Week 4
while glucocorticoid dosage remained stable. The treatment difference was -268 (95% CI: -403,
-132). Key secondary endpoints included percent change in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 28
while androstenedione levels were controlled and change from baseline in serum 17hydroxyprogesterone at Week 4. In subjects receiving crinecerfont, glucocorticoid daily dose
was lowered by 18% (1.8) compared to an increase of 6% (2.6) in the placebo group at Week 28
while androstenedione levels were controlled. The treatment difference was -24% (95% CI: -30,
-17). Additionally, crinecerfont lowered 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels at Week 4 by
5865 ng/dL (compared to an increase of 556 ng/dL in the placebo group).

In summary, these trials compellingly demonstrated that crinecerfont allowed for adrenal
androgen control with decreasing doses of glucocorticoids. In fact, many subjects achieved
physiologic glucocorticoid dosing with continued androgen control. The significant decrease in
glucocorticoid dose is clinically meaningful because lowering glucocorticoid dose can have a
direct impact on the subsequent adverse events associated with glucocorticoid excess.

Current
treatment
options

•

The standard-of-care treatment for the adrenal insuffiiency
aspect of CAH includes glucocorticoid replacement (e.g.,
hydrocortisone) and mineralocorticoid replacement
(fludrocortisone).
Stress dosing of glucocorticoids is needed for acute illness
and other situations associated with increased cortisol
requirements.
Suppression of excess adrenal androgen is achieved with
physiologic glucocorticioid dosages in some patients, but
many patients require supraphysiologic dosages of
glucocorticoid to achieve androgen control.
Chronic exposure to supraphysiologic glucocorticoid has
adverse effects on body weight, metabolic parameters, and
bone health.

Standard-of-care therapy includes glucocorticoid and
mineralocorticoid replacement. Additional glucocorticoid is often
needed to suppress elevated adrenal androgen levels, and this
supraphysiologic glucocorticoid can have long-term adverse
effects on body weight, metabolic parameters, and bone health.

By reducing ACTH production via corticotropin-releasing
factor-1 receptor antagonism, crinecerfont lowers adrenal
androgen levels so that the disease can be managed with
lower, more physiologic, total daily glucocorticoid dosages.
In two phase 3 trials, one in adults and one in pediatric
subjects (aged 4 to 17 years) with CAH, crinecerfont
significantly lowered adrenal androgen levels at Week 4
while glucocorticoid dosage remained stable, and allowed
for a significant decrease in glucocorticoid daily dosage at
Week 24 (adult trial) or Week 28 (pediatric trial) while
androgen levels were controlled.
Crinecerfont lowered androstenedione levels at Week 4 by
299 ng/dL (compared to an increase of 46 ng/dL in the
placebo group) in the adult trial and by 197 ng/dL
(compared to an increase of 80 ng/dL in the placebo group)
in the pediatric trial.
Crinecerfont lowered 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels at
Week 4 by 5865 ng/dL (compared to an increase of
556 ng/dL in the placebo group) in the pediatric trial.

In adult and pediatric subjects aged 4 years and older with
CAH, crinecerfont allowed for adrenal androgen control at lower
glucocorticoid dosages, many at physiologic or nearphysiologic replacement dosages. Decreased exposure to
supraphysiologic glucocorticoid is clinically meaningful because
excess glucocorticoid has adverse effects on body weight,
metabolic parameters, and bone health. Changes in body
weight and metabolic parameters were not improved compared
to placebo after 24 weeks of crinecerfont treatment in adults.

Risk and risk
management

•

•

The crinecerfont safety database was adequate in size and

were generally considered tolerability issues (e.g.,

in the postmarketing setting and require that the Applicant
implement enhanced pharmacovigilance for adverse events of
suicidality and neutropenia.

illness or other physiologic stressors.

8.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a rare disease most commonly caused by deficiency of
the adrenal enzyme 21-hydroxylase. The lack of 21-hydroxylase activity results in deficiencies
of cortisol and, in some cases, aldosterone. Because the adrenal gland tries to compensate for the
lack of cortisol production, excessive adrenal androgens are produced. Glucocorticoid
replacement is necessary for the underlying adrenal insufficiency associated with CAH.
Additionally, mineralocorticoid replacement may be needed. Treatment of the excessive adrenal
androgen production associated with CAH can be challenging and generally requires
glucocorticoid dosing that exceeds the needed physiologic replacement. Therefore, control of
adrenal androgens with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosing can be associated with adverse
effects on body weight, growth, metabolic parameters, and bone health.
Crinecerfont is a selective antagonist of the corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor
intended to decrease ACTH stimulation of the adrenal gland’s hormone production. This is a
novel approach to allow for control of adrenal androgen production as an adjunct to the required
physiologic glucocorticoid therapy for treatment of the underlying adrenal insufficiency.
The Applicant conducted two adequate and well-controlled clinical trials in the CAH population:
one in adults and one in pediatric subjects aged 4 years and older. These trials demonstrated that
crinecerfont allowed for adrenal androgen control with decreasing doses of glucocorticoids. In
fact, many subjects achieved physiologic glucocorticoid dosing with continued androgen control.
The significant decrease in glucocorticoid dose is clinically meaningful because lowering
glucocorticoid dose can have a direct impact on the subsequent adverse events associated with
glucocorticoid excess.
The safety profile of crinecerfont was adequately characterized in the context of this rare disease.
Based on crinecerfont’s mechanism of action, adrenal insufficiency was a clinical concern and
was monitored throughout the development program. Cases of adrenal insufficiency, some with
fatality, did occur in the setting of stress situations for subjects. The adrenal insufficiency and
crisis were not caused by crinecerfont itself but the underlying disease state. Therefore, patients
will need to continue physiologic glucocorticoid replacement and to be advised of the need for
increased glucocorticoid doses as the time of stress from concurrent illness or other reasons. This
will be addressed in product labeling as a Warning and Precaution.
Crinecerfont was previously evaluated as a treatment for depression, and the activity of
crinecerfont on the CRF receptors in the pituitary indicate that the drug crosses the blood-brain
barrier. Therefore, the clinical development program assessed the risk of suicide with the use of
the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). One subject in the adult trial attempted
suicide during the conduct of the trial. The assessment of the C-SSRS in the adult trial revealed
3/120 subjects in the crinecerfont group and 1/58 subjects in the placebo group reported suicidal
ideation, evident by an increase in their C-SSRS score. In the pediatric trial, 4/67 subjects in the
crinecerfont group and 0/31 subjects in the placebo group increased their C-SSRS score. The
relationship of these findings to study drug is unclear, given the very low event rates, remote
history of suicidality in some of the subjects who had an increase on their Columbia-Suicide
Severity Rating Scale, lack of neuropsychiatric findings in animals, and no increase in suicidality
when crinecerfont was studied in a major depressive disorder trial.
12
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
Neutropenia was observed in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont for major depressive disorder. In the
adult and pediatric CAH studies, decreased neutrophil counts also occurred more frequently in
study subjects treated with crinecerfont compared to placebo. The etiology for this is unclear and
the findings were not associated with increased risk of infection.
Hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema, were reported with crinecerfont treatment.
Other noted adverse reactions (e.g., headache, fatigue) may be tolerability issues.
In summary, crinecerfont use as an adjunct to glucocorticoid therapy has been shown to reduce
androgen levels in adults and pediatric subjects with CAH and lower glucocorticoid dose
requirements, with many subjects able to achieve physiologic or near-physiologic glucocorticoid
replacement doses. The decreased exposure to supraphysiologic glucocorticoid is clinically
beneficial because of the well-known adverse effects of excess glucocorticoid. The safety profile
is adequately characterized, and risks (e.g., adverse reactions such as headache and fatigue;
contraindication if prior hypersensitivity reaction to crinecerfont; need for adequate
glucocorticoid replacement to avoid adrenal insufficiency/crisis) can be adequately addressed
through product labeling. Other findings of unclear clinical significance (e.g., minor neutrophil
count reductions) and unclear relation to study drug (e.g., suicidality) will be included in labeling
for prescriber awareness. These risks and uncertainties are outweighed by the benefits when
crinecerfont is used according to the approved labeling.

II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
9. Introduction
Crinecerfont, a new molecular entity, is a first-in-class selective antagonist of the pituitary
corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor. The Applicant submitted two crinecerfont
(b) (4)
NDAs (for two formulations) for the proposed indication
caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency:
•

NDA 218808 for soft gelatin capsules (25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg)

•

NDA 218820 for oral solution (50 mg/mL)

The proposed dosing regimen is:
•

100 mg twice daily for adults (aged 18 years and older)

•

100 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing greater than or equal to 55 kg

•

50 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 20 kg to less than 55 kg

•

25 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 10 kg to less than 20 kg

In patients with classic CAH, deficiency of 21-hydroxylase enzymatic activity causes deficiency
of adrenal glucocorticoid (cortisol) and mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) production. The
glucocorticoid deficiency stimulates excess adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) production
from the pituitary gland, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce excess androgens.
Levels of androstenedione (A4) and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) are measured clinically
as biomarkers of adrenal androgen production and disease control in patients with CAH.
Standard of care treatment of classic CAH consists of glucocorticoid (e.g., hydrocortisone) and
mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) replacement. Exogenous glucocorticoids remedy adrenal
insufficiency as well as suppress excess adrenal androgen production, while mineralocorticoids
are used to correct salt-wasting in the setting of insufficient aldosterone production. While
physiologic glucocorticoid doses are required to remedy adrenal insufficiency, supraphysiologic
glucocorticoid dosages are often necessary to suppress the high ACTH levels and control adrenal
androgen production.
The use of supraphysiologic glucocorticoid doses creates a clinical management challenge of
balancing disease control (by lowering adrenal androgen levels) with avoiding iatrogenic
Cushing’s syndrome due to excess glucocorticoid exposure. Elevated androgen levels cause
hirsutism, acne, subfertility (in females), and short adult stature (because of accelerated growth
in childhood and premature epiphyseal fusion). Elevated ACTH levels promote growth of
testicular adrenal rest tumors, which may cause subfertility in males. Long-term exposure to
excess glucocorticoid causes weight gain and adverse effects on metabolism, the cardiovascular
system, bone health, and growth (in children) (Merke and Auchus 2020).
The Applicant hypothesizes that by reducing pituitary ACTH production via CRF1 receptor
antagonism, crinecerfont lowers adrenal androgen levels so that the disease can be managed with

glucocorticoid requirements, crinecerfont treatment as an adjunct to glucocorticoid replacement
ultimately minimizes the adverse health consequences of long-term exposure to supraphysiologic
glucocorticoid.

provide a substantial improvement over available therapy based on statistically significant

9.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
Trial CAH3003 in adults with classic CAH and Trial CAH2006 in pediatric subjects aged 4 to
17 years with classic CAH are the pivotal phase 3 trials reviewed as primary evidence of
crinecerfont’s efficacy and safety (Table 4). Crinecerfont was evaluated in a double-blind,
placebo-controlled fashion for 24 weeks (Trial CAH3003) or 28 weeks (Trial CAH2006),
followed by an open-label treatment period through 12 months (both trials). These trials are fit
for purpose to support this application.
Efficacy results submitted for Trial CAH3003 include analysis of the completed double-blind
period (Day 1 to Week 24) and an interim analysis for the ongoing open-label period (Week 24
to Month 12) at the data cutoff (July 19, 2023). Efficacy results submitted for Trial CAH2006
include analysis of the completed double-blind period (Day 1 to Week 28) and an interim
analysis of the available data for the ongoing open-label period (Week 28 to Week 52) at the data
cutoff (August 9, 2023). Data from the 120-Day Safety Update were incorporated into the
review.
We also independently reviewed the literature and the literature review submitted by the
Applicant justifying the clinical meaningfulness of the studies’ efficacy findings.

11. Pharmacologic Activity,
Pharmacokinetics, and Clinical
Pharmacology
11.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential
Effectiveness
Cortisol (glucocorticoid) deficiency in patients with CAH causes an increase in corticotropinreleasing factor (CRF hormone from the hypothalamus, which stimulates excessive
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary. Excessive ACTH
secretion stimulates the adrenal cortex, which leads to adrenal hyperplasia.
Crinecerfont is a selective first-in-class CRF1 receptor antagonist that reduces the excess ACTH
secretion caused by elevated CRF in response to low glucocorticoid levels in patients with CAH.
The Applicant provided a series of in vitro and in vivo nonclinical pharmacology studies to
demonstrate that crinecerfont binds CRF1 receptors and inhibits CRF-induced cyclic adenosine
monophosphate (cAMP) synthesis and ACTH release. The nonclinical pharmacology data were
provided to support the proposed mechanism of action of crinecerfont.
Crinecerfont inhibited the ability of CRF to bind human and rodent CRF1 receptors with halfmaximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 0.6 to 3.99nM and showed no affinity for
related receptors human CRF2a or human CRF-binding protein (limited to 11.5% inhibition at
10µM crinecerfont). The most abundant crinecerfont metabolite (NBI-756179, M6), which
represented 6% of human crinecerfont exposure, bound to CRF1 receptors with nanomolar
affinity (Ki =1.14nM), but no inhibitor constant (Ki) was provided for crinecerfont. The
contribution of this metabolite to CRF1 receptor antagonist activity was considered minor due to
its low abundance. In the in vitro functional assays, crinecerfont inhibited CRF-induced cAMP
production in Y79 cells with an IC50 value of 3.1nM (1.5 ng/mL), and blocked ACTH secretion
in AtT-20 mouse pituitary tumor cells, demonstrating that crinecerfont acts as a functional
antagonist of CRF1 receptors (Figure 1).

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)

CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
Figure 1. Crinecerfont Antagonizes CRF-Induced Pituitary ACTH Secretion (AtT-20 Cells)

Source: Applicant’s NDA submission
Abbreviations: ACTH, adrenocorticotropin hormone; CRF, corticotropin-releasing factor

The in vivo primary pharmacodynamic studies reiterated the findings of the in vitro binding and
functional studies. The binding of crinecerfont to pituitary and brain CRF1 receptors was
evaluated in crude tissue homogenates from rats administered crinecerfont hydrochloride (HCl)
orally (PO) or intraperitoneally. The results demonstrated that crinecerfont binds to CRF1
receptors in pituitary and brain, with higher occupancy of CRF1 receptors in pituitary (67 to
81%) than in brain (13 to 29%) at early timepoints (0.5 to 1 hour postdose). The CRF1 receptor
binding of crinecerfont was comparable between pituitary and brain at 2 to 24 hours postdose. In
vivo, CRF administration caused an increase in plasma ACTH levels. In studies in rats,
administration of crinecerfont PO (Figure 2), intravenously (IV), or intraperitoneally showed a
dose-dependent inhibition of CRF-stimulated ACTH secretion with 50% inhibitory dose of 1.3 to
4.9 mg/kg crinecerfont HCl, further demonstrating the antagonist action of crinecerfont on CRF1
receptors. The CRF1 receptor antagonist effects of crinecerfont were further investigated in a
stressed rat model. Stress was induced by restraining rats for 15 minutes, which caused up to a 6fold increase in ACTH plasma levels. When crinecerfont HCl was administered PO to male rats
1 hour before inducing stress, crinecerfont significantly antagonized the stress-induced ACTH
increase at 10 mg/kg but not at 3 mg/kg crinecerfont HCl. Crinecerfont did not significantly
affect basal plasma ACTH level when administered PO daily up to 1000 mg/kg in nonstressed
rats, indicating that physiological ACTH levels were not affected by crinecerfont, which likely
reflects maintenance of endogenous positive and negative feedback signals within the
hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis.

Drug Information
• Adults: Based on the phase 2 dose-finding study NBI-74788-2001 in adults with CAH, crinecerfont decreased serum A4
levels in a dose-dependent manner, from 50 mg once daily to 100 mg bid, with maximal A4 reduction observed at 100 mg

the 100 mg bid dose and showed similar reduction in A4 levels as seen with the phase 2 dose finding study.

selected to match the exposure seen in adults at 100 mg bid and had similar reduction in serum A4 levels as those in adults
with CAH. In the phase 3 clinical trial, CAH2006, 100 mg bid and 50 mg bid were studied in pediatric subjects with CAH >4

Drug Information
Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Population pharmacokinetic analyses indicated that body weight is a significant covariate affecting the pharmacokinetics of
crinecerfont. Therefore, body weight-banded dosing was used in the pediatric study to ensure comparable exposures to those
of adult subjects across pediatric weight groups (i.e., 100 mg bid for subjects weighing ≥55 kg and 50 mg bid for subjects
weighing 20 to <55 kg). For pediatric subjects between 10 to <20 kg, crinecerfont dose of 25 mg bid is recommended based
on exposure-matching to pediatric subjects between 20 to <55 kg.
No clinically significant differences in the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont were observed based on age ranging from 5 to
54 years.
Mass balance study indicates that renal excretion is unlikely to be a major elimination pathway of crinecerfont. Population PK
analysis indicates that the median decreases in AUC24 with mild and moderate renal impairment relative to normal renal
function was 2.7% and 8.4%, respectively. Therefore, dosage adjustment is not needed in patients with mild or moderate
renal impairment. Considering the potential impact of severe renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont, and
the lack of clinical experience in these patients, crinecerfont is not recommended in patients with severe renal impairment or
end-stage renal disease.
Crinecerfont exposure for subjects with mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment decreased by 9%, 15%, and 17%,
respectively, for Cmax and 27%, 34%, and 20%, respectively, for AUC0­∞, relative to subjects with normal hepatic function. The
90% CI values for GMR for Cmax and AUC for all the hepatic impairment groups included unity as compared to the normal
hepatic function group. Therefore, hepatic impairment has no clinically significant effect on crinecerfont pharmacokinetics, and
dose adjustment is not needed in patients with hepatic impairment.
Drug Interaction Liability (Drug as a Precipitant)
• Effect of crinecerfont on the pharmacokinetics of CYP3A substrates:
Concomitant administration of repeated 100-mg daily doses of crinecerfont increased midazolam (sensitive CYP3A
substrate) AUC by 23% (90% CI: 9% to 38%) and did not affect the pharmacokinetics of oral contraceptive (nonsensitive
CYP3A substrate, 90% CI of GMR for AUC and Cmax within 0.80 to 1.25). Therefore, crinecerfont is considered a weak
CYP3A inhibitor and is unlikely to significantly increase the systemic exposures of glucocorticoids, which are generally not
sensitive CYP3A substrates.
• Crinecerfont is unlikely to induce CYP3A, CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2B6 or inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9,
CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1 at clinically relevant doses.
Crinecerfont is not an inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, organic anion transporter (OAT) 1, OAT3,
organic cation transporter (OCT) 2, multidrug and toxin extrusion transporter (MATE)1, or MATE2-K.

12. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
12.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential
Effectiveness
The Applicant has proposed the following crinecerfont dose regimens:
•

Adults and pediatric patients weighing >55 kg: 100 mg twice daily PO with food

•

Pediatric patients aged 4 years and older weighing 20 kg to <55 kg: 50 mg twice daily PO
with food

•

Pediatric patients aged 4 years and older weighing 10 kg to <20 kg: 25 mg twice daily PO
with food

The proposed dosing regimens for adult patients and pediatric patients weighing ≥20 kg are the
same as those in Trial CAH3003 (adult trial) and Trial CAH2006 (pediatric trial; see details in
Section 12.2). Therefore, the appropriateness of the proposed doses is supported by the safety
and efficacy data from these pivotal phase 3 trials. The proposed dosing regimen for pediatric
patients weighing 10 to <20 kg is supported by exposure matching to pediatric subjects weighing
20 to <55 kg and is considered acceptable (see Section 12.1.3).

12.1.1. Dose Selection Rationale for Pivotal Trials
12.1.1.1. Adult Phase 3 Trial Dose Selection
The dose selection for the phase 3 adult study, Trial CAH3003, was based on the phase 2 study,
Trial CAH2001, an open-label, multiple-dose, sequential dose-escalation study to assess the
pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, safety, and tolerability of crinecerfont in adult male and
female subjects 18 years to 50 years of age with a documented medical diagnosis of classic
21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH. The study assessed four crinecerfont dosing regimens
administered for 14 days in a sequential manner. Dose cohorts with sample sizes are listed
below:
•

Cohort 1 (N=8): 50 mg once daily at bedtime with Ensure Plus® (350 calories, 11 grams total
fat, 20 grams sugars, 13 grams protein, and 50 grams carbohydrate)

•

Cohort 2 (N=7): 100 mg once daily at bedtime with Ensure Plus

•

Cohort 3 (N=8): 100 mg once daily with the evening meal

•

Cohort 4 (N=8): 100 mg twice daily at breakfast and dinner

29
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
The doses selected for this phase 2 dose-finding study were based on the following data:
•

Crinecerfont 50 mg was well tolerated in single- and repeat-dose safety and pharmacokinetic
(PK) studies in healthy volunteers.

•

Doses up to 200 mg were well tolerated in single-dose and repeat-dose studies in healthy
subjects.

•

Crinecerfont 100 mg daily was well tolerated in an 8-week double-blind study in adult male
and female subjects with major depressive disorder.

•

The anticipated steady-state exposures with the selected crinecerfont doses, using the
predicted maximum observed plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentrationtime curve (AUC), were within the acceptable safety margins defined by the nonclinical
toxicology studies.

Per the Applicant, reductions in ACTH, 17-OHP, and A4 relative to baseline levels were
observed in most of the subjects across all dose regimens after receiving 14 days of treatment
with crinecerfont. A dose response was observed for androstenedione reduction, with the greatest
median reduction observed in the 100 mg twice daily dose group (64%) compared to the other
dose groups (21%, 42%, and 51% change from baseline, with 50 mg at bedtime, 100 mg at
bedtime, and 100 mg with evening meal, respectively; Table 9).
In addition, the responder rate (i.e., >50% reduction of A4) was greatest in the crinecerfont
100 mg twice daily (bid) group (75%) compared to responder rates between 50% and 63% for
the other dose groups. It should be noted that crinecerfont needs to be administered with food
due to low bioavailability under fasting conditions. Various meal types (i.e., Ensure Plus versus
breakfast and dinner) were used across the cohorts. Similar crinecerfont drug exposures were
observed between cohort 2 (100 mg with Ensure Plus) and cohort 3 (100 mg with evening meal).
Therefore, the use of different meal types across treatment arms is unlikely to confound the dosefinding results.
Crinecerfont was generally well tolerated in all four dosing cohorts, and there was no dose
relationship in the incidence, type, or severity of adverse events. Therefore, 100 mg twice-daily
dosing was selected for the phase 3 adult study, CAH3003. It should be noted that interpretation
of the dose response for A4 reduction may be confounded by different baselines of A4 among
the four dosing cohorts, between-subject variabilities of this pharmacodynamic marker, and
relatively small sample sizes across dose groups (refer to Section 20.2.10 for details).
12.1.1.2. Pediatric (Weight >20 kg) Phase 3 Dose Selection
The dose selection for the phase 3 pediatric trial, CAH2006, was based on the following:
•

Clinical benefits observed in the phase 2 study, NBI-74788-CAH2008, an open-label
multiple-dose study to assess the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and
pharmacodynamics of crinecerfont in eight pediatric subjects (14 to 16 years old with mean
body weight of 70 kg) with a documented medical diagnosis of classic CAH.

•

An exposure-matching approach to the adult 100 mg twice-daily dose using population
pharmacokinetic (popPK) analysis for pediatric subjects with CAH.

In the phase 2 study, NBI-74788-CAH2008, pediatric subjects with mean body weight of 70 kg
received crinecerfont 50-mg capsules twice daily at breakfast and dinner for 14 consecutive days.
Study results indicated that on Day 14, compared to baseline, median A4 levels decreased by
58%, and ACTH and 17-OHP as key secondary endpoints decreased by 57% and 69%,
respectively (Table 9). It is interesting that the degree of A4 reduction appears to be comparable
to that in adult subjects, despite the fact that these adolescents received only half the dose the
adults received (50 mg bid versus 100 mg bid). Nonetheless, in the phase 3 pediatric study, the
Applicant selected the same dose as adults for pediatric subjects with body weight ≥55 kg based
on the exposure-matching approach rather than relying on the pharmacodynamic (PD) findings.
As body weight is a significant PK covariate, body weight-banded dosing was used in pediatric
subjects with varying body weights. Specifically, the population PK model informed the doses
selected for the pediatric phase 3 study, Trial CAH2006, (i.e., 100 mg bid for pediatric subjects
weighing ≥55 kg and 50 mg bid for those weighing 20 to <55 kg), as these doses in children
provide comparable crinecerfont exposures to those of adult subjects across pediatric weight
groups. Refer to Sections 20.2.11 and 20.5 for the in vivo study details and pharmacometrics
assessment, respectively.

12.1.1.3. Dose for Pediatric Patients Weighing 10 to <20 kg
The phase 3 pediatric clinical trial (CAH2006) did not enroll any subjects in the 10 to <20 kg
weight band; instead, the Applicant relied upon popPK modeling and exposure matching to
support the proposed dosing of 25 mg twice daily in the pediatric subgroup of 10 to <20 kg
weight band and down to 4 years of age. The dose for the 10 to <20 kg pediatric subgroup was
informed by the dose for pediatric subjects weighing 20 kg to <55 kg. The 20 kg to <55 kg
subgroup was chosen as the reference population because of similarities between the two groups
with respect to disease state, pathophysiology, disease progression, and expected efficacy
response. Furthermore, efficacy was demonstrated at the dose administered to the 20 kg to
<55 kg pediatric subgroup, which provided additional support to rely on that subgroup for dose
determination for the <20 kg weight group (refer to Section 12.3.1).
Utilizing modeling and simulation in virtual pediatric subjects of 10 to <20 kg and at least
4 years of age, 25 mg twice daily is projected to produce similar exposures (i.e., 24-hour area
under the concentration-time curve and 24-hour maximum concentration) to those of the 50 mg
twice daily regimen in pediatric subjects of 20 to <55 kg. Additionally, a high proportion of
virtual pediatric subjects weighing 10 to <20 kg is expected to have crinecerfont exposures
within the model-predicted adult exposure (Figure 3). Collectively, the proposed dosage of
25 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 10 kg to <20 kg is expected to have similar
safety and efficacy based on comparable exposures observed in pediatric subjects weighing
20 kg to <55 kg and in adults (refer to Section 20.5.5).

12.1.2. Exposure Response
Utilizing the final popPK model and phase 3 clinical data, the Applicant performed exposureresponse (E-R) analyses in adults and in pediatric subjects with CAH independently in each
population. The efficacy endpoints in the phase 3 clinical trials included the change from
baseline in serum A4 prior to morning glucocorticoid dose at Week 4, the percent change from
baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24 for adults and at Week 28 for pediatric subjects,
and the achievement of a reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose to physiologic levels at Week 24
for adults and Week 28 for pediatric subjects while maintaining androgen control. For safety
E-R, the most frequent adverse events for adult (i.e., fatigue) and pediatric subjects (i.e.,
headache) were selected as exploratory safety endpoints for independent analyses in each
population.
The E-R efficacy analyses demonstrated that across the studied exposure ranges, for the
proposed adult and pediatric dosing regimens (i.e., 100 mg twice daily dose in adults and
pediatric subjects weighing ≥55 kg; 50 mg twice daily in pediatric subjects weighing 20 to
<55 kg), the E-R efficacy relationships were relatively flat for change from baseline in serum A4
(prior to morning glucocorticoid dose) at Week 4 and percent change from baseline in
glucocorticoid daily dose (Figure 4).
The E-R analyses demonstrated an increase in probability of achieving a reduction in
glucocorticoid daily dose to physiologic levels (while maintaining serum A4 control) across
studied exposure ranges in the adult and the pediatric E-R models. However, the 95% confidence
interval of the slope (i.e., log-odds ratio) for drug exposure contains zero in the pediatric model
and is numerically close to zero in the adult model, suggesting that other factors in addition to
crinecerfont exposure may be driving the probability of glucocorticoid response.
The following limitations should also be considered when interpreting the E-R findings:
•

The exposure ranges in the E-R analysis were relatively narrow. Specifically, the E-R
analysis was based on data from the phase 3 trials in adult and pediatric subjects (i.e., Trials
CAH3003 and CAH2006). It should be noted that only one dose level was studied in the
adult phase 3 trial, data of which was used for the E-R analysis, and pediatric doses were
selected to match the adult population.

•

An E-R analysis was performed for the most common treatment-emergent adverse event in
the adult and pediatric phase 3 trials. There was no apparent relationship between
crinecerfont exposure and proportion of adults with fatigue at Week 24 across the studied
exposure range. In pediatric subjects, the probability of headache increased across studied
exposures at Week 28; however, this finding may have limited interpretation given the small
number of pediatric subjects who experienced this adverse event in the crinecerfont arm
versus placebo (17 and 2 subjects, respectively).

Overall, the results from the exposure-efficacy and exploratory exposure-safety analyses support
the proposed doses for adult and pediatric subjects with CAH (refer to Section 20.5 for details on
the E-R analyses.

12.1.4. Switching Between Oral Solution and Capsule
Formulation
Crinecerfont is available as an oral solution and as capsules. Study NBI-74788-1716 compared
the crinecerfont exposure between the oral solution and the phase 2 capsule formulation. The
results show the two formulations were not bioequivalent and crinecerfont exposure (Cmax and
AUC) from the oral solution was ~15% less than the phase 2 capsule formulation6 (refer to
Section 20.2.4). In addition, the popPK analysis indicates that the mean exposure for the oral
solution is expected to be 26% lower than that for the capsule formulation (Figure 5).
Nonetheless, the Applicant is proposing that the oral solution and the commercial capsule
formulation can be switched based on patient preference.
The review team agrees with the Applicant’s proposal based on the following considerations:
•

This is consistent with the phase 3 pediatric clinical trial (NBI-74788-CAH2006), where
subjects were allowed to switch from the oral solution to the capsule formulation in the openlabel phase. In clinical practice, we expect the most common scenario to be a switch from
oral solution to capsule when pediatric patients become old enough to swallow the capsule.
Given that the capsule formulation has slightly higher bioavailability than the oral solution,
we do not expect a loss of efficacy when switching to the capsule formulation. In addition,
the safety with the capsule formulation has been established in the phase 3 clinical trials.

•

Simulation results show that, despite numerically lower exposure (i.e., steady-state AUC)
with the oral solution, a large percentage of the simulated exposures in subjects receiving the
oral solution fall within those of the capsule formulation.

•

The Applicant is proposing the 25 mg bid solution for pediatric patients weighing 10 to
<20 kg, and the 50 mg bid solution for pediatric patients weighing 20 to <55 kg. In the
randomized, placebo-controlled portion of the pediatric phase 3 trial, about 50% of the
subjects were in the 20 to <55 kg weight band (37 crinecerfont, 14 placebo) and received the
50 mg bid (or placebo) solution. The remaining ~50% of subjects were in the ≥55 kg weight
band (32 crinecerfont, 20 placebo) and received the capsule. These subgroups achieved
similar reductions in glucocorticoid doses. Although the trial did not enroll pediatric subjects
weighing <20 kg, the pharmacokinetic exposure with the 25 mg bid solution in the 10 to
<20 kg weight band is expected to match that of the 50 mg bid solution in the 20 to <55 kg
weight band (see Section 12.3).

•

Exposure-efficacy models based on phase 3 clinical data with both oral solution and capsule
formulations demonstrate that the E-R relationships are relatively flat across studied
exposure for adult and pediatric subjects, respectively.

Based on these considerations, we conclude that the difference in crinecerfont exposure between
the oral solution and capsule is not considered clinically meaningful.

6 The phase 2 capsule formulation is expected to have a similar crinecerfont exposure to the commercial

formulation, as it is nearly identical in composition to the phase 3 capsule formulation, which is bioequivalent to the
commercial capsule formulation. The GMRs and 90% CIs for AUC0-∞, and Cmax of the commercial capsule
compared to the phase 3 capsule at the 100 mg dose were 1.01 (0.94, 1.09), 0.99 (0.91, 1.08), and 1.07 (0.98, 1.16),
respectively.

12.2.2. Trial CAH3003
12.2.2.1. Design, Trial CAH3003
Overall Design
Trial CAH3003 is titled “A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the
safety and efficacy of crinecerfont in adult subjects with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia,
followed by open-label treatment.” The study design is appropriate to demonstrate efficacy and
is depicted in Figure 6.
This phase 3 trial consisted of a 4-week screening period; a 24-week double-blind, placebocontrolled treatment period; a 6-month open-label treatment period; a 6-month open-label or
36
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
double-blind, active-controlled treatment period; and an open-label extension. The primary
objective was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily
compared with placebo in reducing daily glucocorticoid dosage while maintaining adrenal
androgen control.
24-Week Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Treatment Period (Day 1 to
Week 24)
A total of 182 adult subjects with classic CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency who
required supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids to control androgen excess (i.e.,
glucocorticoid dose >13 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents) were randomized in a 2:1 ratio
(active: placebo) to receive crinecerfont 100 mg taken orally twice daily with breakfast and the
evening meal or placebo. The 24-week treatment period consisted of a 4-week glucocorticoid
stable dose phase, an 8-week glucocorticoid reduction period, and a 12-week glucocorticoid
optimization period.
Week 1 to Week 4
During the first 4 weeks of the study, subjects were maintained on their baseline glucocorticoid
regimen.
Week 4 to Week 12
Subjects underwent downward dose-titration of their glucocorticoid dosage to a target of
8 to 10 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents by Week 12.
Week 12 to Week 24
Glucocorticoid dosage was adjusted if needed based on androstenedione (A4) levels, presence of
symptoms of glucocorticoid insufficiency, or hyperandrogenism. The treatment goal was to
maintain A4 levels at ≤120% of the subject’s baseline or upper limit of normal (ULN) for age
and sex.
Open-Label Treatment Period (Week 24 to Month 12)
At Week 24 (Month 6), subjects transitioned to a 6-month open-label period during which all
subjects received crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily until Month 12. During Months 7 through 10,
glucocorticoid dosage was reduced as tolerated if androstenedione levels were controlled (i.e.,
≤120% of the subject’s baseline or ≤ULN for age and sex) to a goal of 8 to 10 mg/m2/day
hydrocortisone equivalents by Month 10.
In all parts of the study that allowed for glucocorticoid dose reduction, dose was reduced at a rate
of approximately 10% to 20% per month.
Open-Label or Double-Blind Active-Controlled Treatment Period (Month 12 to Month 18)
At Month 12, subjects whose glucocorticoid dosage remained greater than 11 mg/m2/day
hydrocortisone equivalents were rerandomized (2:1 ratio) to receive crinecerfont 100 mg every
morning and 200 mg every evening, or to continue 100 mg twice daily, in a blinded fashion.
Glucocorticoid reduction could be reattempted after the first month of blinded treatment, as

37
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
tolerated, with the goal of achieving a glucocorticoid dose of 8 to 10 mg/m2/day by Month 18
while maintaining control of A4.
Subjects who had been successfully able to reduce their glucocorticoid dosage to ≤11 mg/m2/day
hydrocortisone equivalents continued to receive crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily in an open-label
fashion.
Open-Label Extension Period (Month 18 Onward)
After Month 18, subjects could enter an open-label extension period during which they initially
received crinecerfont 100 mg bid with adjustment as needed to a maximum crinecerfont dose of
100 mg every morning (qAM) and 200 mg every evening (qPM). Glucocorticoid dose was
adjusted as needed to achieve the lowest dose required to maintain adequate disease control.
After the Month 24 visit, subjects could consider transitioning to crinecerfont 200 mg qPM.
A final posttreatment visit occurred approximately 1 month after the subject’s final dose of study
drug.

Efficacy Endpoints
The primary efficacy endpoint was the percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid (GC)
daily dose (in hydrocortisone equivalents adjusted for body surface area [BSA] in mg/m2/day) at
38
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
Week 24 while also achieving Week 24 androstenedione levels in the controlled range (i.e.,
≤120% of baseline or ≤ULN for age and sex).
Glucocorticoid daily dose was calculated at baseline and at Week 24. If glucocorticoid dosing
alternated over the course of 2 consecutive days, then the average of the glucocorticoid dose on
those days was used to calculate the glucocorticoid daily dose. If glucocorticoid dosing
alternated between weekdays and weekends (or another weekly regimen that varied by day of the
week), then the average daily dose was calculated as the sum of the glucocorticoid doses over the
7-day period divided by 7.
According to the statistical analysis plan, the androstenedione level prior to morning
glucocorticoid dose served as the baseline and Week 24 level. If androstenedione levels prior to
morning glucocorticoid were not available, then androstenedione levels after morning
glucocorticoid dose were used.
Subjects who had a decrease in glucocorticoid daily dose but did not meet the definition of
androstenedione control at Week 24 were considered to have a zero percent change from
baseline in the glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24.
Key secondary efficacy endpoints were the following:
•

Change from baseline in serum androstenedione at Week 4 (while glucocorticoid dose was
stable)

•

Achievement of a reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose to ≤11 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone
equivalents at Week 24 (while Week 24 androstenedione was adequately controlled)

•

Change from baseline in homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR; in
fasting subjects not on insulin, at Week 24

•

Percent change from baseline in weight at Week 24

•

Change from baseline in percent total fat mass at Week 24

The study design was adequate to meet its stated objectives. The data from Trial CAH3003 that
were submitted with the NDA are results from the 24-week (i.e., Weeks 0 to 24) randomized,
double-blind, placebo-controlled treatment period and the open-label treatment period, which
capture treatment Week 24 through Month 12 (data cutoff of July 19, 2023). The 120-day Safety
Update included new data obtained in the open-label extension treatment period from Month 12
through the data cutoff of January 16, 2024. The trial is ongoing.
The efficacy analysis is based primarily on data obtained during the initial 24-week placebocontrolled treatment phase.
12.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial CAH3003
The eligibility criteria are reflective of the patient population who would benefit from a reduction
in glucocorticoid dose. Study subjects were required to be taking supraphysiologic
glucocorticoid doses (total daily dosage >13 mg/m2/day in hydrocortisone dose equivalents).
The study enrolled adult male and nonpregnant, nonlactating female subjects aged 18 years and
older with a diagnosis of classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH (accepted diagnostic criteria
were an elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level, confirmed cytochrome P450 (CYP) 21A2
39
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
genotype, positive newborn screening with confirmatory second-tier testing, or cosyntropin
stimulation testing). Individuals with other forms of classic CAH were excluded.
Subjects were also required to be on a stable supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dose regimen
(defined as >13 mg/m2/day in hydrocortisone dose equivalents; prior to protocol Amendment 5,
the threshold was >14 mg/m2/day) and consisting of one or more of the following orally
administered glucocorticoids: hydrocortisone, prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, or
dexamethasone.
If treated with fludrocortisone for salt wasting, the dosage was stable for at least 1 month prior to
screening, with an upright plasma renin activity (PRA) during screening that was not greater than
ULN while maintaining a usual sodium intake. If PRA was >ULN, the subject must have systolic
blood pressure >100 mm Hg, without orthostatic hypotension, and with serum sodium and
potassium in the normal range.
Additional exclusions were conditions requiring chronic glucocorticoid therapy at systemic
exposures that may interfere with study endpoints; increased risk of adrenal crisis; history of
malignancy; laboratory findings consistent with impaired hepatic or renal function; anemia,
thrombocytopenia, neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count [ANC] <1.0×103/mm3), or impaired
coagulation; and active suicidal ideation in the 6 months prior to screening or any history of
suicidal behavior within the past year based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale
collected at screening.
Contraception was required in female subjects of childbearing potential with fertile male partners
from screening until the final study visit or 30 days after the last dose of study drug, whichever
was longer.
Medications prohibited during the trial were:
•

Orally administered glucocorticoids for indications other than CAH

•

Strong inducers of CYP3A4 or CYP2B6 except topically administered medications

•

Medications that affect cortisol or glucocorticoid metabolism (e.g., phenytoin, mitotane,
phenobarbital, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors) except topically administered medications

•

Aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole, testolactone)
12.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial CAH3003

The full analysis set (FAS), defined as all randomized subjects regardless of adherence to study
treatment administration, was used for all efficacy analyses. Continuous efficacy endpoints were
analyzed using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model assuming equal variance between
the placebo and the treatment group. The ANCOVA model included respective baseline
measurement as a covariate and stratification factors and treatment group (crinecerfont 100 mg
bid or placebo) as factors. Categorical efficacy endpoints were analyzed using the CochranMantel-Haenszel (CMH) test. The CMH test compared treatment groups (crinecerfont 100 mg
bid versus placebo) and included the stratification factors used in the randomization.

40
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
The protocol prespecified testing procedure described below was used to control the familywise
Type I error rate for the primary and key secondary endpoints (Figure 7). All significance levels
noted below were two-sided.
•

The primary endpoint was tested using a significance level of 0.05.

•

If the primary endpoint was statistically significant, then the first two key secondary
endpoints were tested using an unequal allocation of significance levels. The change from
baseline at Week 4 in androstenedione was tested using a significance level of 0.02. The
achievement of a reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose to physiologic levels
(≤11 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalent adjusted for BSA) with androstenedione control
(as defined for the primary endpoint) was tested using a significance level of 0.03.

•

The significance level for the family of the remaining three key secondary endpoints was
dependent on whether the first two key secondary endpoints were statistically significant. If
both were statistically significant, then the significance level for this family of endpoints was
0.05. If only one was statistically significant, then the significance level for that endpoint was
used for this family of endpoints. If neither was significant, then this family of endpoints will
not be tested for statistical significance.

Missing Data Handling
The primary efficacy endpoint requires the availability of both the glucocorticoid dose at
Week 24 as well as androstenedione values used in the assessment of androstenedione control.
The missing data corresponding to the subjects with a missing glucocorticoid dose,
androstenedione, or both at Week 24 were multiply imputed as follows:
•

For subjects who were on study drug at Week 24 and had missing one or both components of
the primary endpoint, their missing Week 24 data were imputed from Week 24 Completers
(subjects who completed through the time of the endpoint on study drug) within the same
treatment group.

•

For subjects who were off study drug at Week 24 and had missing one or both components of
the primary endpoint, their missing Week 24 data were imputed from subjects who were
classified as “retrieved dropouts” (subjects in the FAS who discontinued study drug but
remained in the study and had an evaluable measurement). If there were five or fewer
retrieved dropouts, the missing endpoint values would be imputed from subjects in the
placebo treatment group. For subjects in the placebo treatment group, missing data were
imputed using nonmissing data from subjects in the placebo treatment group.

12.2.2.4. Results of Analyses, Trial CAH3003
12.2.2.4.1. Disposition, Baseline Demographics, and
Baseline Clinical Characteristics
Disposition During Double-Blind Treatment Period (Baseline to Week 24)
A total of 182 subjects were randomized (122 crinecerfont; 60 placebo). All subjects were
included in the FAS. One subject (1.7%) in the placebo group was not dosed and was excluded
from the double-blind period safety analysis set. The double-blind period safety analysis set
includes all randomized subjects who took at least one dose of study treatment in the doubleblind, placebo-controlled period. Most subjects (95.9% crinecerfont; 95.0% placebo) completed
the double-blind period and completed study treatment in this period (Table 11). Reasons for
study discontinuation (and study treatment discontinuation) before Week 24 were withdrawal by
subject (2.5% crinecerfont; 3.3% placebo), lost to follow-up (0.8% crinecerfont; 1.7% placebo),
and an adverse event (AE) (0.8% crinecerfont; 0% placebo).

Disposition During Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 24 to 48)
Of the 182 randomized subjects, 174 (96%) completed the double-blind treatment period. All
174 entered the open-label treatment period (117 crinecerfont; 57 placebo) and were treated with
open-label crinecerfont 100 mg bid starting at Week 24. As of the data cutoff date (July 19,
2023), 45% (39% placebo/crinecerfont; 49% crinecerfont/crinecerfont) had completed the study
through Month 12 and are included in the efficacy analysis. Data from subjects who had not yet
completed the open-label treatment period through Month 12 as of the data cutoff date are not
included in the efficacy analyses but are included in the safety analyses. The remainder of the
subjects who entered the open-label treatment period completed treatment after the data cutoff
date.
Disposition During the Open-Label Extension (Month 12 Onward)
Of the 174 subjects who started the open-label treatment period, 167 (96%) completed openlabel treatment through Month 12. All of the 167 who completed the open-label treatment period
continued into the open-label extension, 50 of whom were rerandomized at Month 12 and
entered the double-blind active-controlled treatment period (Month 12 to Month 18). Their data
are not included in the safety analysis. Data from the remaining 117 subjects who were not
rerandomized are included in the safety analysis.
Baseline Demographics and Clinical Characteristics
Demographics were generally similar between the treatment groups (Table 12). The mean age of
randomized subjects was 31.3 years (range: 18 to 54 years) in the crinecerfont group and
29.8 years (range: 18 to 58 years) in the placebo group. All subjects were younger than age
65 years. The percentage of male and female subjects was approximately 50% in both treatment
groups. Most subjects were White (90.1%) and not Hispanic or Latino (92.3%). Geographic
region was the United States for 37.9% of subjects and outside the United States for 62.1% of
subjects.
Baseline disease characteristics were generally similar between the treatment group and the
placebo group (Table 13). Participants, on average, were taking supraphysiologic glucocorticoid
dosages and had mean androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels significantly above
43
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
the clinical guideline-specified goal ranges (androstenedione within the reference range for age
and sex and 17-hydroxyprogesterone in the upper normal reference range to mildly elevated
(Speiser et al. 2018). A target 17-hydroxyprogesterone level of less than approximately
1200 ng/dL has been suggested, although target levels are individualized in clinical practice
(Merke 2008).
The mean glucocorticoid total daily dose in hydrocortisone equivalents was 17.6 mg/m2/day
(absolute dose 32 mg/day). In adults, a daily absolute hydrocortisone dose of 15 to 25 mg is
widely accepted clinically as physiologic replacement (Bornstein et al. 2016; Husebye et al.
2021). For a typical adult with a body surface area of 1.8 m2, this absolute dose translates to 8 to
14 mg/m2/day.
The mean androstenedione level was 619 ng/dL prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose
(approximately 3 to 4× treatment goal of A4 level below the upper limit of normal) and
349 ng/dL after the morning dose. The androstenedione reference range for males aged 15 to 60
years is about 15 to 150 ng/dL. For females aged 15 to 60 years, the androstenedione reference
range is about 40 to 260 ng/dL.
The mean 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was 9467 ng/dL (about 8× treatment goal of 17-OHP
values less than approximately 1200 ng/dL) prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose and
3299 ng/dL after the morning dose. The 17-hydroxyprogesterone reference range for adult males
is about 30 to 200 ng/dL. For adult females, the 17-hydroxyprogesterone reference range is about
15 to 70 ng/dL in the follicular phase and 35 to 290 ng/dL in the luteal phase.

12.2.2.4.2. Efficacy Results
Efficacy results for Trial CAH3003 include analysis of the completed double-blind period
(Day 1 to Week 24) and an interim analysis of the available data for the ongoing open-label
period (Week 24 to Month 12) at the data cutoff (July 19, 2023).
12.2.2.4.2.1. Primary Analysis
For the primary efficacy endpoint, the least-squares (LS) mean percent change from baseline in
glucocorticoid daily dose at Week 24, while Week 24 androstenedione was controlled at ≤120%
of baseline or ≤ULN for age and sex, was -27.3% (standard deviation [SD] 2.4) for the
crinecerfont group and -10.3% (SD 3.2) for the placebo group, with an LS mean difference
(crinecerfont - placebo) of -17.0% (95% confidence interval [CI]: -23.8, -10.2; p<0.0001) (Table
14). For the primary analysis of the primary endpoint, subjects who did not achieve
androstenedione control were assigned a change in glucocorticoid dose of 0%.

A sensitivity analysis was performed to test the equality of variances between the placebo and
treatment group. Based on the Bartlett’s 𝜒2 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐=0.34517 with p-value=0.56, there was not
enough evidence (at 0.05 significance level) found against the equal variance assumption. Also,
the least squares mean treatment difference (95% CI) obtained from the ANCOVA model
adjusted for unequal variances was ‑17.0 (‑23.7, ‑10.4) is almost identical to what was observed
in the primary analysis in Table 14.
A two-way tipping point sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the
primary efficacy analysis. The significance at p<0.05 was maintained for the primary endpoint
when the delta shift for the multiply imputed values was up to 25 mg/m2/day for crinecerfont or
up to -25 mg/m2/day for placebo. Table 16 contains all combinations of delta values that tipped
the result from statistically significant to not statistically significant. The tipping point (p≥0.05)
was reached when the combined delta shift was 43 mg/m2/day or greater (for example
23 mg/m2/day for crinecerfont and -20 mg/m2/day for placebo). These very extreme values for
the tipping point are supportive of the primary results.

There were 57 subjects (27 in the placebo group and 30 in the crinecerfont treatment group) who
did not achieve androstenedione control by Week 24. In the primary analysis, if a subject did not
meet androstenedione control criteria, the change (and percentage change) in glucocorticoid
daily dose from baseline was set to zero at each visit where control was not met. As an
exploratory analysis, the primary analysis was repeated without setting the change in
glucocorticoid daily dose to zero for subjects with loss of androstenedione control. In this
analysis, the least squares mean treatment difference (-16.3, 95% CI [-22.5, -10.1]) at Week 24
was consistent with that of the primary efficacy analysis. Figure 9 below summarizes the
findings of this exploratory analysis at each visit.
Another sensitivity analysis of the primary endpoint was done where the percentage changes in
glucocorticoid daily dose for the 57 subjects who did not achieve androstenedione control by
Week 24 were replaced with the worst percentage change among all the subjects. Results from
this analysis were also consistent (treatment difference of –20.75 with 95% CI [-29.25, -12.26])
with that of the primary efficacy analysis.

Given the mean baseline glucocorticoid daily dose of 17.6 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents
(absolute dose of 32.3 mg hydrocortisone equivalents) in all study subjects, a mean decrease of
17% (placebo-subtracted difference in the primary analysis of the primary endpoint) would
correspond to a mean dose of 14.6 mg/m2/day (absolute mean dose of 26.8 mg/day), for an
absolute mean decrease of 3 mg/m2/day (mean decrease of 5.5 mg) hydrocortisone equivalents.
A decrease of 2 to 3 mg/m2/day (about 3.5 to 5.5 mg/day) hydrocortisone equivalents in subjects
with CAH treated with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages is clinically meaningful.
Published studies show a high prevalence of adverse effects on body weight and bone health in
individuals with classic CAH treated with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages. Studies in
individuals requiring replacement glucocorticoid therapy show improvements in body mass
index, metabolic parameters, and quality of life when supraphysiologic glucocorticoid is
decreased to more physiologic levels. In adults, a daily absolute hydrocortisone dose of 15 to
25 mg is widely accepted clinically as physiologic replacement (Bornstein et al. 2016; Husebye
et al. 2021). For a typical adult with a body surface area of 1.8 m2, this absolute dose translates to
8 to 14 mg/m2/day.
In published cohort studies, adults and children with classic CAH have a relatively high
prevalence of obesity, and adults also have a high prevalence of low bone density. In a cohort of
139 pediatric patients and 44 adults with classic CAH and mean glucocorticoid daily dose in
hydrocortisone equivalents of 17.9 mg/m2/day in adults and 15 mg/m2/day in children (similar to
the study populations), the prevalence of obesity was 33% in adults and 35% in children.
Furthermore, obesity was associated with higher glucocorticoid dose (Finkielstain et al. 2012).
In a cohort of 165 adults with classic CAH in the United Kingdom, a mean age of 33 years in
women and 32 years in men, and median daily dosages of hydrocortisone (25 mg in males,
20 mg in females), prednisone (7.5 mg in males, 6 mg in females), and dexamethasone (0.5 mg
49
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
in males, 0.375 mg in females), the prevalence of obesity was 37% in men and 52% in women.
In the same study, prevalence of osteopenia and osteoporosis at the lumbar spine for those with
available data was 39.2% and 6.8%, respectively.
In a study of adults with primary adrenal insufficiency caused by Addison’s disease, decreasing
the absolute glucocorticoid dose by 5 mg/day hydrocortisone equivalents and switching from
immediate-release to dual-release glucocorticoids for 6 months led to statistically significant
improvements in body mass index, hemoglobin A1c, lipid levels, and quality of life (Delle Cese
et al. 2020).
Below we further explore the impact of the changes in glucocorticoid dose on other endpoints in
the trial and also assess the proportion of subjects who were able to achieve physiologic-range
glucocorticoid doses in the setting of androgen control.
Secondary Efficacy Endpoint Results
The primary analyses of the five key secondary endpoints are given in Table 17. The LS mean
change from baseline in serum androstenedione at Week 4 was ‑299 (37.7) ng/dL for the
crinecerfont group, compared with an increase of 46 (51.0) ng/dL for the placebo group. The LS
mean treatment difference (crinecerfont - placebo) of ‑345 ng/dL (95% CI: ‑457, ‑232) was
statistically significant. There was a statistically significant difference between the treatment
groups in the percentage of subjects achieving a reduction to a physiologic glucocorticoid daily
dose (≤11 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents adjusted for BSA) at Week 24, while
androstenedione was controlled (≤120% of baseline or ≤ULN for age and sex): 62.7% for the
crinecerfont group and 17.5% for the placebo group (see Figure 10).
The three key secondary endpoints—change from baseline in HOMA-IR, percent change from
baseline in weight, and change from baseline in total fat mass—were not statistically significant.

12.2.3. Trial CAH2006
12.2.3.1. Design, Trial CAH2006
Overall Design
Trial CAH2006 is titled “A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the
safety and efficacy of crinecerfont in pediatric subjects with classic congenital adrenal
hyperplasia, followed by open-label treatment.” The study design is appropriate to demonstrate
efficacy and is depicted in Figure 12. This phase 3 trial consisted of a 4-week screening period, a
28-week double-blind placebo-controlled treatment period, and a 6-month open-label treatment
period through Week 52. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the efficacy of
crinecerfont, compared with placebo, in reducing adrenal androgen levels during a
glucocorticoid-stable period.
Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Treatment Period (Day 1 to Week 28)
A total of 103 pediatric subjects aged 4 to 17 years with classic CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase
deficiency and who required supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids to control androgen
excess (>12 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents) were randomized in a 2:1 ratio
(active:placebo) to receive a weight-based dosage of crinecerfont orally twice daily with
breakfast and the evening meal (25 mg oral solution twice daily for subjects weighing 10 to less
than 20 kg; 50 mg oral solution twice daily for subjects weighing 20 to less than 55 kg; and
100 mg oral capsule for subjects weighing 55 kg or more) or placebo. Randomization was
stratified by pubertal stage (Tanner breast or genital stage 1 or 2 versus 3, 4, or 5) and sex.
During the first 4 weeks of the study, subjects maintained their baseline glucocorticoid regimen.
Serum androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels were measured at Week 4 to evaluate
the change from baseline.
From Week 4 to Week 28, glucocorticoid dosage was adjusted to a target of 8 to 10 mg/m2/day
hydrocortisone equivalents while maintaining goal androstenedione levels (<ULN for sex and
age or if pubertal, pubertal stage; or ≤120% of the subject’s baseline) as long as there was no
evidence of glucocorticoid insufficiency.
Open-Label Treatment Period (Week 28 to Week 52)
At Week 28, subjects transitioned to a 6-month open-label period during which all subjects
received a crinecerfont dosage based on their Week 28 body weight. During Week 32 through
Week 52, glucocorticoid dosage was reduced as tolerated if androstenedione levels were
controlled (≤120% of baseline or ≤ULN for sex, age, or pubertal stage) to a goal of 8 to
10 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents by Week 52.
In all parts of the study allowing for glucocorticoid dose reduction, the attempted dose reduction
was approximately 1 to 4 mg/m2/day per month.
After Week 52, subjects could enter an open-label extension period allowing for crinecerfont
dose adjustment with the goal of maintaining adequate disease control at the lowest possible
glucocorticoid dosage.

12.2.3.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial CAH2006

The eligibility criteria are reflective of the patient population with uncontrolled disease who
would benefit from a reduction in glucocorticoid dose. Study subjects were required to be taking
supraphysiologic glucocorticoid doses (i.e., total daily dosage >12 mg/m2/day in hydrocortisone
dose equivalents). Androstenedione levels (prior to morning glucocorticoid dose) were required
to be greater than the midpoint of the reference range and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels (prior
to the morning glucocorticoid dose) were required to be greater than twice the upper limit of
normal. Key eligibility criteria are summarized below.

12.2.3.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial CAH2006
The full analysis set, defined as all randomized subjects regardless of adherence to study
treatment administration, was used for all efficacy analyses. Continuous efficacy endpoints were
analyzed using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model assuming equal variance between
the placebo and treatment groups. The ANCOVA model included the respective baseline
measurement as a covariate and stratification factors and treatment group (crinecerfont; placebo)
as factors. Categorical efficacy endpoints were analyzed using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel
(CMH) test. The CMH test compared treatment groups (crinecerfont versus placebo) and
included the stratification factors used in the randomization.
For analysis of the primary and key secondary endpoints, the fixed-sequence testing procedure
described below was followed to control for the treatment-group comparisons of multiple
endpoints. Each step in the sequential testing procedure used a two-sided 0.05 level of
significance for the null hypothesis being tested; testing of hypotheses at each step of the
procedure commenced only if all null hypotheses in prior steps were rejected.
1. Primary endpoint: change from baseline in serum androstenedione at Week 4.
2. Key secondary endpoint: change from baseline in serum 17-OHP at Week 4.
3. Key secondary endpoint: percent change from baseline in daily glucocorticoid dose (in
hydrocortisone dose equivalents adjusted for BSA) at Week 28, while Week 28 serum
androstenedione was ≤120% of the baseline value or ≤ULN, according to sex and either age
(for Tanner stage 1) or pubertal stage (for Tanner stages 2 to 5).
Missing data imputation for the primary and key secondary endpoints was handled similar to
Trial CAH3003, i.e., for the primary and key secondary endpoints, the following steps were
taken:
•

For subjects on study drug who were missing the endpoint at the timepoint of interest, their
missing Week 4 (or Week 28 for secondary endpoints) data were imputed from Completers
(subjects who completed through the time of the endpoint on study drug) within the same
treatment group.

•

For subjects in the crinecerfont treatment group off study drug prior to the timepoint of
interest who were missing the endpoint at the timepoint of interest, their missing endpoint
was imputed from subjects who were classified as “retrieved dropouts” (subjects in the FAS
who discontinued study drug but remained in the study and had an evaluable measurement).
If there were five or fewer retrieved dropouts, the missing endpoint values would be imputed
from subjects in the placebo treatment group. For subjects in the placebo treatment group,
missing data were imputed using nonmissing data from subjects in the placebo treatment
group.

discontinued the study after completing the Week 28 visit and thus had study data contributing to
the key secondary endpoint of glucocorticoid dose.

Disposition During Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 28 to 52)
Of the 103 randomized subjects, 97 (97%) completed the double-blind treatment period. All 97
subjects entered the open-label treatment period (66 crinecerfont; 31 placebo) and were treated
with open-label crinecerfont, with dosing recalculated based on the current body weight at
Week 28. As of the data cutoff date (August 9, 2023), 45% (48% placebo/crinecerfont; 44%
crinecerfont/crinecerfont) completed the study through Week 52 and are included in the efficacy
analysis. Data from subjects who had not yet completed the open-label treatment period through
Week 52 as of the data cutoff date are not included in the efficacy analyses but are included in
the safety analysis. The remainder of subjects who entered the open-label treatment period
completed treatment after the data cutoff date.
Disposition During Open-Label Extension (Week 52 Onward)
All 97 subjects who started the open-label treatment period completed open-label treatment
through Week 52. Of the 97 who completed the open-label treatment period, 93 (97%) continued
in the open-label extension.

Baseline Demographics and Clinical Characteristics
Subjects 2 years to 17 years of age were eligible for the study. Randomization in the study was
stratified by pubertal stage (Tanner breast or genital stage 1 or 2 versus 3, 4, or 5) and sex.
Demographics were generally similar between the treatment groups (Table 21). The mean age of
randomized subjects was 12.1 years (range 4.6 to 17.8 years). Approximately 45% of
randomized subjects in each treatment group were <12 years of age. There was an equal
distribution of male and female subjects in both treatment groups. Most subjects in the study
were White (63.1%) and not Hispanic or Latino (74.8%). Geographic region was the United
States for 56.3% of subjects and outside the United States for 43.7% of subjects.
Baseline disease characteristics were generally similar between the treatment group and the
placebo group (Table 22). Subjects, on average, were taking supraphysiologic glucocorticoid
dosages and had mean androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels significantly above
the clinical guideline-specified goal ranges (i.e., androstenedione within the reference range for
age and sex (Speiser et al. 2018)). A target 17-hydroxyprogesterone level of less than
approximately 1200 ng/dL for children with CAH has been suggested (Merke 2008).
The mean glucocorticoid total daily dose in hydrocortisone equivalents was 16.4 mg/m2/day. In
pediatrics, glucocorticoid dosages of 8 to 10 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalent are clinically
accepted as physiologic replacement (Husebye et al. 2021).
The mean androstenedione level was 431 ng/dL prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose (about
3 to 4 times the goal of less than the upper normal range). The androstenedione reference range
for prepubertal males and females is up to about 50 ng/dL. During puberty, the androstenedione
reference range varies by pubertal stage but generally ranges from a lower limit of 30 to
65 ng/dL to an upper limit of 65 to 210 ng/dL for males and a lower limit of 40 to 80 ng/dL to an
upper limit of 100 to 240 ng/dL for females.
The mean 17-hydroxyprogesterone level was 8682 ng/dL (about 7 times the suggested goal of
less than approximately 1200 ng/dL) prior to the morning glucocorticoid dose. The 17-OHP
reference range for prepubertal males and females is about 0 to 90 ng/dL. During puberty, the
17-hydroxyprogesterone reference range varies by pubertal stage but generally ranges from a
lower limit of 0 to 30 ng/dL to an upper limit of 115 to 180 ng/dL for males and a lower limit of
10 to 20 ng/dL to an upper limit of 100 to 265 ng/dL for females.
There were no enrolled pediatric subjects with body weight <20 kg. Therefore, the 25 mg bid
solution was not tested in this trial (see Section 12.3 for further details). There were 51 subjects
in the 20 to <55 kg weight band (37 crinecerfont, 14 placebo) and 52 subjects in the ≥55 kg
weight band (32 crinecerfont, 20 placebo).
