12.2.3.4.2. Efficacy Results
Efficacy results for Trial CAH2006 include analysis of the completed double-blind period (i.e.,
Day 1 to Week 28) and an interim analysis of the available data for the ongoing open-label
period (i.e., Week 28 to Week 52) at the data cutoff (August 9, 2023).
12.2.3.4.2.1. Primary Analysis
For the primary efficacy endpoint, the LS mean change from baseline in serum androstenedione
at Week 4 following the initial 4-week glucocorticoid stable dose period, was ‑196.8 (standard
error [SE] 39.4) ng/dL for the crinecerfont group compared with 71.0 (SE 56.2) ng/dL for the
placebo group. The LS mean treatment difference (crinecerfont - placebo) of -267.8 ng/dL (95%
CI: -403.4, -132.1) was statistically significant (p-value=0.0002) (Table 23).

A two-way tipping point sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the
primary efficacy analysis. Significance at p<0.05 was maintained for change from baseline in
serum androstenedione at Week 4 when the delta shift for the multiply imputed values was up to
2006 ng/dL for crinecerfont or ‑2006 ng/dL for placebo. Table 25 contains all combinations of
delta values that tip the result from statistically significant to not statistically significant. The
tipping point (p≥0.05) was reached when the combined delta shift was 3926 ng/dL or greater
(1920 ng/dL for crinecerfont and ‑2006 ng/dL for placebo), which is an extreme value that
supports the robustness of the primary results.

Results of the primary analyses of the two key secondary endpoints are shown in Table 26. The
LS mean change from baseline in serum 17-OHP at Week 4 was ‑5865 (SE 572.0) ng/dL for the
crinecerfont group compared with 556 (SE 818) ng/dL) for the placebo group. The LS mean
treatment difference (crinecerfont - placebo) of ‑6421 ng/dL (95% CI: ‑8387, ‑4454) was
statistically significant. Similarly, the percent change from baseline in glucocorticoid daily dose
at Week 28, while Week 28 androstenedione was controlled at ≤120% of baseline or ≤ULN for
sex and either age (for Tanner stage 1) or pubertal stage (for Tanner stages 2 to 5), was
statistically significant. The LS mean reduction in glucocorticoid daily dose was ‑18.0% (SE 1.8)
for the crinecerfont group and 5.6% (2.7) for the placebo group, with an LS mean difference
(crinecerfont - placebo) of ‑23.5% (95% CI: ‑29.9, ‑17.2).

Subjects not meeting the androstenedione control criteria will have their glucocorticoid daily dose percent change from baseline

Abbreviations: CFT, crinecerfont 100 mg bid; PBO, placebo

In the primary analysis, if a subject did not meet androstenedione control criteria, the change
(and percentage change) in glucocorticoid daily dose from baseline was set to zero at each visit
where control was not met. As an exploratory analysis, the primary analysis of this key
secondary endpoint was repeated without setting the glucocorticoid daily dose to zero for these
subjects. In this analysis, the least square mean difference (-25.9% and 95% CI: [-32.5, ‑19.2]) at
Week 28 was similar to that of the primary analysis.
Given the mean baseline glucocorticoid daily dose of 16.5 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents
in the crinecerfont group, a decrease of 18% (decrease observed in the crinecerfont group) would
correspond to a dose of 13.5 mg/m2/day, for an absolute decrease of 3 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone
equivalents. A decrease of 3 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents in pediatric subjects with
CAH treated with supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dosages is clinically meaningful. See
Section 12.2.2.4 for a discussion of the clinical meaningfulness of this reduction.
A secondary endpoint of clinical importance, reduction in physiologic glucocorticoid doses while
maintaining androstenedione control (defined as serum androstenedione <120% of baseline or
≤ULN, according to sex and either age for Tanner stage 1 or pubertal stage for Tanner stages 2 to
5) at Week 28, showed a 30% responder rate with crinecerfont versus a 0% responder rate for
placebo (Table 27).

12.3. Key Efficacy Review Issues
12.3.1. Appropriate Dosage in Pediatric Patients
Weighing 10 kg to Less Than 20 kg
Issue
No pediatric subjects weighing 10 kg to less than 20 kg were enrolled in the pediatric phase 3
Trial CAH2006. Therefore, the proposed crinecerfont dosage of 25 mg twice daily (oral solution)
for this patient population was not evaluated in a phase 3 clinical trial.
Background
The Applicant selected a dosing regimen of 25 mg bid for the pediatric 10 to <20 kg weight band
based on exposure matching to the adult regimen of 100 mg twice daily using popPK modeling
and simulation.
Assessment
Leveraging popPK modeling and simulation, an exposure-matching approach was employed by
the Applicant to propose dosing regimens for pediatric patients by weight bands (10 to <20 kg,
20 to <55 kg, and ≥55 kg), corresponding to doses of 25 mg solution bid, 50 mg solution bid, and
100 mg capsule bid, respectively. The simulated results demonstrate that the percent of pediatric
subjects (10 to <20 kg) falling within the 90% prediction interval of the adult exposure (i.e., 24hour AUC) was relatively low at 68.4% (as compared to 76.8% and 91.6% for the other pediatric
weight bands). As such, approximately 31% of the pediatric subjects of 10 to <20 kg are
projected to have exposures lower than the 5th percentile of the reference adult exposure (Figure
3).
In regard to the exposure-matching approach, the Applicant used the adult subjects as the
reference exposure; however, the review team considers the 20 to <55 kg pediatric subgroup to
be more similar to those weighing 10 to <20 kg based on physiology, disease state, and disease
progression. Furthermore, the review team assessed efficacy in these pediatric subgroups in the
phase 3 clinical trials and found the pediatric subgroup of 20 to <55 kg to be an acceptable
efficacy reference group for exposure matching for the 10 to <20 kg group based on the percent
change from baseline in glucocorticoid dose and proportion of subjects achieving a
glucocorticoid dose ≤11 mg/m2/day at Week 28 (Table 30).
Based on popPK modeling and simulation, the proposed 25 mg bid dosing regimen for the 10 to
<20 kg pediatric subgroup is expected to produce similar exposures to those of 50 mg bid for the
20 to <55 kg pediatric subgroup, and therefore, efficacy is expected to be similar between these
two pediatric subgroups. Additionally, the relatively higher exposure in adult subjects serves as
an appropriate safety exposure coverage. Overall, the exposures of the proposed 25 mg bid
dosing regimen in the 10 to <20 kg pediatric subgroup is expected to be safe and effective. Refer
to Section 20.5 for details on exposure comparison and matching.

Conclusion
The Applicant’s proposed dosage of 25 mg twice daily for pediatric patients weighing 10 kg to
less than 20 kg is acceptable.

13. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
13.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Nonclinical Data
The safety of crinecerfont was evaluated in nonclinical safety pharmacology studies, subchronic
and chronic toxicology studies in rats and dogs, reproductive and developmental studies in rats
and rabbits, genetic toxicology studies, juvenile studies in rats, and 2-year rat and 6-month
transgenic mouse carcinogenicity studies. Systemic steady-state crinecerfont exposures increased
with dose in a less than dose-proportional manner and approached or reached saturation in the
pivotal nonclinical studies. Maximum plasma exposures declined after repeated dosing, likely as
a result of induced liver drug-metabolizing enzymes, which contributed to the saturation of
exposure observed in the toxicity studies. Thus, clinical exposure multiples at the no-observedadverse-effect levels (NOAELs) in the pivotal nonclinical studies were limited to one- to
fourfold the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD). Nonclinical data relevant to clinical
risk assessment or safety concerns are discussed below (see Section 19 for the detailed
nonclinical assessment). Overall, nonclinical data support the safe use of crinecerfont for the
indicated patients with CAH ≥4 years old.
Safety Pharmacology
Crinecerfont administered as a single oral or IV dose had no significant effects on
neurobehavioral function in rats, cardiovascular function in dogs, respiratory function in guinea
pigs, renal function in rats, or gastrointestinal function in rats at clinically relevant doses.
Crinecerfont showed no potential for clinical arrhythmia risk in vitro in human ether-à-go-gorelated gene (hERG) current (<5% inhibition at 10µM) or isolated rabbit Purkinje fiber action

70
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
potential. Overall, the safety pharmacology data demonstrated that crinecerfont did not pose
acute safety concerns at clinically relevant exposure levels.
General Toxicology
The toxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated in a series of single- and repeat-dose studies in mice,
rats, and dogs. The target organs for crinecerfont were liver (mouse, rat, and dog), thyroid gland
(rat and dog), gastrointestinal (GI) tract (mouse and rat), and coagulation-associated effects. GI
tract findings were not clinically relevant and thyroid gland findings are discussed in the context
of carcinogenic potential (below). Clinical trial data identified neutropenia and neuropsychiatric
safety as potential clinical risks. Neutropenia was not observed in the pivotal rat or dog toxicity
studies and there were no nonclinical signals for immunosuppression or neurobehavioral effects.
Mechanistic studies showed crinecerfont is active at the pituitary and can cross the blood-brain
barrier, but distribution to the central nervous system was low, with an observed brain to plasma
ratio of 0.1. In comparison, crinecerfont was highly distributed to liver (where it is metabolized)
as evidenced by a ≥8.5 liver-to-plasma ratio.
Initial studies with a crinecerfont tosylate formulation were associated with coagulopathy
(prolongation of prothrombin time [PT] and activated partial thromboplastin time [APTT] and/or
bleeding) and mortality in repeat-dose rat studies. Subsequently, the tosylate salt formulation was
replaced with a free base form of crinecerfont for evaluation in the pivotal chronic toxicology,
carcinogenicity, prenatal and postnatal and juvenile nonclinical studies, and for the clinical
studies. In chronic rat studies with crinecerfont free base, no mortality or bleeding effects were
noted; however, changes in coagulation parameters (prolongation of PT up to 60%, and APTT up
to 90%) were observed at 1250 mg/kg/day (6-fold MRHD exposure). Similar findings
(prolongation of PT) were observed in the chronic dog study conducted with crinecerfont free
(b) (4)
base, without any other coagulopathy up to 1000 mg/kg/day (5-fold MRHD exposure).
. Drug-related effects
on coagulation were routinely monitored in clinical trials with the crinecerfont free base
formulation.
Crinecerfont is predominantly metabolized by CYP3A4 in the liver in animals and in humans. In
rats and dogs, crinecerfont induces drug-metabolizing enzymes, which resulted in increased liver
weight and hepatocellular hypertrophy in both species. Mechanistic studies confirmed that
induction of metabolizing enzymes contributed to dose- and duration-dependent signs of liver
toxicity. In rodents only, higher crinecerfont doses (approximately seven times MRHD
exposures) caused a low incidence of more advanced liver injury, including multinucleated
hepatocytes and anisokaryosis and minimal hepatocyte necrosis. There were no liver findings of
concern at doses corresponding to one- to fourfold clinical exposures, and induction or inhibition
of liver metabolizing enzymes is unlikely to occur at clinically relevant doses. Routine
monitoring for biomarkers and signs of drug-induced liver injury was conducted throughout the
clinical development program.
Reproductive, Developmental, and Juvenile Toxicology
The effects of crinecerfont on fertility, reproduction, early embryonic and embryo-fetal
development, and juvenile development were evaluated in rat and rabbit toxicology studies.
Investigations with the crinecerfont tosylate salt did not identify effects on male or female
71
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
fertility or early embryonic development at low clinical exposure margins (two- to fourfold
clinical MRHD exposures).
There were also no effects of crinecerfont on rat embryo-fetal development, pre- and postnatal
development, or juvenile development that raised concerns about clinical safety. Exposure was
limited by tolerability in the rat studies, reaching approximately four times maximum clinical
exposure. The toxicity profile of crinecerfont in juvenile rats was comparable to the adult
toxicity profile. Juvenile animal findings support the safety of crinecerfont in the indicated
pediatric patients ≥4 years of age.
In the embryo-fetal development study in rabbits, there were multiple craniofacial malformations
in a few fetuses, from multiple litters, which were not present in the concurrent control and were
outside the historical control range. The malformations included microcephaly, microstomia,
acephalostomia, misshapen cerebrum and/or cerebellum, among others. Exposure attained in the
rabbit study ranged between 2× to 3× MRHD, without a dose dependency, despite a 10-fold
increase in nominal dose (100 mg/kg low dose to 1000 mg/kg high dose), indicating saturation of
absorption. The absence of a dose-related increase in exposure confounds identification of an
exposure/response relationship on embryo-fetal development. We therefore assessed the
incidence of malformations across all treatment groups because of the similar crinecerfont
exposures—there were 4 fetuses from four litters with craniofacial poly-malformations of
interest, for a total fetal incidence of 0.8% (4/525) in 7% (4/59) of litters. These specific findings
were not present in the historical control data from the same study site. The overall incidence of
fetal malformations was low and there was no clear relationship to drug, but absent similar
findings in concurrent control fetuses, and with the incidence being outside the historical control
range for individual malformations, we cannot rule out a possible effect of crinecerfont treatment
on rabbit embryo-fetal development. Rabbit findings and potential implications for clinical risk
of special populations will be addressed in labeling.
Additional details of the developmental, reproductive, and juvenile development toxicity studies
can be found in Section 19. A discussion of the developmental and reproductive toxicology data
relevant to crinecerfont use in pregnant people can be found in Section 14.4.
Carcinogenicity
The oncogenic potential of crinecerfont was evaluated in two-year rat and 6-month transgenic
mouse carcinogenicity studies. Crinecerfont did not show oncogenic effects in transgenic mice.
In the 2-year rat study, crinecerfont increased the incidence of thyroid gland follicular cell
adenoma and carcinoma in females at 100 mg/kg crinecerfont (4-fold MRHD exposure). Thyroid
gland follicular cell tumors arise from excessive clearance of thyroid hormone from induction of
liver drug-metabolizing enzymes, which results in release of, and continuous stimulation by,
thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) on the thyroid follicular cells. This mechanism of inducing
thyroid gland follicular cell hyperplasia and subsequent tumor development in rats is considered
not relevant in humans (Wu and Farrelly 2006; Bartsch et al. 2018). Additional evidence from
the chronic 6-month rat toxicity study showed increased thyroid gland weights and follicular cell
hypertrophy and hyperplasia, with increased TSH measured in the subchronic rat study further
supporting thyroid hormone stimulation leading to thyroid gland hypertrophy. Overall, the data
from genotoxicity, 6-month transgenic mouse carcinogenicity, and two-year rat carcinogenicity
studies show that the potential human oncogenic risk of crinecerfont is low.

13.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
Crinecerfont is a first-in-class drug, so there is no marketing experience. Adrenal insufficiency
was identified as a potential safety concern because of the drug’s mechanism of action.
Crinecerfont decreases pituitary ACTH levels, leading to decreased adrenal androgen levels, and
ultimately allowing for reduction in glucocorticoid dosage.
Neuropsychiatric safety was identified as another potential concern because crinecerfont is
centrally acting and was previously in development as a treatment for major depression.
Potential risks of hypersensitivity and neutropenia were identified because of observations in
earlier clinical studies. A hypersensitivity event of angioedema occurred in a phase 1 study
(Study NBI-74788-1724) of two dose regimens of crinecerfont (100 mg qAM/200 mg qPM, or
100 mg qAM/150 mg qPM) in healthy adult volunteers. According to the Applicant, the 41-yearold male with no relevant past medical history developed a moderate-grade generalized rash after
3 days of crinecerfont treatment with 100/150 mg. He subsequently experienced perioral edema
and throat tightness. No symptoms of shortness of breath or difficulty swallowing were reported,
and vital signs were stable. These signs and symptoms resolved following treatment with
dexamethasone, inhaled epinephrine, and an oral corticosteroid taper. The study drug was
discontinued because of the hypersensitivity event. The investigator considered the event
possibly related to study drug. Hypersensitivity reactions are discussed further in Section 13.7.2.
Neutropenia was observed in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont for major depressive disorder
(Study DFI5687). There was a higher incidence of transient low neutrophil counts
(<1.5×103 cells/µL for non-Black subjects, <1×103 cells/µL for lack subjects) in the crinecerfont
100 mg group (12.9%) compared with the placebo and escitalopram groups (3.5% and 6.1%,
respectively) in this study. Neutropenia is discussed further in Section 13.7.3.

13.3. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns
Identified Through Postmarket Experience
Not applicable. The drug is not marketed in any country.

13.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
The phase 3 trials, CAH3003 (conducted in adults with CAH) and CAH2006 (conducted in
children aged 4 years to 17 years with CAH), were used to support the safety review. The
Applicant’s safety analysis included results of the completed 6-month double-blind treatment
period for both studies and the subset of available data from ongoing open-label periods through
Month 12 for Trial CAH3003 (data cutoff July 19, 2023) and Week 52 for Trial CAH2006 (data
cutoff August 9, 2023). The Applicant subsequently submitted the completed 120-day Safety
Update (data cutoff January 16, 2024, for Trial CAH3003 and February 6, 2024, for Trial
CAH2006), which was incorporated into the safety review and included data from the open-label
extension (post-Month 12). We present the safety data from each distinct period (i.e., 24-week
double-blind treatment period, open-label treatment Months 6 to 12, followed by open-label

adverse events. All AEs in the reviewed trials were graded by investigators using a threecategory intensity scale, shown in Table 31, with options of mild, moderate, or severe, which

13.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database
Incorporating the two pivotal phase 3 studies, the safety database is adequate for the proposed
CAH indication, dosage regimens, and patient population. Total exposure to crinecerfont in both
trials was 216 person-years, with 134 person-years in Trial CAH3003 and 82 person-years in
Trial CAH2006. The majority of subjects in both trials completed the full one-year treatment
period. A total of 179 subjects were exposed to crinecerfont for ≥46 weeks in the two trials
combined. Extent of exposure in each phase 3 trial is shown in Table 32 and Table 33,
respectively. The exposure is adequate to evaluate the safety of chronic use.

are not included in the open-label extension safety analysis.
The adverse event rate decreased to 51% in the open-label extension, with the majority of events
graded as mild or moderate (Table 36).

13.6.2.2.1. Open-Label Extension (Month 12 Onward)
One death occurred in a subject on study drug (crinecerfont 100 mg in the morning and 200 mg
in the evening) during the open-label extension period. The cause of death was an adrenal crisis.
The adrenal crisis was precipitated by an acute infectious illness that was not adequately treated
with stress-dose steroids. The death was not likely study-drug-related.
The subject, a 56-year-old male with classic CAH, died during an episode of acute adrenal
insufficiency. Approximately 19 months after starting crinecerfont and 15 months after achieving
a lower glucocorticoid dose of 9.8 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalent, he developed a flu-like
illness with nausea, vomiting, and lethargy. He had recently been exposed to visiting family
members with similar symptoms. The following day, he vomited 3 times. That evening, he
informed his visiting family members that he would start stress dosing of steroids with his next
glucocorticoid dose and was going to bed. He was found dead on the floor the next morning.
Autopsy findings showed inflammatory infiltrates in his lungs consistent with his reported flulike syndrome, and cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly thought to be related to his uncontrolled
diabetes.
13.6.2.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial
CAH3003
13.6.2.3.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
The overall rate of serious TEAEs during the 24-week double-blind treatment period of Trial
CAH3003 was 3.3% (in four subjects) in the crinecerfont group and none in the placebo group
(Table 37).
Four subjects experienced serious TEAEs during the double-blind treatment period. One event
was presyncope, the cause of which is unclear, but did not recur despite resuming study drug:
•

Presyncope occurred in a 48-year-old female who developed fatigue, general malaise, and
myalgias on Study Day 64 (Week 9, during the glucocorticoid reduction period) and was
admitted to the hospital for evaluation. Her glucocorticoid dose was decreased from
14.5 mg/m2/day at baseline to 11.6 mg/m2/day at Week 6 and she remained at a dose of
11.6 mg mg/m2/day at Week 9. The evaluation was unremarkable, without orthostatic
hypotension or laboratory signs of adrenal insufficiency. She was successfully treated with
intravenous fluids, electrolytes, and hydrocortisone. Study drug was interrupted for 1 day and
she continued study drug into the open-label treatment period with no recurrence of
presyncope.

The three remaining serious TEAEs occurring during the double-blind treatment period are not
likely study-drug-related:
•

A serious adverse event (SAE) of acute adrenocortical insufficiency during the double-blind
treatment period occurred in a 24-year-old female. Concomitant medications administered
within 30 days before the event included fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone. On Day 30, the
subject experienced vomiting for which she self-administered emergency hydrocortisone.
Her glucocorticoid dose at Week 4 was 16 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalents, which had
not changed from baseline.

13.6.2.3.2. SAEs During Open-Label Treatment Period
(Weeks 24 to 48)
Table 38 shows the serious TEAEs that began during the open-label treatment period according
to treatment received in the double-blind phase (i.e., placebo or crinecerfont). There were nine
events in eight subjects. Acute adrenal insufficiency was the only preferred term that occurred in
more than one subject.
The events (preferred terms) of tympanic membrane perforation, gastroenteritis viral,
coronavirus infection, and Bell’s palsy are considered unrelated to study drug due either to
identification of an alternate cause, or unlikely relationship to pharmacology of crinecerfont. The
event of joint injury was a case of right knee torsion injury sustained during a skateboarding
accident.
The two cases of adrenocortical insufficiency were both preceded by acute infection
accompanied by vomiting. In one of the two cases, the subject had been unable to take stressdose steroids due to vomiting. Both events were attributed to infection and not considered related
to study drug.
There was a serious AE of suicide attempt, for which a drug effect cannot be excluded:
•

The serious adverse event of suicide attempt involved a 29-year-old female with a history of
acne who had received crinecerfont 100 mg bid starting in the double-blind treatment period
and continuing during the open-label treatment period. Concomitant medications
administered within 30 days of the event included hydrocortisone and paracetamol/tramadol.
On Study Day 320 (also Day 320 of study drug administration), she was hospitalized after
taking 19 tramadol tablets and thiocodin as well as intentionally injuring her arm. Three days
prior to hospital admission she had ended a seven-year romantic relationship and experienced
significant deterioration of her mental condition. Computed tomography scanning showed
cortical brain atrophy. Study drug was discontinued because of the suicide attempt. The
investigator considered the suicide attempt to be unrelated to study treatment.

The remaining SAE described below, was not considered related to study drug following review
of the narrative:
•

A 46-year-old male had an anaphylactic reaction to tree nuts. He had a history of a tree nut
allergy and ate cake containing nuts on Study Day 332 during the open-label treatment
period. He was treated with antihistamine and hydrocortisone in the emergency department
with resolution the same day. He continued on study drug after the event. This SAE was not
drug-related.

13.6.2.3.3. Serious Adverse Events Reported in OpenLabel Extension (Month 12 Onward)
Nine subjects experienced serious adverse events in the open-label extension through the data
cutoff date of the 120-day safety update submission (Table 39). There were three cases of acute
adrenocortical insufficiency, one of which was fatal and is described in Section 13.6.2.2.1 above.
Review of this narrative and the other nonfatal cases of acute adrenocortical insufficiency do not
suggest a relationship to crinecerfont treatment. All events except one were preceded by acute
illness and associated with inadequate stress dosing of steroids. The remaining event involved a
52-year-old male who was hospitalized for vomiting and hypoxia. He reported an antecedent
history of several months of generalized weakness and chronic diarrhea. Hospital evaluation
yielded no evidence of underlying infection, and no unifying diagnosis was made. However, the
subject’s symptoms improved with stress-dose steroids, and he resumed crinecerfont without
recurrence of symptoms. The cause of adrenal insufficiency in this subject is unclear but could
relate to dehydration from chronic diarrhea, or to a subacute non-bacterial infectious or other
inflammatory etiology. Negative rechallenge with study drug suggests the event was not related
to crinecerfont.
The remaining narratives for SAEs were reviewed and there is no suggestion that the events were
related to study drug, as events resolved while the subjects continued on crinecerfont and/or an
alternative etiology was identified.

13.6.2.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment
Discontinuation, Trial CAH3003
13.6.2.4.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
A total of four subjects (3.3%) in the crinecerfont group and none in the placebo group
experienced an adverse event leading to study drug discontinuation during the double-blind
treatment period (Table 40). No single preferred term occurred in more than one subject.
During the double-blind treatment period, adverse events of restlessness, apathy, dyspepsia,
nausea, and vomiting, involving two subjects described below, are possibly study-drug-related:
•

A 28-year-old male developed restlessness on Study Day 3 and apathy on Study Day 54. He
also had an increase in his Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale from 0 to 2 (nonspecific
active suicidal thoughts). He discontinued crinecerfont on Study Day 380 during the
extended open-label period due to restlessness, with resolution of the restlessness 11 days
after discontinuation. The adverse event of restlessness is possibly study-drug-related
because crinecerfont is centrally acting and the restlessness resolved after drug
discontinuation. Drug-relatedness for apathy and suicidal ideation cannot be excluded.

•

Dyspepsia, nausea, and vomiting developed in a 39-year-old female without any noted
medical history other than CAH on Study Day 167, which resolved on Study Day 169. She
then discontinued study drug on Day 184 due to nausea, vomiting, and dyspepsia.
Information is not available regarding resolution of symptoms off study drug.

The adverse events of rash, and gastric ulcer leading to study drug discontinuation are not likely
study-drug-related:
•

Rash occurred in a 26-year-old female on Study Day 166. She was treated with clobetasol
and discontinued the study on Day 589 because of the rash. The rash was still present on
Day 671. The rash is not likely study-drug-related because the rash did not resolve after study
drug discontinuation.

•

Gastric ulcer occurred in a 31-year-old female on Study Day 10. Her medical history
included headache, hypertension, menstrual disorder, and sleep apnea. Concomitant
medications included hydrocortisone and propranolol. The timing of a gastric ulcer occurring
after only 10 days of study drug treatment makes it unlikely to have been related to study
drug.

13.6.2.5.2. Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 24 to
48)
During the open-label treatment period, the rate of any AE decreased from 83% in the
crinecerfont DB group to 62% in the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group and decreased from 81% in
the placebo DB group to 70% in the placebo/crinecerfont group (Table 43).
Adverse events occurring in ≥4% of subjects in the placebo/crinecerfont group were fatigue,
headache, coronavirus infection, nasopharyngitis, diarrhea, dizziness, back pain, and abdominal
pain (see Table 43).
Fatigue, dizziness, arthralgia, back pain, increased creatine phosphokinase (CPK), and decreased
appetite all decreased in frequency from the crinecerfont DB period to the
crinecerfont/crinecerfont open-label period, suggesting drug tolerance. Overall AE incidence
also decreased. These data raise no concerns with respect to the longer-term safety of
crinecerfont.

13.6.2.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial CAH3003
See the schedule of assessments in Section 21 for the frequency of laboratory monitoring.
Laboratory data for CPK, neutrophil count, and coagulation parameters were examined more
closely for the following reasons:
•

The adverse event preferred term of blood creatine phosphokinase increased occurred with
greater frequency in the crinecerfont versus placebo group (see Section 13.6.2.5).

•

A higher incidence of neutropenia was noted in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont in subjects
with major depressive disorder (see Section 13.2).

•

Nonclinical studies of crinecerfont tosylate formulation were associated with coagulopathy
(prolongation of PT and APTT and/or bleeding) and mortality in repeat-dose rat studies.
Subsequently, the tosylate salt formulation was replaced with a free base form, which was
used for the clinical studies. In chronic rat studies with crinecerfont free base, no mortality or
bleeding effects were noted; however, changes in coagulation parameters (prolongation of PT
88

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
up to 60%, and APTT up to 90%) were observed at 1250 mg/kg/day (6-fold MRHD
exposure). Similar findings (prolongation of PT) were observed in the chronic dog study
conducted with crinecerfont free base but without any other coagulopathy up to
1000 mg/kg/day [5-fold MRHD exposure].
13.6.2.6.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
13.6.2.6.1.1. Chemistry Parameters
Elevated CPK levels occurred more frequently in the placebo group, but CPK levels greater than
5× ULN occurred more frequently in the crinecerfont group. The mean change in CPK levels
from baseline over time was slightly higher in the crinecerfont group compared to placebo
(Figure 16).
Although more subjects in the placebo group (12%) had CPK levels >3× ULN (Level 1
abnormality) compared to the crinecerfont group (9%), more crinecerfont-treated subjects had
CPK values >5× ULN (Level 2 abnormality) and >10× ULN (Level 3 abnormality) than subjects
receiving placebo (Table 44).
Of the five subjects with CPK values >10× ULN (Level 3) in the crinecerfont group during the
double-blind treatment period, all elevated levels were documented on a single blood draw and
had resolved by the subsequent blood draw. According to the Applicant, most instances of
increased CPK levels were associated with significant physical exertion and improved with
cessation of the inciting activity. No cases of increased CPK resulted in study treatment
discontinuation. There were no reported cases of rhabdomyolysis.
The elevated CPK levels are not likely drug-related because elevated levels >3× ULN occurred
more frequently in the placebo group, most instances of elevated CPK levels were explained by
other factors, and there is no mechanistic evidence of causality.

13.6.2.6.1.2. Hematology Parameters
As noted above, because of the higher incidence of neutropenia noted in the major depression
study, we examined laboratory data for neutropenia and those findings are discussed further in
Section 13.7.3.There was also a decrease in white blood cell count over time in the crinecerfont
group during the double-blind treatment period compared to placebo. This issue is addressed
further in Section 13.7.3.
There was no notable difference in mean change or outlier incidence in hemoglobin, hematocrit,
or platelets (see Table 198 in Section 23.2.2).
With respect to coagulation parameters, mean PT and partial thromboplastin time (PTT)
increased slightly over time in both treatment groups, but the effect was larger in the crinecerfont
group (see Figure 17). INR remained stabled in both groups (Figure 17). There was no notable
difference in incidence of outliers in coagulation parameters of INR or PTT between crinecerfont
and placebo groups (Table 46). For study subjects with adverse events classified under the
narrow FDA medical query (FMQ) of hemorrhage (Table 47), all had coagulation study
parameters within normal limits, that includes PT, PTT, and INR.

13.6.2.6.2. Open-Label Treatment Period and Open-Label
Extension
Laboratory parameters that were abnormal in the double-blind treatment period were the focus of
the assessment of laboratory data from the open-label treatment period and, as needed, the openlabel extension data that were submitted in the 120-Day Safety Update.
The incidence of elevated CPK levels in the open-label period decreased compared to the
double-blind period, which suggests the effect was not due to study drug. As shown in Table 48,
creatine phosphokinase values >3× ULN (Level 1 abnormality) decreased in frequency from
11.9% in the placebo double-blind group to none in the placebo/crinecerfont group. The
frequency of elevated CPK values at all levels decreased from the crinecerfont DB group to the
crinecerfont/crinecerfont group. See Table 48.

13.6.2.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial
CAH3003
In rat and dog studies, increased liver weight and hepatocellular hypertrophy were observed,
likely due to crinecerfont’s induction of drug-metabolizing enzymes. Laboratory data were
screened for evidence of drug-induced liver injury to determine cases meeting Hy’s Law criteria,
defined as any postbaseline total bilirubin equal to or exceeding two times the upper limit of
normal (2× ULN) after a postbaseline alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate
aminotransferase (AST) equal to or exceeding 3× ULN. There were no potential cases of Hy’s
Law during the double-blind (Figure 18) or open-label treatment periods.
As shown in Table 49, the incidence of excursions in liver parameters outside the normal range
during treatment were similar between the crinecerfont and placebo groups. A single subject
receiving crinecerfont experienced increase in total bilirubin to >2× ULN without associated
transaminase elevation.

13.6.2.8. Vital-Sign Analyses, Trial CAH3003
Review of the vital-sign data did not reveal any safety concerns. There were no clinically
significant changes from baseline over time in mean systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood
pressure, orthostatic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, or body temperature in the
crinecerfont versus placebo group during the 24-week double-blind treatment period. See Section
23 for additional details (Figure 78, Figure 79, Figure 80, Figure 81, Figure 82, and Table 199).

13.6.3. Safety Results, Trial CAH2006
13.6.3.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, Trial CAH2006
13.6.3.1.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
During the 28-week double-blind placebo-controlled period of Trial CAH2006, the overall rates
of adverse events were similar in the crinecerfont (84%) and placebo (82%) groups. One subject
in the crinecerfont group (1.4%) compared to four subjects in the placebo group (12%)
experienced serious adverse events. Adverse events leading to interruption of study drug
occurred more frequently in the placebo group (15%) compared to the crinecerfont group (3%)
(Table 52).

13.6.3.1.2. Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 28 to
52)
The overall rate of any adverse event decreased from 82% in the placebo DB period to 74%
during the open-label period in the placebo/crinecerfont group and decreased from 84% in the
crinecerfont DB period to 70% during the open-label period in the crinecerfont/crinecerfont
group (Table 53), which suggests improved tolerability of crinecerfont for the subjects who
remained in the trial and continued treatment with crinecerfont. The rate of serious adverse
events decreased from 12% in the placebo DB period to 6.5% during the open-label period in the
placebo/crinecerfont group and were similar to the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group (6%). These
data do not raise any concerns with longer-term treatment.

13.6.3.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial
CAH2006
13.6.3.3.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
In Trial CAH2006, the overall rate of serious TEAEs was higher in the placebo group (12%, four
subjects) compared to the crinecerfont group (1.4%, one subject) during the 28-week doubleblind treatment period (Table 55).
The one serious TEAE of pyrexia occurring in the crinecerfont group during the double-blind
treatment period was more likely related to an infectious etiology, given the subject’s
improvement with treatment in the emergency department and in the setting of continued
crinecerfont treatment:
•

Pyrexia occurred in a 12-year-old-male who presented to the emergency department with a
temperature of 38.2°C, vomiting, and headache on Study Day 61. Attempts at oral stressdose hydrocortisone at home were unsuccessful due to vomiting. In the emergency
department, he was treated with intravenous hydration, fluids, dextrose, and hydrocortisone.
His condition improved and he was discharged the same day. No changes were made to his
study drug regimen.

13.6.3.3.2. SAEs During Open-Label Treatment Period
(Weeks 28 to 52)
Table 56 lists the serious TEAEs that began during the open-label treatment period, according to
treatment received in the double-blind phase (i.e., placebo or crinecerfont). There were six events
in six subjects.
Narratives for the events (preferred terms) of vomiting and gastritis were reviewed and are
considered unrelated to study drug, due either to identification of an alternate cause or an
unlikely relationship to pharmacology of crinecerfont.
Details of the three remaining SAEs, none of which are likely study-drug-related, follow:
•

An SAE of hypotension occurred in a 6-year-old female on amlodipine. Her hypotension
resolved when her amlodipine dose was reduced. This event can be attributed to effect of
antihypertensive medication.

•

A seizure occurred in a 5-year-old female on Study Day 222 that led to hospitalization and
study drug interruption for 1 day. Initial laboratory evaluation and brain imaging was normal.
Further evaluation included chromosomal microarray testing that was suspicious for 15q
duplication syndrome, which may be associated with epilepsy. This case represents initial
presentation of epilepsy secondary to a chromosomal abnormality.

•

An SAE of acute adrenocortical insufficiency occurred in a 7-year-old female on Study
Day 223 that led to interruption of study drug for 2 days. She was admitted to the hospital
after presenting with vomiting and diarrhea. She vomited her stress-dose hydrocortisone.
Evaluation was consistent with adrenal crisis (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, metabolic
acidosis). A viral gastroenteritis panel was positive for norovirus. She was treated with
intravenous fluids, dextrose, stress-dose hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, and ondansetron.
Her condition significantly improved after two days. In this case, acute adrenal insufficiency
was considered secondary to norovirus gastroenteritis.

13.6.3.3.3. Serious Adverse Events Reported in the OpenLabel Extension (Week 52 Onward)
Three subjects experienced serious adverse events in the open-label extension that were newly
reported in the 120-day safety update. Narratives for the events (preferred terms) of blood CPK
increased, Norovirus infection, and cerebrospinal fluid leakage were reviewed, and these events
are considered unrelated to study drug due either to identification of an alternate cause, or
unlikely relationship to the pharmacology of crinecerfont. The event of blood CPK increased was
temporally related to isotretinoin. The event of cerebrospinal fluid leakage was related to craniospinal surgery for Chiari malformation.

13.6.3.4.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
Two subjects (3%) in the crinecerfont group and none in the placebo group experienced an
adverse event leading to study drug discontinuation during the 28-week double-blind treatment
period (Table 57).

The symptoms occurring in the two subjects leading to study drug discontinuation (abdominal
pain, nausea, motion sickness, retching, myalgias, dizziness) are described below:
•

Abdominal pain, nausea, and myalgias occurred in a 15-year-old female on Study Day 126.

Dizziness, nausea, motion sickness, and retching occurred in a 15-year-old female leading to

occurred on Study Day 58. Motion sickness occurred on Study Day 149. Anxiety,
depression, and suicidal ideation occurred after about 5 months on study drug. Retching
occurred after about 6 months on study drug. Dizziness and retching were resolved about
5 months after study drug was discontinued.

13.6.3.4.3. Open-Label Extension (Week 52 Onward)
One subject, a 14-year-old male, discontinued study drug during the open-label extension for a
suicide attempt (preferred term) as specified per protocol. After the data cutoff, the investigations
indicated that the event term should be corrected to “suicidal ideation” because the subject did
not have a plan and did not make a suicide attempt. He had a history of anxiety, depression, and
attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Concomitant medications included bupropion, fluoxetine,
hydroxyzine, aripiprazole, and isotretinoin. The subject visited his family home construction site
and had a thought that if he fell off the roof, he would die.

13.6.3.5.2. Open-Label Treatment Period (Weeks 28 to

During the open-label treatment period, the rate of any AE decreased from 84% in the
crinecerfont DB group to 70% in the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group and decreased from 82% in
the placebo DB group to 74% in the placebo/crinecerfont group (Table 59).

to crinecerfont were considered possibly related to study drug with the caveat that the small
sample size significantly limits interpretation. As shown in Table 59 in the column labeled
“Placebo (DB) to Crinecerfont (OL) Week 28 to Week 52,” only headache and abdominal pain
met those criteria. It is possible that these events relate to symptoms of glucocorticoid
withdrawal rather than crinecerfont itself. Both headache and abdominal pain also decreased in
frequency from the crinecerfont DB group to the crinecerfont/crinecerfont group, suggesting
development of tolerance to reduction in glucocorticoid dose or to crinecerfont treatment.

13.6.3.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial CAH2006
See the schedule of assessments in Section 21 for the frequency of laboratory monitoring.
Laboratory data for CPK, neutrophil count, and coagulation parameters were examined more
closely for the following reasons:
•

Elevated CPK levels were noted in the adult study.

•

A higher incidence of neutropenia was noted in a phase 2 study of crinecerfont in subjects
with major depressive disorder (see Section 13.2).

•

Nonclinical studies of crinecerfont tosylate formulation were associated with coagulopathy
(prolongation of PT and APTT and/or bleeding) and mortality in repeat-dose rat studies.
Subsequently, the tosylate salt formulation was replaced with a free-base form, which was
used for the clinical studies. In chronic rat studies with crinecerfont free base, no mortality or
bleeding effects were noted; however, changes in coagulation parameters (prolongation of PT
up to 60%, and APTT up to 90%) were observed at 1250 mg/kg/day (6-fold MRHD
exposure). Similar findings (prolongation of PT) were observed in the chronic dog study
conducted with crinecerfont free base but without any other coagulopathy up to
1000 mg/kg/day (5-fold MRHD exposure).

•

Neutropenia and white blood cell count findings are discussed in detail in Section 13.7.3.

13.6.3.6.1. Double-Blind Treatment Period
13.6.3.6.1.1. Chemistry Parameters
The mean change in CPK levels from baseline over time was similar in both the crinecerfont and
placebo groups, with a peak at Week 8 in the crinecerfont group (Figure 19). Elevated CPK
values occurred in one subject in both the crinecerfont (1.4%) and placebo (3%) groups during
the 28-week double-blind treatment period, without significant difference between the two
groups (Table 200).
According to the Applicant, the instances of increased CPK levels were associated with
significant physical exertion and an increased isotretinoin dose in one case. The levels improved
with cessation of the inciting factor. No cases of increased CPK resulted in study treatment
discontinuation. There were no reported cases of rhabdomyolysis. The elevated CPK levels are
not likely drug-related because elevated levels were explained by other factors and there is no
mechanistic evidence of causality.

13.6.3.6.1.2. Hematology Parameters
There was no notable difference in mean change or outlier incidence in hemoglobin, hematocrit,
or platelets (see Table 203 in Section 23.4).
There was no notable difference in mean change in coagulation parameters (Figure 20) over the
28-week treatment period. There was a higher incidence of transitions from normal at baseline to
above normal during treatment in elevated PTT for the crinecerfont group (7%) compared to the
placebo group (3%) (Table 62). However, all such excursions were Level 1 in severity and are
not considered clinically meaningful. None of the five subjects with elevated PTT experienced
an adverse event related to hemorrhage.

13.6.3.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial
CAH2006
In rat and dog studies, increased liver weight and hepatocellular hypertrophy were observed,
likely due to crinecerfont’s induction of drug-metabolizing enzymes. Laboratory data were
screened for evidence of drug-induced liver injury to determine cases meeting Hy’s law criteria,
defined as any postbaseline total bilirubin equal to or exceeding 2× ULN after a postbaseline
ALT or AST equal to or exceeding 3× ULN. There were no potential cases of Hy’s Law during
the double-blind (see Figure 21) or open-label treatment periods. In addition, outlier analysis
showed no increased incidence of abnormal liver function tests for the crinecerfont group
compared to placebo (see Figure 21).

the 28-week double-blind treatment period. See Section 23.5 for additional details (Table 85,
Table 86, Table 87, Table 88, and Table 89).

13.7. Key Safety Review Issues
13.7.1. Potential for Adrenal Insufficiency
Issue
Adrenal insufficiency can occur given crinecerfont’s mechanism of action of decreasing pituitary
ACTH levels, leading to reduced adrenal androgen levels, and ultimately allowing for a
reduction in glucocorticoid dose. Acute adrenal insufficiency as a serious adverse event was
observed in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006.
Background
Glucocorticoid deficiency is a clinical feature of CAH and requires replacement glucocorticoid
therapy. Additional glucocorticoid is often needed to lower adrenal androgen levels into the
recommended goal range. By reducing elevated adrenal androgen levels, crinecerfont may allow
for a reduction in glucocorticoid dose to more physiologic levels. Adrenal insufficiency could
occur if the glucocorticoid dose is reduced too much or if an inadequate glucocorticoid dose is
given at times of stress.
Assessment
We devised and performed a customized grouped query of preferred terms that could potentially
signal acute adrenocortical insufficiency for the double-blind treatment periods of both Trials
CAH3003 and CAH2006. Results are shown in Table 69 and Table 70 below.
In Trial CAH3003, adverse events in the adrenal insufficiency grouped query occurred at a
greater frequency in the crinecerfont group (43%) compared to the placebo group (27%) (see
Table 69). In contrast, in Trial CAH2006, adverse events in the grouped query occurred at a
greater frequency in the placebo group (42%) compared to the crinecerfont group (36%). (see
Table 70).
Time of onset of events in the adrenal insufficiency grouped query is shown in the figures below
(Figure 22 and Figure 23). The pattern of time to onset is similar between crinecerfont and
placebo groups in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006.
This grouped query search has important limitations. First, most of the preferred terms are
nonspecific and may not necessarily reflect adrenal insufficiency. Second, it is possible some of
these symptoms could be related to a reduction in the glucocorticoid dose in subjects who are not
adrenally insufficient. Third, these symptoms could occur noncontemporaneously, and therefore
could reflect different clinical entities at different timepoints. Given these limitations, we next
focus on an analysis of specific preferred terms of adrenal insufficiency.

The Applicant provided narratives for all treatment-emergent adverse events with the preferred
terms adrenocortical insufficiency acute and adrenal insufficiency. None were likely drugrelated. In almost all cases, the adrenal crisis was precipitated by an acute illness and was not
adequately treated with stress-dose steroids.
The only case of an adrenal crisis not precipitated by an acute illness was one subject in the
placebo group of Trial CAH3003, who experienced an adrenal crisis during the double-blind
period after stopping her maintenance hydrocortisone upon advice of her endocrinologist (not a
study investigator) because she was thought to be on study drug. This endocrinologist
erroneously assumed that crinecerfont treated all aspects of CAH, including the adrenal
insufficiency. This case illustrates the importance of ensuring patients and healthcare
professionals know to continue at least replacement doses of glucocorticoid therapy while taking
crinecerfont as adjunct therapy to reduce residual androgen excess.
Of the eight subjects experiencing an adrenal crisis in Trial CAH3003 while taking crinecerfont,
all episodes were secondary to an acute illness coupled with lack of adequate stress-dose steroid.
Two episodes of adrenal crisis occurred during the double-blind treatment period, two in the
open-label treatment period, and four in the open-label extension beyond Month 12. One subject
died from his adrenal crisis in the open-label extension period.
Similarly, the two subjects with narratives related to adrenal crisis while taking crinecerfont in
Trial CAH2006 had episodes secondary to acute illness coupled with lack of adequate stress122
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
dose steroid. One episode of adrenal crisis occurred during the open-label treatment period, and
one occurred during the open-label extension beyond Month 12. One subject in Trial CAH3003
experienced a serious TEAE of presyncope during the glucocorticoid reduction period, which is
potentially related to glucocorticoid withdrawal (see Section 13.6.2.3).
Conclusion
In conclusion, adrenal insufficiency does not appear to be drug-related but rather related to the
underlying disease process of CAH, for which glucocorticoid deficiency is a prominent clinical
feature. The adrenal insufficiency case narratives highlight the importance of continuing
physiologic replacement glucocorticoid, not decreasing the glucocorticoid below physiologic
replacement levels, and taking appropriate stress-dose steroids during times of illness. One case
illustrates the importance of ensuring that healthcare professionals know that crinecerfont is
adjunctive therapy to at least replacement doses of glucocorticoid therapy.
Action Taken
•

Added the description of crinecerfont as adjunctive therapy to physiologic glucocorticoid
replacement in the indication statement

•

Ensured directions in the Prescribing Information state not to decrease the glucocorticoid
dose below physiologic replacement levels

•

Ensured directions in the Prescribing Information state that stress-dose glucocorticoid
continues to be necessary during acute illnesses and other situations of increased need

•

Added directions for timing of monitoring of androstenedione levels after initiation of
crinecerfont so the glucocorticoid dose can be evaluated at appropriate time periods

13.7.2. Potential for Hypersensitivity
Background
Throat tightness, perioral edema, and generalized rash (coded as angioedema) occurred in one
subject in a phase 1 study (NBI-74788-1724) of crinecerfont in healthy subjects, prompting
closer evaluation of potential hypersensitivity events in the phase 3 studies of crinecerfont for the
treatment of CAH. The event of angioedema occurred after 3 days of crinecerfont treatment with
100 mg qAM plus 150 mg qPM.
Assessment
To capture potential hypersensitivity events, we examined narrow FMQs within the “immune
system disorders” and “skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders” system organ class (SOC). The
narrow FMQs (and also the preferred terms) “anaphylactic reaction” and “hypersensitivity” fall
under the “immune system disorders” SOC.
During the double-blind treatment period of Trial CAH3003, narrow FMQs within the “skin and
subcutaneous tissue disorders” SOC occurred more frequently (and with similar frequency) in
the placebo group (12%) compared to the crinecerfont group (11%) during the double-blind
period (Table 71). There were no reported AEs within the narrow FMQs in the “immune system
disorders” SOC in either group during the double-blind treatment period of Trial CAH3003.

One Trial CAH3003 subject experienced a rash during the double-blind treatment period (Study
Day 166) that led to study drug discontinuation. The rash was not likely study-drug-related
because skin findings remained present months after study drug discontinuation (see
Section 13.6.2.4.1 for additional details).
In the open-label treatment period of Trial CAH3003, events of anaphylaxis, bullous dermatitis,
and urticaria led to study drug discontinuation. None of the events were likely study-drugrelated. The anaphylactic reaction occurred in a subject with a history of a tree nut allergy and
exposure to tree nuts. Bullous dermatitis (rash with bullous eruptions) was reported in a subject
on Study Day 76 and resolved after about 1 week without treatment or effect on study drug
administration. Urticaria occurred on Study Day 197 and the skin findings were still present
1 month after study drug discontinuation. See Section 13.6.2.4.2 for additional details.
During the double-blind treatment period of Trial CAH2006, narrow FMQs of “hypersensitivity”
and “rash” occurred more frequently in the crinecerfont group versus placebo group (3% versus
0 for “hypersensitivity” and 4% versus 3% for “rash”). However, the two events of
“hypersensitivity” consisted of a reaction to a cat and occurred in the same subject (Table 72).
There were no hypersensitivity-related serious AEs or TEAEs that led to study drug
discontinuation in Trial CAH2006.

13.7.3. Potential for Neutropenia and Reduction in
Total White Blood Cell Count
Background
Neutropenia was observed in a phase 2 study (Study DFI5687) of crinecerfont for major
depressive disorder. The pathophysiology of this observation is unclear.
Issue
Decreased neutrophil counts occurred more frequently in study subjects treated with crinecerfont
compared to placebo in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006. Decrease in mean white blood
count over time was also observed in Trial CAH3003 and was more pronounced in the pediatric
study.
Assessment
In the adult trial (CAH3003), the mean change in neutrophil count was slightly decreased
compared to baseline at Week 24 in the crinecerfont group, but the decrease was not notably
different from placebo Figure 24.

from 5% in the placebo DB group to 19% in the placebo/crinecerfont group. In Trial CAH2006,
the frequency increased from 16% in the placebo DB group to 23% in the placebo/crinecerfont

laboratory assessment.

As shown in Table 80, over the 36-month treatment period, the median white blood count ranged
from 7.6×103 cells/µL at baseline to 7.1×103 cells/µL at Month 36. It is reassuring that the
median count did not continue to decline over this exposure period. It is possible that some of the
decline is due to reduction in glucocorticoid dose in the crinecerfont-treated subjects. Both acute
and chronic treatment with glucocorticoids have been shown to increase peripheral white blood
cell count (Shoenfeld et al. 1981)and it is possible that this slight decline reflects withdrawal of
glucocorticoids rather than an effect of crinecerfont itself.

open-label treatment period was similar to the frequency in the placebo group during the doubleblind treatment period (Table 81).

To further examine the potential signal of reduction in white blood cells (WBCs) with treatment,
laboratory data from the major depression study (Study DFI5687) were reviewed. Adults with
major depressive disorder (N=580) were randomized to receive one of three doses of
crinecerfont (20 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg daily), placebo daily, or escitalopram 10 mg daily, for 8
weeks. Median white blood cell count was stable over 8 weeks of treatment in each crinecerfont
dose group –median values of 5.8 to 6.0×103 cells/µL for the 100 mg group, 6.1 to
6.2×103 cells/µL for the 50 mg group and 5.7 to 6.0×103 cells/µL for the 20 mg group. In this
study, however, subjects received once-daily dosing compared to twice-daily dosing in the CAH
studies.
Conclusion
Decreased neutrophil counts (<2×103 cells/µL) occurred more frequently in study subjects
treated with crinecerfont compared to placebo during the double-blind treatment periods of both
Trials CAH3003 (14% versus 5%) and CAH2006 (37% versus 16%). The frequency increased
from 5% in the placebo DB group to 19% in the placebo/crinecerfont group in Trial CAH3003
134
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
and from 15.6% in the placebo DB group to 26% in the placebo/crinecerfont group in Trial
CAH2006. The clinical significance of these decreased neutrophil counts is unclear, but adverse
event data do not suggest an association with increased bacterial infections occurring in children
in Trial CAH2006
The reduction in WBCs is more pronounced in children, but in both populations the absolute
changes were small, and the absolute values remained within the normal range. Reduced
glucocorticoid dose is a possible explanatory factor for the decreased WBCs observed with
crinecerfont. The change does not appear to be of clinical significance to treated subjects.
Additional postmarketing investigation to evaluate these minor changes in absolute WBC count
is unlikely to yield meaningful data that will change the benefit-risk evaluation of crinecerfont.
Given that the absolute WBC values stayed in the normal range, we are not requesting the
Applicant to include the WBC data in prescribing information.
Action Taken
Added the observation of decreased neutrophil counts to the adverse reactions table in Section 6
(Adverse Reactions) of the Prescribing Information as follows so prescribers are aware that
reductions in neutrophils can occur:
Laboratory Findings
•

Adults with CAH: Neutrophil count less than 2×103 cells/µL occurred in 14% (17 of 120) of
CRENESSITY-treated subjects, compared to 5% (3 of 58) of subjects in the placebo group.
Neutrophil count less than 1×103 cells/µL occurred in 0.8% (1 of 120) of CRENESSITYtreated subjects, compared to 1.7% subjects (1 of 58) in the placebo group.

•

Pediatric subjects with CAH: Neutrophil count less than 2×103 cells/µL occurred in 37% (25
of 68) of CRENESSITY-treated subjects, compared to 16% (5 of 32) of subjects in the
placebo group. Neutrophil count less than 1×103 cells/µL occurred in 4% (3 of 68) of
CRENESSITY-treated subjects, compared to no subjects (0 of 32) in the placebo group.

•

We will also request that the Applicant conduct enhanced pharmacovigilance of
postmarketing safety data for serious adverse events of bacterial infection and concurrent
neutropenia.

13.7.4. Neuropsychiatric Safety Concerns
Issue
A suicide attempt occurred in a Trial CAH3003 subject taking crinecerfont, and more study
subjects taking crinecerfont in both Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006 increased their score on the
Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale compared to placebo.
Background
The Applicant prospectively identified neuropsychiatric safety as a potential concern because
crinecerfont was previously in development as a treatment for depression. The rationale for
studying crinecerfont in major depressive disorder was that evidence suggests that CRF1
receptors in the brain mediate CRF-induced anxiety and depression-like behaviors. According to
135
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
the Applicant’s submission, probes to CRF1 receptors decreased anxiety-like behavior in
stressed rats and CRF1 knockout mice showed less anxiety-like behaviors when stressed.
Despite the drug’s lack of efficacy in the phase 2 major depressive disorder trial, and limited
brain distribution of crinecerfont, the Applicant prospectively monitored for development of
suicidality in Trials CAH3003 and CAH2006 using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale
(C-SSRS).
The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS), a validated instrument to assess suicidal
ideation and behavior, was administered at screening and at regular intervals during treatment.
The C-SSRS consists of a series of six yes/no questions pertaining to suicidal ideation with each
question indicating progressively more severe suicidality. The score ranges from 0 (no thoughts
of suicide) to 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent). See Section 21.3 for the
C-SSRS questionnaire and scoring.
In Trial CAH3003, the C-SSRS was administered at the following intervals (screening; baseline;
Weeks 4, 9, 12, 16, 20, and 24; Months 7, 8, 9, 10, and 12). Subjects with any suicidal behavior
within the past year or suicidal ideation of type 4 (active suicidal ideation with some intent to act,
without specific plan) or type 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent) in the
6 months before screening based on the C-SSRS were excluded from the study. These were also
study drug discontinuation criteria.
In Trial CAH2006, the C-SSRS was administered at the following intervals to individuals aged
>6 years (screening; baseline; Weeks 4, 16, 28, 40, 52, and 56). Subjects aged >6 years with a
lifetime history of suicidal behavior or suicidal ideation of type 4 (active suicidal ideation with
some intent to act, without specific plan) or type 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and
intent) in the 6 months before screening based on the C-SSRS were excluded from the study.
These were also study drug discontinuation criteria.
Assessment
To examine a possible relationship between crinecerfont and neuropsychiatric adverse events
including suicidality, we searched the safety databases of both trials for events coding to the
psychiatric SOC. We also evaluated for subjects who experienced an increase in C-SSRS score
(indicating increased suicidality) while on treatment.
Neuropsychiatric Adverse Events
A subject in Trial CAH3003 attempted suicide by taking 19 tramadol tablets and thiocodin while
on crinecerfont:
•

The serious adverse event of suicide attempt involved a 29-year-old female with a history of
acne who had received crinecerfont 100 mg bid starting in the double-blind treatment period
and continuing during the open-label treatment period. Concomitant medications
administered within 30 days of the event included hydrocortisone and paracetamol/tramadol.
On Study Day 320 (also Day 320 of study drug administration), she was hospitalized after
taking 19 tramadol tablets and thiocodin and intentionally injuring her arm. Three days prior
to hospital admission the subject had ended a seven-year romantic relationship and as a
result, experienced significant deterioration of her mental condition. Computed tomography

136
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
scanning showed cortical brain atrophy. Study drug was discontinued because of the suicide
attempt. The investigator considered the suicide attempt to be unrelated to study treatment.
Another Trial CAH3003 subject discontinued crinecerfont because of restlessness and apathy.
His C-SSRS score increased from 0 at baseline to 2 (nonspecific active suicidal thoughts).
A subject in Trial CAH2006 who reportedly discontinued crinecerfont for dizziness, nausea,
motion sickness, and retching also experienced anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation.
Narrow FMQs of the psychiatric SOC occurred more frequently in the placebo group (20.3%)

A greater proportion of subjects in both Trial CAH3003 and Trial CAH2006 reported any
suicidality, measured as any score above zero on the C-SSRS compared to placebo (Table 89).
All study subjects had a baseline score of 0 except for one crinecerfont-treated subject in Trial

CAH3003 who had a baseline score of 1 (wish to be dead). This subject’s score shifted to 0

In Trial CAH3003, three subjects (3/120=2.5%) in the crinecerfont group had a C-SSRS score
shift from 0 to a maximum of 2 (nonspecific active suicidal thoughts) versus one subject

behavior. No subjects had an increase in their C-SSRS score during the open-label treatment
period as of the data cut-off date.

placebo group had a C-SSRS score shift from 0 at baseline to a maximum above 0 during the 28week double-blind treatment period. Two subjects in the crinecerfont group shifted from a
baseline C-SSRS score of 0 to a maximum of 1 (wish to be dead) and two shifted to a maximum
of 2 (nonspecific active suicidal thoughts) versus none (0/31) in the placebo group. Two of the
four subjects had a lifetime history of suicidal ideation. At baseline, four subjects (4/63=6%) in
the crinecerfont group versus none (0/31=0%) in the placebo group had a lifetime history of

the open-label treatment period, prior to the data cut-off date, one subject shifted their C-SSRS
score from 0 at baseline to 3 (active suicidal ideation with any methods [not plan] without intent
to act).

Regulatory Tracking System (DARRTS) on November 25, 2024. The Division of Psychiatry

Conclusion
A serious AE of suicide attempt occurred in a study subject taking study drug. Suicidal ideation,
measured by a score above 0 on the C-SSRS, occurred in very few subjects, some of whom had a
history of suicidality. The very low event rates significantly limit conclusions, but a suicidality
risk cannot be definitively excluded.
Action Taken
Added the following to Section 6.1 (Adverse Reactions) of the label:
Suicidal Ideation and Behavior
•

Adults with CAH: Study 1 excluded subjects with active suicidal ideation with intent or plan
within the six months prior to screening and those with a history of suicidal behavior within
the past year, based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) administered
at screening. The C-SSRS was administered to subjects at regular intervals during the study.
Three of 122 (2.5%) CRENESSITY-treated subjects reported suicidal ideation without
method, intent, or plan on the C-SSRS during the 24-week double-blind treatment period
compared to 1 of 59 (1.7%) placebo-treated subjects. One of the three subjects receiving
CRENESSITY and the placebo treated subject reported a lifetime history of suicidal ideation.
One CRENESSITY-treated subject without a history of suicidal ideation or behavior
attempted suicide during the open-label period after 320 days of treatment.

•

Pediatric subjects with CAH: Study 2 excluded subjects with active suicidal ideation with
intent or plan within six months prior to screening or those with a lifetime history of suicidal
behavior within the past year, based on the C-SSRS administered at screening. Four of 67
(6%) CRENESSITY-treated subjects and 0 of the 31 (0%) placebo-treated subjects reported
suicidal ideation without method, intent, or plan on the C-SSRS during the 28-week double
blind treatment period. Two of the four CRENESSITY-treated subjects reported a lifetime
history of suicidal ideation. There were no completed suicides or suicide attempts.

•

We will also request that the Applicant conduct enhanced pharmacovigilance of
postmarketing safety data for serious and non-serious adverse events of suicidal behavior
and/or ideation.

14. Therapeutic Individualization
14.1. Intrinsic Factors
Hepatic Impairment
Study NBI-74788-1717 was a phase 1, single-dose, open-label study comparing the PK of
crinecerfont in subjects with normal hepatic function (n=6) and mild (n=6), moderate (n=6), and
severe hepatic impairment (n=7). All subjects received 100 mg (two 50-mg capsules)
crinecerfont with Ensure Plus (350 calories, 11 grams total fat, 20 grams sugars, 13 grams
protein, and 50 grams carbohydrate). PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points from
predose to 504 hours postdose. Based on the study results, the mean AUC0-∞ was 27%, 34%, and
20% lower in the mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment groups, respectively, as
compared to the normal hepatic function group. The 90% CI values for the geometric mean
ratios (GMRs) for Cmax, AUCtlast, and AUC0-∞ for all the hepatic impairment groups as compared
to the normal hepatic function group included unity (Table 90, see details in Section 20.2.5).
Therefore, we conclude that hepatic impairment does not have a clinically significant impact on
crinecerfont PK and agree with the Applicant’s proposed labeling that no dose adjustment of
crinecerfont is necessary in patients with mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment.

Renal Impairment
The Applicant did not conduct a dedicated renal impairment study. Per the Applicant, the mass
balance study (BEX5094) suggested limited renal elimination. In Study BEX5094, a single dose
of 100-mg crinecerfont capsule with 2.59 MBq (70 µCi) [14C]-crinecerfont was administered
with a high-fat breakfast. PK samples were collected at prespecified times from 1- to 3-day
intervals through Day 37 postdose. The recovery of radioactivity was not complete by Day 37,
and only 49.4% of the administered dose was recovered on average. Of the total amount of
radioactivity recovered, 47.3% of the administered dose was recovered in the feces and less than
2% (mainly as metabolites with undetectable crinecerfont) was recovered in the urine (see
Section 20.2.14). Despite the limitations of the mass balance study, considering the negligible
amount of crinecerfont in the urine, the review team agrees that renal excretion is unlikely to
significantly contribute to the elimination of crinecerfont.
142
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
The popPK analysis included estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR; Chronic Kidney
Disease Epidemiology Collaboration 2009 formula for adult subjects and bedside Schwartz
formula for pediatric subjects) as a covariate for crinecerfont clearance. The range of eGFR
(indexed to BSA) was evaluated against random effect of crinecerfont apparent clearance (in the
base popPK model), and no obvious trend was observed. Additionally, the 95% CI of the eGFR
effect on crinecerfont clearance included the null effect of zero, indicating minimal effect of
eGFR on crinecerfont PK (refer to Section 20.5). Based on covariate effect assessment shown in
Figure 28, the median AUC24 for crinecerfont in subjects with mild and moderate renal
impairment were 0.973 and 0.916, respectively of the median crinecerfont AUC24 in subjects
with normal renal function. The 95% confidence intervals included 1, indicating no statistically
significant impact on crinecerfont AUC24 due to mild to moderate renal impairment. Of note,
only a limited number of subjects with moderate renal impairment (n=2, based on BSA-indexed
eGFR) in the popPK analysis contributed to a relatively wide 95% CI for the estimated moderate
renal impairment impact on crinecerfont AUC (Figure 28).
Overall, mild to moderate renal impairment is unlikely to have clinically meaningful impact on
crinecerfont exposure. Therefore, the review team agrees with the proposed labeling that no dose
adjustment for crinecerfont is needed in patients with mild or moderate renal impairment.
Crinecerfont was not studied in patients with severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease.
According to the FDA’s guidance for industry Pharmacokinetics in Patients With Impaired
Renal Function (March 2024), impaired renal function can be associated with changes in
absorption, plasma protein binding, or alterations in some drug metabolism and transport
pathways in the liver and gut. These changes can be particularly prominent in patients with
severely impaired renal function and those with kidney failure. Considering the potential impact
of severe renal impairment on the PK of crinecerfont, and the lack of experience in these
patients, the review team recommends avoiding the use of crinecerfont in patients with severe
renal impairment and end-stage renal disease.

Other Intrinsic Factors
Based on popPK analysis, no clinically significant differences in the PK of crinecerfont were
observed based on age (range: 5 to 54 years), sex (58.7% male), and race (4.8% Asian, 9.7%
Black, 77.5% White).
Body weight is a significant PK covariate of crinecerfont. Therefore, weight-band dosing in
pediatric patients is proposed to account for the weight impact on crinecerfont PK (refer to
Sections 12.1.1, 12.1.3, and 20.5).

14.2. Extrinsic Factors
Food Effect
Food has a significant impact on crinecerfont absorption. In Study NBI-74788-1736 (n=19), a
single dose of crinecerfont 100-mg commercial capsule was administered with a high-fat, highcalorie meal or under fasted conditions. The GMRs for AUC0-tlast, AUC0-∞, and Cmax were 3.78,
3.27, and 4.95, respectively, in the fed state compared to the fasted state (Table 91). A similar
magnitude of food effect was observed with earlier capsule formulations (Studies NBI-747881712 and NBI-7478-1601, see Sections 20.2.3 and 20.2.1).

Based on significantly enhanced bioavailability of crinecerfont for both oral solution and capsule
formulations, pediatric and adult subjects with CAH were instructed to take crinecerfont with
breakfast and dinner in the pivotal clinical trials, CAH2006 and CAH3003. Additionally, popPK
analysis indicates that fasted status (relative to fed status) has a clinically meaningful reduction
in crinecerfont exposure (Figure 28). Overall, the review team agrees with the proposed labeling
that crinecerfont should be administered with food.
Drug Interactions
Crinecerfont as a Victim
Based on in vitro studies, crinecerfont is metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 (fraction
metabolized [fm] ~68 to 74%) and to a lesser extent by CYP2B6 (fm~11 to 25%). Crinecerfont is
not a substrate for transporters including P-glycoprotein (P-gp), breast cancer resistance protein
(BCRP), bile salt export pump (BSEP), organic anion transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, or
OATP1B3. Metabolism studies in vitro identified a single active metabolite, M6, with a similar
affinity for the CRF1 receptor compared to the parent drug. However, due to limited systemic
exposure (i.e., approximately 6% relative to crinecerfont), M6 is not expected to significantly
contribute to the pharmacological activity of crinecerfont.
Effect of Strong CYP3A Inhibition on Crinecerfont PK
Study INT5449 evaluated the effect of a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (ketoconazole) on crinecerfont
PK in 16 healthy subjects. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 50 mg crinecerfont was
administered with a moderate fat breakfast. Following a 22-day washout period, in treatment
period 2, ketoconazole 400 mg once daily was administered for 5 days with standardized
breakfast, and on Day 6 subjects received ketoconazole 400 mg and 50 mg crinecerfont with a
moderate-fat breakfast. Ketoconazole dosing continued from Day 7 to Day 14 of treatment
period 2. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours postdose. The
study results show that coadministration with ketoconazole increased crinecerfont AUC and Cmax
by ~45% and ~25% respectively (Table 94, see details in Section 20.2.15). According to the
International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guideline M12 Drug Interaction Studies (May
2024), “Sensitive index substrates are index drugs that demonstrate an increase in area under the
concentration versus time curve (AUC) of greater than or equal to 5-fold with strong index
inhibitors of a given metabolic pathway in clinical DDI [drug-drug interaction] studies.”
Therefore, crinecerfont is not considered a sensitive CYP3A substrate.
