In terms of clinical relevance of the DDI, crinecerfont has been studied at daily doses of 300 mg
for 28 days, and no major safety concerns were identified. Additionally, in the open-label
extension of Trial CAH3003, subjects with CAH who did not have adequate treatment response
to crinecerfont were allowed to have a 50% dose increase (e.g., increase from 100 mg bid to 100
mg in the morning and 200 mg in the evening). Therefore, the 45% exposure increase when
coadministered with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor is not expected to fall outside the safety margin
seen in the subjects studied and does not necessitate dose adjustment.

Effect of Strong CYP3A Induction on Crinecerfont PK
Study NBI-74788-1718 investigated the effect of a strong CYP3A4 inducer (rifampin) on
crinecerfont PK in 16 healthy subjects. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 100 mg
crinecerfont was administered with Ensure Plus. Following a 21-day washout period in treatment
period 2, subjects received 600 mg rifampin once daily for 29 days in the fasted state. On Day 9
of period 2, subjects received 100 mg crinecerfont 2 hours after rifampin dosing with Ensure
Plus. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours postdose. The study
results show that coadministration with rifampin decreased crinecerfont AUC by ~62% and Cmax
by ~23% (Table 94).
From a clinical perspective, coadministration of crinecerfont with a strong CYP3A4 inducer
(rifampin) has a significant impact on the exposure of crinecerfont. Based on the magnitude of
exposure reduction, a 2-fold dose increase is necessary to maintain crinecerfont exposure at
levels high enough to be effective. The review team agrees with the Applicant’s proposed
labeling language that crinecerfont dosage should be increased 2-fold (e.g., 200 mg bid in adults)
in subjects on concomitant strong CYP3A4 inducers.

Effect of Moderate CYP3A Induction on Crinecerfont PK
The Applicant did not conduct any clinical DDI studies with moderate CYP3A4 inducers. In
Trial CAH3003, 17 adult subjects were on dexamethasone with or without other glucocorticoids
at the time of enrollment. The Applicant considered dexamethasone as a moderate CYP3A
(b) (4)
inducer

The review team did not agree with the Applicant’s approach based on the following
considerations.

(b) (4)

Despite no observed data to support the dose adjustment for crinecerfont when taken with
moderate CYP3A inducers, the review team expects a reduction of less than 50% in crinecerfont
exposure due to moderate CYP3A induction, considering that (1) crinecerfont is not a sensitive
CYP3A substrate and (2) per the DDI guideline (May 2024), a moderate CYP3A inducer is
defined as decreasing exposure of sensitive CYP3A substrates by 50 to 80%. Thus, the review
team recommends that crinecerfont dosage needs to be adjusted in patients taking moderate
CYP3A4 inducers. For example, the current dosage of 100 mg twice daily with morning and
evening meals should be changed to 100 mg with the morning meal and 200 mg with the evening
meal. Increasing the crinecerfont dose by 50% will ensure clinical benefit in this patient
population.
Crinecerfont as a Perpetrator

maximal clinical dose of 100 mg twice daily. For Study INT6752, the review team concluded
that crinecerfont is a weak CYP3A inhibitor at clinically relevant doses. Based on FDA guidance
on drug interactions with COC (June 2023), weak CYP3A inhibitors are unlikely to cause a
clinically significant increase in COC exposures. Therefore, the review team concludes that
crinecerfont at clinically relevant doses is not expected to affect the PK of COCs containing
ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel.

Effect of Crinecerfont on PK of Glucocorticoids
Glucocorticoids, which are the current standard of care for the treatment of CAH and will be
coadministered with crinecerfont in the target patient population, are generally not sensitive
CYP3A4 substrates. Based on the study results from the midazolam study (sensitive CYP3A4
substrate) and the oral contraceptive study (nonsensitive CYP3A4 substrate), coadministration
with crinecerfont is unlikely to have clinically significant impact on glucocorticoid exposure.
Effect of Crinecerfont on Other CYP Enzymes and Transporters
Crinecerfont is unlikely to induce CYP3A, CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2B6 or inhibit CYP1A2,
CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1 at clinically relevant doses.
Crinecerfont is not an inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, organic anion
transporter (OAT) 1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT) 2, multidrug and toxin extrusion
transporter (MATE) 1, or MATE2-K.

14.3. Plans for Pediatric Drug Development
The proposed indication includes pediatric patients aged 4 years and older. Because crinecerfont
received orphan drug designation, Pediatric Research Equity Act requirements are not triggered
by this application and an agreed pediatric study plan is not required.

14.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males
of Reproductive Potential
The Division of General Endocrinology consulted the Division of Pediatrics and Maternal Health
(DPMH) for review of the nonclinical and clinical pregnancy and lactation data, and for
recommendations on appropriate language for Section 8 (Use in Special Populations) of the
prescribing information based on those data. DPMH also commented on the necessity for
postmarketing studies to further evaluate the safety of crinecerfont in the setting of pregnancy
and lactation.
Their findings regarding each subsection of Section 8 of the label are discussed below.
Pregnancy
Animal Data
Distribution studies in animals indicated that crinecerfont crosses the placenta and is detected at
low levels in fetuses of pregnant rats and rabbits.
Crinecerfont administered during the period of organogenesis in pregnant rats did not result in
embryotoxicity or fetal structural malformations at approximately 4 times MRHD exposures. A
low incidence of malformations (primarily craniofacial defects) was observed in rabbits at
clinically relevant exposures. The incidence of findings in rabbit fetuses was low but exceeded
concurrent and historical controls and, therefore, a relationship to crinecerfont cannot be
excluded. In a pre- and postnatal developmental toxicity study, no developmental toxicity was
observed in rats at 4-fold the MRHD based on exposure.

(b) (6)

1 month after receiving moxifloxacin. Study treatment was discontinued. The subject was

(b) (6)

– A 32-year-old female (Subject
) was found to be pregnant (approximately 5 to

Month 18 visit. Subsequently, she underwent an uncomplicated C-section and delivered a

Lactation
Animal Data
There were no adverse effects on pre- and postnatal development in developing rats when dams
were administered crinecerfont during pregnancy and lactation. Fetuses were exposed to
crinecerfont in utero and through lactation until weaning. Crinecerfont was secreted in the milk
of lactating rats, with a milk-to-plasma ratio of 1.5 to 12.
Human Data
No cases related to crinecerfont use during lactation occurred during drug development.
Females and Males of Reproductive Potential
Animal Data
There were no effects on mating or fertility in male or female rats treated with crinecerfont prior
to mating, with continued treatment in females throughout the early embryonic development
period.

In Subsection 8.2 of the label, include that there are no data regarding the presence of

was excreted in animal milk, the drug is likely be present in human milk.

•

Include text in labeling about monitoring infants exposed to crinecerfont through breast milk
for signs and symptoms of adrenal insufficiency.

•

A PMR for a clinical lactation study to determine the extent to which crinecerfont is present
in human milk is warranted.

III. Additional Analyses and Information
18. Summary of Regulatory History
Crinecerfont (NBI-74788) is a small molecule, selective antagonist of the corticotropin-releasing
factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor. Sanofi (formerly Sanofi-Synthelabo, Inc., and then Sanofi Aventis
US Inc.) originally developed NBI-74788 (then known as SSR125543) and initiated its clinical
(b) (4)
development for the treatment of major depressive disorder in May 2005 under IND
(b) (4)
regulated by the Division of Psychiatry Products. Sanofi withdrew the IND
Neurocrine Biosciences, Inc. (Neurocrine) licensed the compound from Sanofi
in 2015.
The IND application 132849 was submitted by the Sponsor, Neurocrine, on December 23, 2016,
to investigate crinecerfont (NBI-74788) for the treatment for congenital adrenal hyperplasia
(b) (4)
(CAH)
On March 16,
2017, following review of the initial IND, FDA issued nonhold comments and requests for
additional information regarding quality, nonclinical, and clinical topics.
On April 16, 2018, a preliminary breakthrough therapy designation (BTD) request
teleconference was held. FDA determined it was premature to submit a BTD request and the
drug/indication did not meet breakthrough criteria at that stage of development. Three reasons
were provided for discouraging the Sponsor from submitting a BTD request at this stage of
development:
•

CAH is a serious and life-threatening condition because it is associated with adrenal
insufficiency; however, the Sponsor’s study drug has the potential to decrease androgen
levels but does not treat adrenal insufficiency.

•

Approved therapies for treatment of CAH exist and are considered standard of care for this
disease (e.g., glucocorticoid [GC] and mineralocorticoid replacement drugs).

•

There is no evidence to date that the Sponsor’s study drug provides a significant clinical
benefit over existing therapies. This drug has been shown to decrease levels of a surrogate
biomarker, 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP), in adults with classic CAH in a phase 1b
proof-of-concept study. More clinical evidence is needed to demonstrate effects of this drug
on a clinically significant endpoint (for example, reduction in GC requirements that will be
associated with reduction in frequency or severity of adverse events related to GC
overreplacement, or improvement in symptoms related to CAH).

On November 7, 2018, the Sponsor requested a Type C written responses only meeting, to
address the Division of General Endocrinology’s (DGE’s) nonclinical comment regarding new
excipients in drug formulations used in the IND-opening study and to obtain agreement on the
appropriateness of the drug product formulation proposed for use in the long-duration phase 3
clinical studies and in a commercial setting in adult and pediatric subjects. FDA agreed that the
(b) (4)
amount of medium-chain triglycerides, lauroyl polyoxylglycerides, and
excipients
in the proposed formulation present no specific safety concerns for chronic oral use. Also, the
(b) (4)
Sponsor’s proposed excipient propylene glycol dicaprylocaprate
and its daily

within the publicly available and manufacturer-supplied literature to support safety.
On March 15, 2019, Orphan Drug designation was granted to crinecerfont for the treatment of

On April 24, 2019, the Sponsor submitted a Fast Track designation request. They identified CAH
as a serious condition and hypothesized that treatment with crinecerfont may potentially decrease
the need for supraphysiologic glucocorticoid regimen to suppress hyperandrogenism in patients
with CAH. The request was denied due to the limited data provided from the ongoing phase 2
trial, NBI-74788-CAH2001 (hereafter Trial CAH2001), regarding the potential of crinecerfont to
provide a clinically meaningful benefit, or to address an unmet medical need in the patients with
CAH population, or to address a serious aspect of CAH. The denial letter was issued on June 20,
2019.
On May 29, 2019, the Sponsor requested a Type C meeting, to discuss and obtain agreement on
the nonclinical and clinical development plan to support an NDA for the treatment of CAH. A
written response letter was issued, August 12, 2019, to address the Sponsor’s questions regarding
the proposed product development plans. In brief, DGE communicated agreement that
glucocorticoid dose reduction may be clinically beneficial in patients with CAH and that
assessment of glucocorticoid dose reduction and control of adrenal steroid hormone levels was
an acceptable approach for the planned phase 3 registration study. Also, DGE agreed that the
nonclinical program as described in the meeting briefing materials, as well as the number of
subjects and duration of exposures in the clinical safety database, were sufficient to support an

evaluation.

19.1. Summary Review of Studies Submitted With
the Investigational New Drug Application
Crinecerfont is a selective antagonist of CRF1 receptors. Crinecerfont blocks the binding of CRF
to CRF1 receptors in the pituitary but not to CRF2 receptors. Studies in the nonclinical program
to support crinecerfont clinical studies were conducted with different salt forms of crinecerfont.
The primary pharmacology studies were mainly conducted with crinecerfont hydrochloride

19.1.1. ADME/PK
Crinecerfont absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) and PK parameters
were characterized in a series of in vitro and in vivo studies. In vivo studies were conducted in
rat, dog, mouse, rabbit, and monkeys. The nonclinical PK studies are summarized below.
Absorption
Crinecerfont absorption and pharmacokinetics were evaluated in vitro and in nonclinical species
using intravenous (IV) and oral administration of crinecerfont. An in vitro study in colorectal
adenocarcinoma (Caco)-2-TC7 cells with [14C]-crinecerfont tosylate showed that crinecerfont
membrane permeability was low and that crinecerfont was not a substrate for P-glycoprotein (Pgp) transporter. Single-dose in vivo PK studies were conducted with tosylate salt and free-base
crinecerfont following oral (PO) or IV administration. Bioavailability from oral dosing was 53%
in rats, 14% in rabbits, and 19% in dogs for tosylate salt, and 49% in monkey for free base.
(b) (4)
Absorption was higher for free-base crinecerfont in
formulation and when administered
with food. The half-life (t1/2) of crinecerfont following single oral or IV administration was 8
hours in mice, 13 to 24 hours in rat, 8 hours in rabbits, 24 to 90 hours in dogs, and 5 to 13 hours
in monkeys. The time to reach maximum observed plasma concentration (Tmax) following a
single oral administration of crinecerfont tosylate ranged from 2 to 6 hours. In general, exposure
of crinecerfont increased less than dose-proportionally and approached saturation or plateaued as
dose increased. In repeated-dose toxicokinetic (TK) analyses in toxicity studies, no accumulation
was observed in rats when crinecerfont was administered as the tosylate salt. Modest
(b) (4)
accumulation was observed for free base administered as
at 5, 15, and 50 mg/kg/day
doses (less than 3-fold accumulation), with a decrease in exposure observed at the high dose after
repeat doses. Exposure was not sex-dependent in rats, but exposure was slightly higher in female
dogs compared to males (<2-fold).
Distribution
Crinecerfont distribution was evaluated in in vitro and in vivo studies, including by whole-body
imaging, tissue distribution and placenta transfer studies. In in vitro binding assays, crinecerfont
exhibited high plasma protein binding with ≥99.9% bound in mouse, rat, rabbit, and human
plasma independent of drug concentration. Distribution to blood cellular components was low,
with blood cell-to-plasma ratios of 0.18 in mouse, 0.17 in rat, 0.14 in dog and 0.08 in human. In
vivo studies in rat and dog demonstrated that there was no significant binding of crinecerfont to
erythrocytes. Crinecerfont was widely distributed in liver, adrenal gland, lung, spleen,
myocardium, fat, and the lymphatic system in tissue distribution studies after oral or IV

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
administration. Crinecerfont crossed the placenta and distributed to the fetal liver (at low levels)
in pregnant rats and rabbits. Low crinecerfont exposure was observed in brain, skin, and testis.
The brain-to-plasma exposure ratio in rat was 0.1 compared to the liver-to-plasma exposure ratio
of ≥8.5.
Metabolism
The metabolism of crinecerfont was evaluated in vitro using liver microsomes and hepatocytes
and in vivo in mouse, rat, rabbit, dog, and monkey. The metabolism of crinecerfont was similar
among species, with no unique or disproportionate human metabolites (Figure 29). Crinecerfont
was primarily biotransformed by phase 1 metabolism (hydroxylation of the fluorophenyl moiety
and N-depropargylation) by cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4, and to a lesser extent by CYP2B6.
The most abundant metabolite, M6 (NBI-756179), was formed by hydroxylation of the
fluorophenyl moiety and represented 6% of human crinecerfont exposure. M6 bound to CRF1
receptors with nanomolar affinity (Ki =1.14nM), which, coupled with a relatively slow
dissociation rate of 0.01 min-1, resulted in a relatively longer receptor residence time (t1/2 of ~63
minutes). Due to its low abundance, the contribution of M6 to CRF1 receptor antagonist activity
was considered minor. In vitro studies showed crinecerfont exhibited low potential for drug-drug
interaction (DDI) based on limited evidence of inhibition or induction of CYP enzymes or drug
transporters.

Excretion
Crinecerfont excretion studies were conducted in mouse, rat, and dog using [14C]-crinecerfont
tosylate. Crinecerfont was mainly excreted through feces in mouse, rat, and dog, indicating
clearance mainly through hepatobiliary system. Renal excretion was negligible (<2%). The
elimination rate of crinecerfont was slow. The recovery of an orally administered dose of
[14C]-crinecerfont was not complete at 1 week in rats, with about 10% of radioactivity remaining
in the tissues in males and 25% in females. In a dog study, 80% of [14C]-crinecerfont
administered orally was recovered at 2 weeks. Crinecerfont was excreted in the milk of rats with
a milk-to-plasma ratio of 1.5 to 12.

19.1.2. Toxicokinetic Data
The TK data from pivotal toxicology studies are summarized under the respective toxicological
study review in Section 19.1.7. TK results from pivotal 6-month rat and 12-month dog studies
are presented in Table 97 and Table 98 below. In general, crinecerfont exposure increases with
dose but in a less than dose-proportional manner following oral administration of crinecerfont
free base both in rats and dogs. In rats, a 25-fold increase in dose resulted in less than a 4-fold
increase in exposure, reaching saturation at doses ≥250 mg/kg/day. No significant accumulation
was observed after repeated oral administration of crinecerfont free base in 6-month rat study. In
dogs, a 10-fold increase in dose resulted in up to a 2-fold increase in exposure and approached
saturation at doses ≥300 mg/kg/day. Accumulation of up to 2-fold was observed in the 12-month
dog study.

19.1.3. Primary Pharmacology
Crinecerfont is a selective antagonist of CRF1 receptors. Crinecerfont blocks the binding of CRF
to CRF1 receptors in the pituitary but not to CRF2 receptors. Data from a series of in vitro and in
vivo nonclinical pharmacology studies of crinecerfont were provided by the Applicant to
demonstrate the pharmacological effects of crinecerfont. Primary pharmacological studies were
conducted with crinecerfont HCl. These studies demonstrated that crinecerfont inhibits CRF1
receptors and antagonizes CRF-induced cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) synthesis and
ACTH secretion from pituitary, and blocks stress-induced increases in ACTH in rats (Table 99).
In the absence of stress or exogenous ACTH stimulation, crinecerfont had no effect on basal
ACTH or adrenal hormones, suggesting low potential for adrenal insufficiency based on
mechanism of action of crinecerfont. No signs of adrenal insufficiency were observed in
pharmacology (or toxicology) studies in vivo.

19.1.4. Secondary Pharmacology
The off-target activity of crinecerfont was evaluated by in vitro binding and enzyme activity
assays for 10 receptors and 12 enzymes, and by binding assays against more than 100 receptors,
transporters, enzymes, and ion channels. Crinecerfont (10µM) inhibited acetylcholinesterase
activity (88% inhibition), the sigma-1 receptor (54% inhibition), and the serotonin transporter
(half-maximal inhibitory concentration [IC50] of 3.0µM). Crinecerfont did not show any effect
on contractility of isolated pig vas deferens up to 10µM, indicating lack of notable functional
effects on the sigma-1 receptor. The potential off-target effects of crinecerfont on
acetylcholinesterase and serotonin transporter were considered negligible when the micromolar
affinity of crinecerfont to the nonspecific targets was compared with nanomolar affinity to CRF1
receptors. Therefore, clinically relevant off-target activities of crinecerfont were not identified.

19.1.5. Safety Pharmacology
Crinecerfont’s effects on cardiovascular, autonomic nervous system, central nervous system
(CNS), respiratory, renal, and gastrointestinal (GI) systems were assessed using in vitro and in
vivo safety pharmacology studies (Table 100). Crinecerfont tosylate salt was used in safety
pharmacology studies. No significant acute effects were observed on neurobehavioral function in
rats, cardiovascular function in dogs, respiratory function in guinea pigs, renal function in rats, or
gastrointestinal function in rats at clinically relevant doses. Crinecerfont showed no potential for
clinical arrhythmia risk based on human ether-à-go-go-related gene (hERG) current (<5%
inhibition) or isolated rabbit Purkinje fiber action potential assays at up to 10µM crinecerfont
concentrations. Respiratory depression (increased inspiratory, expiratory, and relaxation times,
accompanied by airway obstruction indicated by increased pause and enhanced pause) was
observed in anesthetized guinea pigs at a 1000 mg/kg oral dose. No effects on respiratory
parameters were observed at doses ≤100 mg/kg (0.2-fold maximum recommended human dose
[MRHD]). Anesthetized guinea pigs may have been more sensitive to crinecerfont than other
species, as all animals had tonal loss in hind paws under sedation. There were no significant
effects of crinecerfont on the respiratory system in repeat-dose toxicity studies in mice, rats, and
dogs, indicating the respiratory safety risk of crinecerfont is low. Overall, the safety
pharmacology data supported crinecerfont clinical investigations and no remarkable acute safety
concerns were identified at clinically relevant exposure levels.

19.1.6. Pharmacodynamic Drug Interactions
No data were provided on nonclinical pharmacodynamic drug interactions.

19.1.7. Toxicology
19.1.7.1. General Toxicology
The toxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated in a series of single- and repeat-dose studies in mice,
rats, and dogs. The target organs for crinecerfont were liver (mouse, rat, and dog), thyroid gland
(rat and dog), and GI tract (mouse and rat). In early toxicology studies in rats with the tosylate
salt, crinecerfont was associated with mortality due to hemorrhage and changes in coagulation
parameters (increase in fibrinogen and prolonged prothrombin time [PT] and activated partial
thromboplastin time [APTT]), in addition to the findings in liver, thyroid gland, and GI tract. The
bleeding adverse effects were not observed in the pivotal nonclinical studies conducted with
free-base crinecerfont, the form of crinecerfont proposed for the commercial drug product. The
assessment of the pivotal chronic 6-month rat and 12-month dog studies are summarized in
Sections 19.1.7.1.1 and 19.1.7.1.3, respectively.
19.1.7.1.1. 6-Month Oral Toxicity Study in Rats With a 6Week Recovery Period, Study TXC1269
Key Findings
The 6-month rat study was conducted with a once-daily oral gavage dose of 0, 50, 250 or
1250 mg/kg crinecerfont free base. No crinecerfont-related mortality or clinical signs were
observed. Crinecerfont was associated with partially reversible mild hematological changes
(decreased red blood cell parameters and increased lymphocytes at ≥250 mg/kg/day, at exposure
≥7-fold MRHD). Marked increases in PT (+52 to 60%) and APTT (+80 to 90%) were noted in

Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
males at ≥250 mg/kg/day (total exposure ≥7-fold MRHD) without any signs of hemorrhage,
which were likely associated with changes in liver function.
Crinecerfont was associated with partially reversible minimal to moderate liver lesions
(centrilobular hypertrophy, vacuolation, multinucleated hepatocytes, hepatocyte anisokaryosis,
and minimal hepatocyte necrosis) that correlated with liver enlargement and change in clinical
chemistry (such as increased γ-glutamyl transferase, cholesterol, and decreased triglycerides) in
all dose groups (≥50 mg/kg/day, 4-fold MRHD). The liver findings were mainly related to the
induction of hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes, which was consistent with the finding of the
decrease in exposure following repeated dosing in rats.
Reversible minimal to mild thyroid follicular cell hyperplasia was observed in males at
1250 mg/kg/day (7-fold MRHD) and in females at ≥50 mg/kg/day (4-fold MRHD) with doserelated increase in incidence and severity, and may be secondary to liver enzyme induction (Wu
and Farrelly 2006).
Crinecerfont was associated with forestomach lesions which included epithelial hyperplasia with
hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and/or dyskeratosis to erosion, ulceration, and epithelial necrosis.
The forestomach lesions were observed in all groups (≥50 mg/kg/day, 4-fold MRHD), and in the
vehicle control group, with increasing incidence and severity with increasing dose of
crinecerfont. One control female found dead on Day 116 had stomach perforations possibly
related to the irritant action of the vehicle or to trauma. The lesion in rat forestomach was
considered species-specific and may not be clinically relevant based on the absence of a
nonglandular stomach in humans and the tolerability of the final clinical oral formulations.
Crinecerfont exposure saturation was observed in both sexes at doses ≥250 mg/kg. The NOAEL
was not determined (≤50 mg/kg/day) for this study, and the exposure multiple for this study was
≤4-fold at MRHD. In a complementary 6-month rat study, the NOAEL was 15 mg/kg/day with
exposure comparable to the MRHD (see below, Section 19.1.7.1.2).

8-Week Recovery Period, Study TXC1204
Key Findings
The 12-month dog study was conducted with once-daily oral gavage doses of 100, 300 or
1000 mg/kg crinecerfont. Crinecerfont caused reversible minimal to moderate liver lesions
(centrilobular hypertrophy, eosinophilic droplets, and pigmented hepatocytes) that correlated
with liver enlargement and change in clinical chemistry (such as increased alkaline phosphatase
and decreased albumin) at ≥100 mg/kg/day. Mild decreases in red cell parameters and increases
in platelets were noted at ≥100 mg/kg/day. All the findings observed were not considered
adverse effects based on their low magnitude, low incidence, reversibility, and/or lack of dose
response. The NOAEL for this study was 1000 mg/kg/day. The AUC24 values at the NOAEL
were 399,000 ng∙hr/mL for males and 804,000 ng∙hr/mL for females. The safety margin based on
exposure was ~4-fold, which was calculated using the AUC24=399,000 ng∙hr/mL (males) at
NOAEL and human PK AUC24=88,802 ng∙hr/mg.9

19.1.7.3. Carcinogenicity
The Applicant evaluated the oncogenic potential of crinecerfont by conducting 2-year rat and
6-month transgenic mouse carcinogenicity studies. Crinecerfont did not increase the incidence of
tumors in Tg.rasH2 mice treated for 26 weeks at oral doses of 5, 50, 500 or 1500 mg/kg/day. In
the 2-year rat study, crinecerfont increased the incidence of combined thyroid gland follicular
cell adenoma and carcinoma in females at 100 mg/kg/day crinecerfont, the highest dose tested
(4-fold MRHD). Crinecerfont did not increase the incidence of tumors in rats at 15 mg/kg/day,
which is approximately 2 times the MRHD based on AUC. There were no statistically significant
crinecerfont-related increases in the incidence of any other tumors. The thyroid gland follicular
cell tumors were likely due to continuous stimulation of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)
secondary to liver enzyme induction that causes increased clearance of thyroid hormones. This
mechanism of inducing thyroid gland follicular cell hyperplasia and subsequent adenoma and
carcinoma development is rodent-specific and is not considered relevant to humans (Wu and
Farrelly 2006; Bartsch et al. 2018).

weight were not considered adverse effect.

unlikely due to crinecerfont and was probably associated with the vehicle.

Key Findings
Statistically significant (in trend and pairwise analyses) increase in the incidence
of combined thyroid follicular cell adenomas and carcinomas was observed in
females at 100 mg/kg/day compared to both water and vehicle control females.
The incidence of benign thyroid follicular cell adenomas in 100 mg/kg/day females
was 8/70 (11.4%) compared to 0/70 (0%) in water controls and 2/70 (2.9%) in
vehicle controls, whereas the incidence of thyroid follicular cell carcinomas in
100 mg/kg/day females was 5/70 (7.1%) compared to 0/70 in both water and
vehicle controls. The incidence of combined thyroid follicular cell tumors was
13/70 (18.6%). These findings were dose-dependent and exceeded the historical
control ranges at the facility. The incidence of combined follicular cell adenoma
and carcinoma was statistically significant both in trend (p<0.05) and pairwise
(p<0.01) analysis and was likely associated with crinecerfont treatment.
The incidence of thyroid follicular cell adenomas (7.1%) and carcinomas (2.9%)
was increased in 100 mg/kg/day males compared to water and vehicle male
controls. The incidence of thyroid follicular cell adenomas was higher than the
historical control range of up to 5.1%, whereas the incidence of carcinomas was
within the historical control range of up to 3.3%. These findings in males were not
statistically significant.
Crinecerfont was associated with increased incidences of chronic progressive
nephropathy, bile duct hyperplasia (mild to moderate) and periportal vacuolation

19.1.7.4. Reproductive Toxicology
19.1.7.4.1. Oral Male and Female Fertility Study in Rats
Key Findings
In a fertility study conducted by daily oral administration of crinecerfont tosylate to mature male
and female rats at dose of 0, 150, 300 or 1000 mg/kg/day, no remarkable toxicities on fertility
were observed in male and female rats up to the dose of 1000 mg/kg/day (2-fold MRHD based
on AUC). However, crinecerfont tosylate was related with deaths or preterminal euthanasia in
mid- and high-dose males, which were associated with hemorrhage and changes in coagulation
parameters (prolongation of PT and APTT, and low platelet counts). The NOAEL for fertility in
males and females was 1000 mg/kg/day which corresponded to exposures 2 times the MRHD.
The NOAEL for paternal toxicity was the low dose (150 mg/kg/day).

19.1.7.4.2. Oral Embryo-Fetal Development in Rat
Key Findings
An embryo-fetal development study was conducted with daily oral administration of crinecerfont
tosylate to pregnant female rats during the period of organogenesis from gestation day (GD) 6 to
17 at 0, 150, 500 or 2000 mg/kg/day. No remarkable toxicological effects on maternal
reproductive performance and fetal development were observed up to 2000 mg/kg/day except for
a slight decrease in food consumption (up to -14%) in dams in treatment groups. The decrease in
food consumption was not associated with decreased body weight gain and was not considered
an adverse effect. The NOAEL for rat maternal and developmental toxicity was 2000 mg/kg/day
(exposure 4-fold MRHD based on AUC). The plasma exposure of crinecerfont reached near
saturation at the low dose of 150 mg/kg/day (AUC24=296,000 ng∙hr/mL), which was comparable
to exposure at the NOAEL of 2000 mg/kg/day (AUC24=328000 ng∙hr/mL).

19.1.7.4.3. Embryo-Fetal Development Study in the Rabbit
(TER0384)
Key Findings
An embryo-fetal development study was conducted with daily oral administration of crinecerfont
tosylate to pregnant female rabbits during the period of organogenesis from GD6 to GD19 at 0,
100, 500, or 1000 mg/kg/day. The plasma exposures of crinecerfont were not dose-dependent
between 100 mg/kg/day (low dose) and 1000 mg/kg/day (high dose), with approximately 2-fold
exposure variation across doses, and similar mean systemic exposures were observed in the low
and high dose groups. Crinecerfont was associated with slightly lower maternal body weight gain
in all treatment groups compared to controls, corresponding with a slight reduction in mean fetal
body weight in the high dose group (37.5 g versus 40.4 g in control group). There were a few
fetuses that exhibited external, visceral, and/or skeletal skull malformations. The skull
malformations included microcephaly, microstomia, acephalostomia, misshapen cerebrum and/or
cerebellum, among others (details shown in Table 123).
There were four fetuses (all females) exhibiting one or more of these malformations, three in the
100 mg/kg/day group and one in the 1000 mg/kg/day group (total incidence of 0.8% fetuses and
7% litters across all dose groups combined). The observed malformations are rare and occurred
at incidences above the historical range reported by the conducting laboratory. The observed
malformations did not correlate with maternal toxicity. The NOAEL for fetal toxicity was not
determined due to the increase in incidence of craniofacial malformations. The potential clinical
relevance of the observed fetal malformations is discussed in Section 13 and the fetal
craniofacial defects will be described in the labeling.

NOAEL

The craniofacial malformations described are rarely observed in NZ white rabbit
based on the conducting laboratory’s historical control data. While the craniofacial
malformations were only observed in female fetuses, any relationship to sex is
unclear. The Applicant concluded that the observed malformations were not
related to crinecerfont treatment because of the low incidence and the absence of
a dose-related increase in malformations. However, given the apparent exposure
saturation and the absence of dose-related increases in plasma drug exposure,
we concluded that malformation incidence should not be delineated between
different dose groups. To assess the overall incidence rate of craniofacial
malformations, we combined all the crinecerfont-treated animals in the study to
compare to concurrent and historical control incidence. The overall incidence of
craniofacial malformations was 4 fetuses (4/525, 0.8%) from 4 different litters
(4/59, 7%). We included the 1000 mg/kg/day fetus with polymalformations in our
grouped analysis, but it was likely a unique case because it was significantly
smaller than other fetuses (~50% lower body weight than the study mean) and had
a different spectrum of malformations than the three 100 mg/kg/day fetuses with
craniofacial malformations. Compared to malformations previously observed in the
conducting lab, the craniofacial malformations in this crinecerfont study were
different. Historical control data from the conducting laboratory included a single
craniofacial malformation of anencephaly (1/1098, 0.09% incidence across 11
studies, ranging 0-0.6% in individual studies). Therefore, it was unclear whether
crinecerfont was associated with the low incidence of malformations observed in
this study. The malformation finding will be described in the labeling.
No dose-specific NOAEL could be established because crinecerfont exposure was
saturated across the dose range (Cmax =8470-15,200 ng/mL, AUC24=138,000260,000 ng∙hr/mL). There was no maternal toxicity identified in the study, up to
approximately 3-times the MRHD exposure.
Potential crinecerfont-related effects on embryo-fetal development observed in the
study at 2 to 3 times MRHD exposures included slightly lower mean fetal body
weight and a low incidence of craniofacial malformations.

19.1.7.4.4. Pre- and Postnatal Development Study in Rats
Key Findings
A pre- and postnatal development study was conducted with daily oral administration of
crinecerfont free base to pregnant rats during the period of organogenesis to weaning from GD7
to lactation day 20 at 0, 15, 150 or 250 mg/kg/day. Crinecerfont was not associated with
remarkable toxicity on reproductive performance or development up to a dose of 250 mg/kg/day
(at 4-fold MRHD based on AUC).

19.1.7.4.5. Juvenile Toxicity Study in Rats on Postnatal
Day 21 Through 49
Key Findings
In a juvenile rat study conducted with oral daily administration of crinecerfont free base on
postnatal day (PND) 21 to PND49 at 0, 15, 100 or 1000 mg/kg/day, the toxicological findings in
juvenile rats were largely comparable to the findings observed in adult rats (liver and thyroid
gland toxicity, and changes in coagulation parameters). Increased liver weight associated with
hypertrophy in females (partially reversed), and increased thyroid/parathyroid weight associated
with thyroid follicular cell hypertrophy, minimal to moderate increase in coagulation times and
decreased triglycerides in males (nonreversible) were observed at ≥100 mg/kg/day.
Hepatocellular hypertrophy in liver and follicular cell hypertrophy of thyroid gland were
possibly related to enzyme induction and were also seen in adult rats. Slightly delayed sexual
maturation in 1000 mg/kg/day males was noted. In females mated with untreated males after a 7week recovery period, a higher mean number of pre- and postimplantation losses at
1000 mg/kg/day was observed. Crinecerfont was not associated with CNS effects. The NOAEL
was the mid dose of 100 mg/kg/day, with exposure of ~2-fold MRHD based on AUC.

19.1.7.4.6. Juvenile Toxicity Study in Rats on PND4
Through PND21, With Developmental Observations
From PND22 Through PND70
Key Findings
For this study, juvenile rats were administered crinecerfont orally once daily at 0, 15, 100, 300 or
1000 mg/kg/day on PND4 to PND21 followed by a treatment-free period PND22 to PND70
before euthanasia on PND71. The recovery phase animals were euthanized on PND119 to
PND121 (males) or GD21 (females).
The juvenile rats did not tolerate 1000 mg/kg/day dose (13-fold MRHD based on AUC), which
resulted in early termination of the dose group. Crinecerfont-related findings in decedent animals
included hepatocellular necrosis and vacuolation, increased hepatocellular mitosis, and thyroid
gland follicular cell hypertrophy.
Crinecerfont was associated with significant decreases in body weight gain (up to -30%) and
absolute body weights in all doses (≤0.5-fold MRHD based AUC) during dosing (PND4 to
PND21) and during the treatment-free period (PND22 to PND70), but these resolved after
PND70. Sexual maturation parameters in both sexes were not affected by decrements in body
weights (delayed growth). The decrease in learning and memory on PND24 (shortly after
weaning) in 300 mg/kg/day males and females (at exposure 3-fold MRHD based on AUC) and
the decrease in femur length in 300 mg/kg/day females on PND71 were considered related to
low body weight gains (delayed growth), which were resolved during recovery period PND71 to
PND121.
Decreases in lymphocytes and total white blood cell count at 300 mg/kg/day (at exposure 3-fold
MRHD based on AUC) were observed on PND71, which were resolved at the end of recovery
period. Increases in triglycerides were noted in 300 mg/kg/day males at the end of recovery
period.
Crinecerfont was associated with thyroid gland follicular cell hypertrophy at all doses. This
finding was not resolved at the end of the recovery period in 300 mg/kg/day males and all doses
in females.
The reproductive and developmental NOAEL was 300 mg/kg/day with exposure approximately
4-fold the MRHD.

The plasma exposures (Cmax and AUC0­t) of crinecerfont increased in a less than
dose-proportional manner from 15 to 300/1000 mg/kg/day. A 20-fold increase in
dose from 15 to 300 mg/kg led to an increase in about 8-fold Cmax and AUC0­t.
The exposures for 1000 mg/kg were for a single dose on PND4. Tmax and Tlast
were 4-6 and 24 hours postdose, respectively. Exposures were comparable
between males and females, with no accumulation after multiple doses.
Exposures for 15 and 300 mg/kg/day doses trended low after multiple doses.
All metabolites (NBI-756179, NBI-742939 (M4), NBI-1084059 (M9) and 1084060
(M11)) increased in less than dose-proportional manner. Plasma levels of
metabolites were <1% for M11, <5% for NBI-756179, <8% for M9, and <14% for
M4. M11 accumulation was noted in all doses in both sex at PND21. The other
metabolite accumulations were noted at 100 mg/kg/day dose in both sexes.

Key Findings
Treatment-related mortalities occurred at 1000 mg/kg/day, which led to early
termination of this dose group and the addition of another high-dose group at
300 mg/kg/day. There were 3, 2, 4, and 14 mortalities in males and 2, 2, 5 and
15 mortalities in females in 0, 15, 100, and 1000 mg/kg/day dose groups. Liver
findings (hepatocellular necrosis, vacuolation, and increased mitosis) and thyroid
gland follicular cell hypertrophy were observed in early decedent animals.
Gavage-related findings were observed in some animals at 1000 mg/kg/day. The
cause of death or clinical decline for some animals were not determined. There
was no increase in treatment-related mortalities at ≤300 mg/kg/day dose groups.
Treatment-related clinical signs (discolored black or purple abdominal skin) were
observed in 15 and 100 mg/kg/day dose groups but not in the extended study at
300 mg/kg/day. The association of these clinical signs with crinecerfont was
unclear.
Treatment-related decrease in body weight gains and absolute body weights
(delayed growth) were observed in all treatment groups during dosing period
(PND4 to PND21) in both sexes (up to -31%), and beyond the dosing period
(PND22 to PND70) and resolved or increased compared to the controls after
PND70. Delayed growth did not affect sexual maturation but affected learning
and memory (by passive avoidance assessments) on PND24 in both sexes and
reduced femur length on PND70 in females at 300 mg/kg/day. Effects on
learning and memory and femur length were reversed during later intervals.
No significant treatment-related effects were noted.
No treatment-related effects on sexual maturation. Delayed preputial separation
in 15 mg/kg/day males and early vaginal potency in 15 and 300 mg/kg/day
females were noted. These effects were not dose-dependent and were within
historical control ranges for the facility and were not considered adverse effects.
No treatment-related effects on learning and memory at 15 and 100 mg/kg/day.
Learning and memory were affected at 300 mg/kg/day on PND24 but resolved in
later intervals (PNDs 31, 101, and 108).
No remarkable treatment-related effects: between PNDs 50 and 54, mean body
temperatures (at 15 and 100 mg/kg/day) and hindlimb strength (100 mg/kg/day
females) were lower compared to controls. The changes in body temperature
were not dose-dependent, and the lower hindlimb strength was likely due to
delayed growth rate. These findings were not observed at the later assessment
intervals (between PNDs 97 and 101), consistent with completion of juvenile
growth and development.
Decreased ambulation at 15 mg/kg/day (PND57 to PND69) and increased
ambulation at 300 mg/kg/day (PND99 to PND103), but the toxicological
significance was unclear as it was not dose-dependent and /or occurred long
after off-drug period.

19.1.7.4.7. Other Toxicology Studies
Comments on Inactive Ingredients
Crinecerfont is presented in two oral dosage forms: soft gel capsules of 25 mg, 50 mg, and
100 mg (NDA 218808); and 50 mg/mL oral solution (NDA 218820). The two proposed clinical
oral dosage formulations contain different excipients. Table 133 and Table 134 show the
components and quantities of the crinecerfont 100 mg soft gel capsule and the 50 mg/mL oral
solution, respectively. All the excipients, except for the propylene glycol (PG) dicaprylocaprate
in soft gel capsules and the orange flavor in 50 mg/mL oral solution, are present in the FDA IID
for oral formulations, and thus are not a safety concern. The safety of the two excipients (PG
dicaprylocaprate and orange flavor) that are not in the IID database is assessed below.

Extractables and Leachables

Immunotoxicity
The potential immunotoxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated by oral dosing of rats at 0, 15, 50 or
250 mg/kg/day for 28 days. Animals were immunized with keyhole limpet hemocyanin on Days
15 and 24 to assess the primary and secondary immune responses. Crinecerfont was associated
with slight to moderate increase in lymphocytes, slight increase in B-cell count and slight
increases in absolute CD3/CD4 T-cell count in females, and a slight decrease in T-cell-dependent
antibody response in males. The changes in leukocytic parameters and lymphocyte
subpopulation and T-cell-dependent antibody responses were small in magnitude and occurred in
one sex (males) and showed no remarkable evidence of immunotoxicity in rats.
Cyclophosphamide (positive control) induced marked immunotoxic effects, indicating the
sensitivity of the assay.
Phototoxicity
A potential risk for phototoxicity of crinecerfont was evaluated in vitro using 3T3 cells at
crinecerfont concentrations up to 20 µg/mL. No cytotoxicity was observed with or without
ultraviolet A irradiation, indicating no phototoxic potential of crinecerfont. Chlorpromazine
(positive control) induced a positive phototoxic effect, indicating the sensitivity of the assay.
Abuse Liability
Crinecerfont acts by inhibiting ACTH release from anterior pituitary, which is outside the bloodbrain barrier. Tissue distribution studies following IV or PO administration in rats showed
crinecerfont brain:plasma ratios of 0.1. The ex vivo binding studies following PO or IV dosing
showed that crinecerfont was bound to CRF1 receptors both in pituitary and brain, with higher
198
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
percentage of CRF1 receptor occupancy in pituitary at early timepoints (0.5 to 1 hour postdose)
than in brain and with similar levels of occupancy in later timepoints (2 to 24 hours postdose).
Crinecerfont was not associated with clinical signs related to CNS effects in single- or repeatdose toxicity studies in mice, rats, rabbits, and dogs dosed up to maximum tolerated doses. There
was no evidence of a withdrawal syndrome during recovery periods of chronic toxicology
studies in rats or dogs. Although the binding and tissue distribution studies were indicative of the
potential for CNS effects, the series of single- and repeat-dose studies in multiple species
indicated crinecerfont risk for potential for physical dependency is low.

20. Clinical Pharmacology
20.1. In Vitro Studies
20.1.1. Plasma Protein Binding in Rat, Mouse, Rabbit,
Dog, and Human Plasma, Study LPR0879
The objective of this study was to assess plasma protein binding of crinecerfont tosylate in
mouse, rat, rabbit, dog, and human plasma. Plasma samples from various species were spiked
with [14C]-crinecerfont tosylate at 50, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000, and 30000 ng/mL and allowed to
equilibrate for 1 hour. Specific binding of crinecerfont tosylate at 500 and 5000 ng/mL to human
serum albumin and human serum α1-acid glycoprotein was also determined. All studies were
done in triplicate and radioactivity was determined by liquid scintillation counting. Results
indicate that plasma protein binding was ≥99.9% at concentrations above 50 ng/mL in all species
evaluated. The mean percentage of binding of [14C]-crinecerfont tosylate to human serum
albumin and α1-acid glycoprotein for both concentrations tested was >99.9% and 96.6%,
respectively. Thus, the in vitro studies indicate that crinecerfont is highly plasma protein bound
and specifically binds albumin and α1-acid glycoprotein.11

20.1.2. Blood to Plasma Partitioning in Mouse, Rat,
Dog, and Human Whole Blood, Study DPK0198
The objective of this study was to assess in vitro blood to plasma partitioning in mouse, rat, dog,
and human whole blood. Whole blood samples from various species were spiked with
[14C]‑crinecerfont free base at 50, 500, 1000, 5000, 10 000 and 30 000 ng/mL and incubated for
0.5 hours. The blood/plasma and blood cells/plasma ratios were determined by assessing
crinecerfont radioactivity by liquid scintillation counting. All studies were done in duplicate.
11 Source: LPR0879 Report

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
Results indicate that whole blood/plasma ratios ranged from 0.5 to 0.7. Blood cell/plasma ratios
were low across the species tested with human blood cell/plasma ratio of 0.08±03. Additionally,
no concentration dependence was observed in terms of blood cell affinity at the concentration
range evaluated.12

20.1.3. In Vitro Hepatic Clearance From Rat, Rabbit,
Dog, and Human Hepatocytes, Study MIV0370
The objective of this study was to determine metabolic clearance of crinecerfont free base from
fresh hepatocyte cultures obtained from rat, rabbit, dog, and humans. Crinecerfont free base was
incubated for 24 hours at 1µM in animal hepatocytes and 0.1 and 1µM in human hepatocytes.
Samples were obtained over 24 hours, supernatant and cellular homogenates were collected and
analyzed by liquid-chromatography tandem mass spectroscopy (LC-MS/MS). All studies were
done in triplicate. The in vitro intrinsic clearance (CLint) values in rat, rabbit, dog, and human
hepatocytes at 1µM concentrations were 0.057, 0.029, 0.059, and 0.028 mL/h/106 cells,
respectively. The CLint at 0.1µM in human hepatocytes was 0.029 mL/hr/106 cells. Results
indicate that the human hepatocytes were not saturable over the concentrations tested, and the
CLint from the hepatocytes of all the species tested was low and not concentration-dependent in
human hepatocytes.13

20.1.4. In Vitro Metabolism in Mouse, Rat, Guinea Pig,
Rabbit, Dog, Monkey, and Human Liver
Microsomes, Study MIV0341
The objective of this study was to characterize the in vitro metabolism of [14C]-crinecerfont in
mouse, rat, guinea pig, dog, monkey, and human liver microsomes. [14C]-crinecerfont tosylate at
5µM and 25µM was incubated up to 60 minutes in microsomes. All studies were done in
triplicate and metabolite profiles were determined by high-performance liquid chromatography
with an online radio-detection and metabolite structures were elucidated by LC-MS/MS. In vitro
metabolism of [14C]-crinecerfont tosylate was characterized at 5µM (9.25 kBq/mL;
0.25 µCi/mL), while the samples at 25µM (18.5 kBq/mL; 0.50 µCi/mL) were used for metabolite
elucidation. Crinecerfont metabolism percentages were 5% in human, 12% in mouse, 14% in
dog, 17% in rabbit, 26% in monkey, 56% in rat, and 61% in guinea pig. Excluding the rat and the
guinea pig, metabolism of crinecerfont was slow. The rank order of liver metabolism in
microsomes, from slowest to fastest, shows the following order: human < mouse ≈ dog ≈ rabbit <
monkey << rat ≈ guinea pig. The primary metabolic pathways in humans were hydroxylation of
the fluorophenyl moiety (M6) and N-dealkylation of the propargyl moiety (M4). Metabolites M6
and M4 constituted 4% and 3% of recovered drug material, respectively. Metabolites M6 and M4
were present in all the species tested.14

20.1.5. In Vitro Metabolic Profile in Rabbit, Dog and
Human Fresh Hepatocytes, Study MIV0358
The objective of this study was to assess the in vitro metabolism of [14C]-crinecerfont in different
animal species (rat, rabbit, dog) and human hepatocytes. Crinecerfont was assessed at 5µM and
25µM in hepatocytes for 24 hours at 37°C. Samples were assessed by high-performance liquid
chromatography with an online radioactivity detector. Metabolites were elucidated using LC/MS.
Crinecerfont was stable, with unchanged crinecerfont accounting for 82% of the recover drugrelated material. The major metabolic pathways and metabolites identified from three human
donors were named HH followed by number. These included hydroxylation on methyl of
fluorophenyl moiety (HH7; M6 from study MIV0341), N-depropargylation (HH8) followed by
hydroxylation (HH6; M4 from study MIV0341) and/or glucuronidation (HH3), hydroxylation on
methyl-cyclopropane moiety followed by glucuronidation (HH5), and O-demethylation followed
by glucuronidation (HH4) or followed by both hydroxylation and glucuronidation (HH2).
Metabolites HH7, HH8, HH3, HH5, and HH4 were found in all the species tested. Metabolite
HH6 was not detected in rabbits, metabolite HH4 was not detected in rats, and metabolite HH2
was not detected in dog. No interindividual variability was detected in the three tested human
donors.15

20.1.6. In Vitro Metabolism in Human Liver
Microsomes and Hepatocytes, Study MIH0179
The objective of this study was to assess the role of CYP450 enzymes on the metabolism of
crinecerfont metabolism in human microsomes or from insect cells transfected with human CYP
cDNA (Supersomes™) or cryopreserved human hepatocytes. In human microsomes, crinecerfont
(0.1 and 1µM) was incubated with or without a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate
(NADPH)-generating system for up to 60 min. In Supersomes, crinecerfont (0.1 and 1µM) was
incubated with or without an NADPH-generating system for 30 min. In human hepatocytes,
crinecerfont (0.1 and 1µM) was incubated with or without selective inhibitors of CYP2D6
(quinidine) or CYP3A (ketoconazole) for up to 6 hours. In human hepatocytes, bufuralol and
midazolam metabolism were used as positive controls to confirm CYP2D6 and CYP3A activity.
All samples were quantified using LC-MS/MS. In human liver microsomes, crinecerfont did not
exhibit NADPH-dependent metabolism at 0.1 and 1µM. In Supersomes, crinecerfont exhibited
metabolism via CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C19 at both 0.1 and 1µM concentrations.
Additionally, crinecerfont at 0.1µM concentration in Supersomes exhibited metabolism (to a
lesser extent) by CYP2A6, and flavin‑containing monooxygenases 1 and 2. In human
hepatocytes, metabolism of crinecerfont was not inhibited by either quinidine (selective for
CYP2D6) or ketoconazole (selective for CYP3A). Per the Applicant, the lack of metabolism by
CYP2D6 and CYP3A is possibly because of the insolubility of crinecerfont in the heatinactivated hepatocyte studies, given that the positive controls established activity for both
enzyme isoforms. The Applicant concluded further investigation was necessary to determine the
in vitro metabolism of crinecerfont.16

20.1.7. In Vitro Clearance and Fraction Metabolized by
CYP3A in Human Hepatocytes Using
Recombinant Human Enzymes, Study MIH0659
The objective of this study was to estimate the percentage of contribution of CYP enzymes
identified in crinecerfont metabolism in Study MIH0179. At 0.1 or 10µM [14C]-crinecerfont
concentrations, crinecerfont metabolism was assessed in human hepatocyte suspensions.
Crinecerfont was incubated with and without 1µM ketoconazole (selective CYP3A inhibitor), or
1mM 1-Aminobenzotriazole (nonselective inhibitor of CYP3A4 and CYP2B6). An LC-MS/MS
method was used to monitor the metabolism of crinecerfont depletion in hepatocytes and human
liver microsomes (Supersomes). Crinecerfont concentrations in this study were 0.15 to 20µM to
determine enzyme maximal velocity (Vmax) and dissociation constant of the enzyme-substrate
complex (Km) for CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4 in Supersomes. Metabolism of
[14C]-crinecerfont did not occur in human hepatocyte suspensions at either 0.1 or 10µM and in
vitro intrinsic clearance and estimations of fraction metabolized (fm) by CYP3A could not be
determined. In Supersomes, crinecerfont is metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 (estimated fm
~68.0 to 83.7%) and, to a lesser extent, by CYP2B6 (estimated fm ~10.7 to 25.2%). Contribution
to crinecerfont metabolism from CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 was minor with estimated fm values
<5%.17

20.1.8. CYP450 Inhibition in Human Liver Microsomes,
Study MIH0178
The objective of this study was to assess in vitro if crinecerfont inhibits CYP1A2, CYP2B6,
CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, or CYP3A. Crinecerfont (200µM), microsomes, and
NADPH were pre-incubated at 37°C for 15 min, then the CYP selective substrates for CYP1A2,
CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, or CYP3A were incubated at prespecified
times to allow for product formation. LC-MS/MS was used to quantify the amount of product
formed from each specific CYP assay. Crinecerfont at 200µM did not inhibit CYP1A2,
CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, or CYP3A. The estimated apparent inhibitor
constant (Ki) values for these isoforms would be ≥233μM.18

and incubated for prespecified times with or without an NADPH-regenerating system, along with
a selective substrate for a particular isoform. Isoform-selective inhibitors for CYP1A2, CYP2B6,
CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, and CYP3A4 were furafylline, monoclonal antibody

20.1.10. Further Assessment on Time-Dependent
Inhibition of CYP450 Enzymes in Human Liver
Microsomes Identified in MIH0437, Study
MIH0438
The objective of this study was to further assess the potential for crinecerfont tosylate to be a
time-dependent inhibitor of CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C10, and CYP3A4 in liver microsomes.
Similar to Study MIH0437, crinecerfont tosylate at 25, 50, and 100µM was pre-incubated for 15
or 30 minutes with or without an NADPH-regenerating system. Postincubation aliquots were
transferred to reaction mixtures containing the CYP isoform-specific substrates at their Km
concentrations along with a fresh NADPH-regenerating system. Selective mechanism-based
inhibitors used included thio-TEPA (CYP2B6), tienilic acid (CYP2C9), ticlopidine (CYP2C19)
and troleandomycin (CYP3A). Each assay was run for a prespecified time and metabolite
concentrations were assessed using LC-MS/MS. Results indicate that under conditions evaluated,
there was no significant time-dependent inhibition of CYP2B6, CYP2C9, or CYP2C19.
Irreversible inhibition of CYP3A activity by crinecerfont between 25–100µM with 30-minute
preincubation was observed in liver microsomes.
Further evaluation with CYP3A4 was performed to determine the kinetic constants, maximal rate
of enzyme inactivation (Kinact), and the concentration of inhibitor that gives half-maximal rate of
inactivation (KI), for time-dependent inhibition of CYP3A4 by crinecerfont in liver microsomes
expressing CYP3A4. The study design was similar to the one outlined in Section 20.1.9 above
with additional preincubation times of 0, 10, 20, and 30 minutes and crinecerfont tosylate
concentrations assessed included 0, 2.5, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 30µM. Testosterone was the substrate
and the amount of 6β-hydroxytestosterone formed was quantified using LC-MS/MS. Results
from this study determined that the apparent Kinact and Ki values for crinecerfont inhibition of
recombinantly expressed CYP3A were 0.0408 min-1 and 8.31µM, respectively. Based on the
results from this study, crinecerfont irreversibly inhibited CYP3A activity when preincubated
with liver microsomes for 30 minutes.20

20.1.11. CYP450 Inhibition in Human Liver
Microsomes, Study MIH0507
The objective of this study was to assess crinecerfont free base inhibition of CYP2C8 in human
liver microsomes. Human liver microsomes with an NADPH-regenerating system were
incubated with paclitaxel at Km, a selective CYP2C8 substrate, and crinecerfont free base
between 0 to 200µM. The hydroxypaclitaxel formed was assessed by LC-MS/MS. Quercetin was
used as a positive control as it is a selective CYP2C8 inhibitor. The IC50 values for CYP2C8
inhibition were calculated using WinNonlin Ver 5.2. The percent inhibition of CYP2C8 by
crinecerfont at 10µM and ≥30µM were 33.9% and between 32.7 and 38.6%. The similarity in
inhibition above 10µM is indicative of low crinecerfont solubility at higher concentrations.
Based on the available data, the IC50 value of CYP2C8 was established as >10µM.21

20.1.12. CYP2C8 Time-Dependent Inhibition in Human
Liver Microsomes, Study XT195084
The objective of this study was to assess the ability of crinecerfont to inhibit CYP2C8 in a timedependent manner in human liver microsomes. Human liver microsomes with and without an
NADPH-regenerating system were preincubated with or without crinecerfont 0.01 to 10µM and
with and without selective inhibitors of CYP2C8 (montelukast (reversible) and gemfibrozil
glucuronide (time-dependent)) for 30 minutes. Amodiaquine, a CYP2C8 substrate, was added to
the preincubated samples and amodiaquine and its N-dealkylation metabolite concentrations
were assessed by LC-MS/MS. Results indicate that crinecerfont directly inhibited CYP2C8 with
a maximum inhibition of 44%. No change in percent inhibition was detected above 3µM up to
10µM and so the IC50 value was reported as >3µM. There was no evidence of time- or
metabolism-dependent inhibition of CYP2C8 by crinecerfont as no change in percent inhibition
was noted with and without preincubation with crinecerfont.22

20.1.13. CYP1A2, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4 Induction in
Human Hepatocytes, Study MIV0413
The objective of this study was to assess whether crinecerfont tosylate at 0.1, 1, 5, 10, and 50 µM
could induce CYP1A2, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4 gene expression and enzyme activity in fresh
human hepatocytes. Human hepatocytes were incubated with crinecerfont tosylate for 72 hours,
the level of induction was determined by evaluating gene expression using reverse transcription
polymerase chain reaction, and enzyme activity was determined by activity using specific probe
substrates. Positive inducer controls included in the study were β-naphthoflavone (50µM) for
CYP1A2 and rifampicin (25µM) for CYP3A4 and CYP2C9. Crinecerfont concentrations at
50µM were found to be cytotoxic and were excluded from analysis. At concentrations up to
10µM, no induction of CYP1A2 in terms of gene expression or enzyme activity levels was
observed. After 72 hours of exposure at 10µM crinecerfont, the level of CYP2C9 mRNA was
increased by 1.9-fold (54% of reference inducer; rifampicin) and enzyme activity decreased to

20.1.14. CYP2B6 Induction in Human Hepatocytes,
Study XT183069
The objective of this study was to determine if crinecerfont is able to induce CYP2B6 gene
expression and enzyme activity when treated with crinecerfont free base between 0.1 to 10µM in
cryopreserved human hepatocytes. Crinecerfont was incubated in human hepatocytes for
72 hours and the level of induction was determined by reverse transcription polymerase chain
reaction and enzyme activity on bupropion hydroxylation (probe substrate) (n=3). Controls
included phenobarbital (1mM; positive control), and flumazenil (25µM; negative control).
Treatment with up to 10µM crinecerfont resulted in concentration-dependent increases in
CYP2B6 mRNA expression up to 3.25 to 5.15-fold in two of three cultures. The increase in
mRNA expression in the two cultures was ≤2.6% of the positive control response. There was
little or no induction of CYP2B6 activity (<2-fold change) following treatment with up to 10 µM
crinecerfont for the third culture.24

20.1.15. Permeability Assessment in Caco-2-TC7 Cells
Expressing P-gp, Study AIV0071
The objective of this study was to assess the apparent permeability coefficient (Papp) of
crinecerfont in Caco-2-TC7 cells and evaluate the role of P-gp in the absorption of crinecerfont.
Caco-2-TC7 cells were seeded in in 12-well plates, incubated at 37°C with 10% CO2 and 95%
relative humidity under a continuous gentle orbital agitation. The transport of [14C]‑crinecerfont
tosylate from apical to basal chamber was tested at 1µM (0.046 µCi/mL), 5µM (0.23 µCi/mL)
and 20µM (0.92 µCi/mL) in the absence and in the presence of cells. Incubation time was
2 hours and at the end of the incubation time, samples were withdrawn from the apical and
basolateral side and radioactivity was determined by liquid scintillation counting to determine
Papp. Bidirectional transport (apical to basolateral and basolateral to apical) of 1, 5, and 20µM
[14C]-crinecerfont tosylate across Caco-2-TC7 monolayers was performed to determine the role
of P-gp in crinecerfont absorption. Controls for the Papp studies included [3H]-mannitol and high
[14C]-testosterone, and the positive control for P-gp studies was [3H]-vinblastine. All studies
were done in triplicate. The Papp of crinecerfont was 2.2×10-7 cm/s at 20µM and was similar to
the low-permeability compound [3H]-mannitol, indicating the crinecerfont has a low
permeability. Results for the P-gp studies indicate that the efflux ratio of crinecerfont was 0.9 at
20 µM and it is not considered a substrate for P-gp.25

20.1.16. Crinecerfont Transporter Substrate Potential
for BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, and OATP1B3, Study
XT198097
The objective of this study was to assess the potential of crinecerfont (0.2, 1, 5, and 10µM) to be
a substrate of transporters breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), bile salt export pump
(BSEP), organic anion transport polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, and OATP1B3. Substrate potential
was defined as uptake or efflux ratio ≥2 that is reduced >50% in the presence of an inhibitor.
Crinecerfont potential as a substrate for BCRP was assessed using bidirectional permeability of
in Madin-Darby canine kidney type II (MDCKII) cells with and without inhibitors (Ko143 and
lopinavir). Samples were drawn from the receiver chamber over 120 minutes and concentrations
were assessed by LC-MS/MS. In BCRP-expressing cells, the crinecerfont uptake could not be
measured, due to poor permeability across these cells. Thus, crinecerfont potential as a substrate
for BCRP could not be evaluated.
Crinecerfont potential as a substrate for BSEP was assessed by determining accumulation of
crinecerfont in transporter-expressing vesicles with and without inhibitors (cyclosporine and
glyburide) and with either ATP or AMP (negative control). At 1, 3, and 10 minutes crinecerfont
accumulation in vesicles was assessed by LC-MS/MS. In BSEP vesicles, the crinecerfont uptake
ratio was <2 compared to control at both 5 and 10 µM concentrations, thus indicating that
crinecerfont is not a substrate for BSEP.
Crinecerfont potential as a substrate for OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 was assessed by determining
accumulation of crinecerfont in transporter-expressing human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293
cells with and without inhibitors (rifampin and cyclosporine). At 1, 3, and 10 minutes
crinecerfont accumulation in vesicles was assessed by LC-MS/MS. In OATP1B3 cells, the
crinecerfont uptake ratio was <2 compared to control at both 5 and 10 µM concentrations, thus
indicating that crinecerfont is not a substrate for OATP1B3. In OATP1B1 cells, the crinecerfont
uptake ratio was >2 (range: 1.36 to 3.70). However, crinecerfont uptake was decreased by <50%
in the presence of inhibitors of OATP1B1. Thus, overall, crinecerfont is not a substrate of
OATP1B1 or OATP1B3.26

20.1.17. P-gp Inhibition in Caco-2 Cells Expressing Pgp, Study AIV0107
The objective of this study was to assess if crinecerfont can inhibit P-gp transport of
[3H]‑vinblastine in Caco-2-TC7 cells. Basal-to-apical transport and apical-to-basal transport of
5µM [3H]-vinblastine in the absence (control) and in the presence of 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30 and
100µM crinecerfont was assessed over a 2-hour incubation period. Crinecerfont was added to
both the apical and basal chambers. Verapamil (200µM) was used as the positive control for Pgp inhibition. Radioactivity in the samples was quantified by liquid scintillation. At 100µM
crinecerfont precipitated and P-gp inhibition could not be quantified at this concentration. At

20.1.18. Crinecerfont Inhibition Potential for
Transporters P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1,
OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1, and
MATE2-K, Study XT188068
The objective of this study was to assess the potential of crinecerfont (10µM) to inhibit
transporters P-gp, BCRP, BSEP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, organic anion transporter (OAT) 1,
OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT) 2, multidrug and toxin extrusion transporter (MATE) 1,
and MATE2-K.
P-gp inhibition was evaluated in Caco-2 cells and in MDCKII cells. Digoxin (10µM) was used
as substrate for P-gp. The bidirectional permeability of the digoxin was assessed and quantified
by LC-MS/MS. At 10µM crinecerfont, digoxin efflux ratio in Caco-2 cells decreased from 16.3
to 10.6, indicating a 37% inhibition in P-gp transport. At 10µM crinecerfont, digoxin efflux ratio
in MDCKII-P-gp cells was not affected, indicating that in this system crinecerfont does not
inhibit P-gp transport.
BCRP inhibition was evaluated in MDCKII cells. Prazosin (1µM) was used as substrate for
BCRP. The bidirectional permeability of the prazosin was assessed and quantified by LCMS/MS. At 10µM crinecerfont, the corrected prazosin efflux ratio in MDCKII-BCRP was not
affected, indicating that crinecerfont does not inhibit BCRP.
Crinecerfont potential as an inhibitor of BSEP was assessed by determining accumulation of
[3H]-taurocholic acid (0.4µM) by LC-MS/MS in transporter-expressing vesicles. At 10µM
crinecerfont, the ATP-dependent uptake of [3H]-taurocholic acid (0.4µM) in BSEP vesicles did
not decrease, indicating that crinecerfont is not an inhibitor of BSEP.
Crinecerfont potential as an inhibitor of OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1,
and MATE2-K was assessed in HEK293 cells. OATP1B1, OATP1B3, MATE1, MATE2-K, and
control cells were incubated with butyric acid (10mM) for 24 hours prior to the experiment to
induce transporter gene expression. Crinecerfont 10µM, positive control, or negative control
were preincubated for 15 minutes or 30 minutes before adding the probe substrate and incubating
for 1 to 5 minutes. Probe substrates used for OATP1B1/B3, OAT 1, OAT 3,
OCT2/MATE1/MATE2-K were [3H]-Estradiol- 17β-glucuronide (50nM), [3H]-paminohippurate (1µM), [3H]-estrone-3-sulfate (50nM), and [14C]-metformin (10µM),
respectively. Positive controls used in this study were rifampin (10µM) and cyclosporine (1µM)
for OATP1B1/B3; probenecid (100µM) and novobiocin (300µM) for OAT 1; probenecid
(100µM) and ibuprofen (100µM) for OAT 3; quinidine (300µM) and cimetidine (2500µM) for
OCT2; cimetidine (20µM) and pyrimethamine (0.5µM) for MATE1; and cimetidine (300µM)
and pyrimethamine (3µM) for MATE2-K. Samples were quantified by liquid scintillation.

20.2. In Vivo Studies
20.2.1. Single Ascending Dose Study of Crinecerfont
Between 20 mg to 800 mg, Study TDU10479
Study Design
This is a phase 1 single oral ascending dose, safety, tolerability, and PK study of crinecerfont in
healthy young male subjects. The primary objectives of this study were to assess safety and
tolerability, and PK of single ascending doses of crinecerfont under fasted conditions or 30
minutes post moderate-fat breakfast. Subjects (n=6 per group) received oral doses of 20, 50, 100,
200, 400 or 800 mg crinecerfont or placebo and PK samples were obtained at prespecified time
points over 504 hours. A total of 64 subjects were randomized with 48 subjects in the
crinecerfont groups. Dropouts included three from the placebo group, one each from the 50 mg
fasted and fed groups, and two each from the 100 mg fed and 800 mg fed groups primarily due to
personal reasons. Crinecerfont PK parameters were calculated and 90% confidence intervals
(CIs) for the geometric mean of fed versus fasted ratio for Cmax, AUC, and AUC0-tlast were
provided for each dose level. The food effect was determined at the 20 mg and 50 mg dose levels
under fed and fasted conditions. Dose proportionality was assessed by regression analysis under
fed conditions for Cmax, AUC0-tlast, and AUC.

Conclusions
•

The apparent terminal elimination half-life of crinecerfont was long and ranged from 7.8 to

20.2.2. Crinecerfont Capsule Dose Linearity 20 mg to
200 mg, Study TDR10671
Study Design
This is a phase 1, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the tolerability and
pharmacokinetics of 14-day repeated ascending oral doses of crinecerfont in 48 healthy young
male subjects. The primary objectives of this study were to assess the tolerability, safety, and
pharmacokinetics after repeated oral ascending doses of crinecerfont. Crinecerfont was
administered at 20, 50, 100, and 200 mg under fed-conditions (moderate-fat breakfast) every day
for 14 days. A total of 48 subjects were enrolled, with 32 subjects in the treatment group (all
subjects in the treatment group completed the study). Dropouts included 4 in the placebo group.
PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours. PK parameters were
calculated from plasma concentrations of crinecerfont and time to steady state, dose
proportionality, and accumulation ratio were calculated.

20.2.3. Mass Balance, Excretion, and Metabolite
Profiling, Study BEX5094
Study Design
This is a phase 1, open-label, nonrandomized, single-dose study to determine the excretion
balance and pharmacokinetics after oral administration of 100 mg of [14C]-crinecerfont to
healthy male subjects.
Objectives
•

Determine the excretion balance and systemic exposure of radioactivity after oral
administration of [14C]-crinecerfont.

•

Determine pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont and its contribution to overall exposure.

•

Determine metabolic pathways of crinecerfont and identify the chemical structures of the
main metabolites.

The study enrolled six subjects, five completed the study and one was lost to follow-up.
Crinecerfont was administered with a high-fat breakfast as two 50 mg capsules containing a total

obtained at prespecified time points over 37 days in whole blood, plasma, urine, feces, and
expired air. PK parameters, Cmax, Tmax, AUClast, AUC0-∞, and t1/2, and blood to plasma

Conclusions
•

Following a single dose of 100 mg crinecerfont, with 2.59 MBq (70 µCi) [14C]-crinecerfont,
only 49.4% of the administered dose was recovered.

•

The total mean amount of radioactivity recovered in the feces over 37 days was 47.3% of the
administered dose. Approximately 2.7% of the parent compound was recovered in the feces
indicating that the parent compound is extensively metabolized.

•

The total amount of radioactivity recovered in the urine over 37 days was <2% of the
administered dose.

•

An abundant metabolite, M6, constituting 14.4% of the parent AUC was identified. All other
metabolites represented <6% of the parent compound.

•

The M6 metabolite has a high affinity for CRF1 with Ki of 1.14nM, similar to crinecerfont
affinity (0.6 to 3.99nM). However, in vivo, due to its limited exposure at steady state in
humans (approximately 6% relative to crinecerfont), M6 is not expected to significantly
contribute to the clinical CRF1 inhibition profile.

20.2.5. Hepatic Impairment Study, Study NBI-747881717
Study Design
This is a phase 1, single-dose, open-label study designed to assess the safety, tolerability, and
pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont and its metabolites in subjects with mild, moderate, or severe
stable chronic hepatic impairment relative to subjects with normal hepatic function. The primary
objective of this study was to assess the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont (NBI-74788) and its
metabolite (NBI-7456179; M6) in subjects with normal, mild, moderate, and severe hepatic
impairment. Hepatic impairment was defined using the Child-Pugh scale. A total of 25 adult
subjects between the ages of 18–75 years were enrolled. The normal, mild, and moderate groups
had six subjects each while the severe hepatic impairment group had seven subjects. The group
219
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
of subjects with normal hepatic function were similar in age (±5 years), sex, race, and weight
(±10%) to the subjects with hepatic impairment. An overnight fast of 10 hours was followed by
the administration of two 50 mg crinecerfont capsules with 237 mL of Ensure Plus and 120 mL
of water. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours. GMRs with 90%
CIs were calculated and compared for AUC0-∞, AUC0-tlast, and Cmax in the mild, moderate, and
severe hepatic impairment groups to the reference normal group. All subjects completed the
study.
Results
The mean plasma crinecerfont concentrations versus time in subjects with normal, mild,
moderate, and severe hepatic impairment are presented in Figure 37. The mean apparent terminal
half-life (± standard deviation [SD]) of crinecerfont in normal mild, moderate, and severe hepatic
impairment were 136 h (96.0), 87.2 h (71.3), 119 h (34.9), and 221 h (87.1), respectively. In
subjects with severe hepatic impairment, apparent terminal half-life did increase, however, the
increase is not significant due to the large standard deviation associated with this parameter.
The effective half-life of crinecerfont is ~14 hours and a PK sampling time of 504 hours is
appropriate as it covers more than five half-lives. Comparison of GMRs with the 90% CIs for
AUC0-tlast, AUC0-∞, and Cmax for 100 mg crinecerfont and its metabolite M6 in the different
hepatic impairment groups are presented in Table 146.
