Conclusions
•

Overall, the mild, moderate, and severe hepatic impairment groups had lower AUC0-tlast,
AUC0-∞, and Cmax compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. The magnitude of
impact on crinecerfont pharmacokinetics seems to be comparable between mild and severe
hepatic impairment. The mechanism of decreased crinecerfont exposures due to hepatic
impairment is not known. However, the 90% CI values for the GMRs all included unity
indicating that while the PK exposure is lower it does not appear to be clinically significant.

•

There were no deaths, severe adverse events (AEs), or discontinuations from the study due to
AEs reported in this study. No safety concerns related to routine clinical laboratory results,
vital signs, or electrocardiogram results were identified.

Metabolite M6 has a similar affinity for the CRF1 compared to the parent drug. However, due to
limited systemic exposure (i.e., approximately 6% relative to crinecerfont), M6 is not expected to
significantly contribute to the pharmacological activity of crinecerfont.

20.2.6. Extrinsic Factors: Rifampin Study, Study NBI74788-1718
Study Design
This is a phase 1, open-label, one-sequence crossover study to assess the effect of rifampin on
the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont (NBI-74788) in healthy subjects. The primary objective of
this study is to evaluate and compare the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont when crinecerfont is
administered alone and concomitantly with rifampin. A total of 16 adult subjects between the
ages of 18–55 years were enrolled. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 100 mg
crinecerfont was administered with 237 mL Ensure Plus following a 10 hour overnight fast.
Following a 21-day washout period, treatment period 2 commenced with subjects receiving
600 mg rifampin once daily for 29 days in the fasted state. On Day 9 of period two subjects
received crinecerfont 2 hours after rifampin dosing with 237 mL Ensure Plus. PK samples were
obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours for crinecerfont and its major metabolite
NBI-756169. GMRs with 90% CIs were calculated and compared for AUC0-∞, AUC0-tlast, and
Cmax for crinecerfont with rifampin versus reference (crinecerfont alone). All subjects completed
the study.
Results
The PK profile of 100 mg crinecerfont with and without rifampin 600 mg is presented in
Figure 38. Comparison of GMRs with the 90% CIs for AUC0-tlast, AUC0-∞, and Cmax for 100 mg
crinecerfont with rifampin and crinecerfont alone are presented in Table 147.

20.2.7. Extrinsic Factors: Ketoconazole Study, Study
INT5449
Study Design
This is a phase 1, open-label, two-treatment, single-sequence crossover pharmacokinetic
interaction study of 14-day repeated oral 400 mg doses of ketoconazole on the pharmacokinetics
of a single oral 50 mg dose of crinecerfont in healthy male subjects. The primary objective of the
study was to assess the PK interaction of 14-day repeated oral 400 mg doses of ketoconazole on
the pharmacokinetics of crinecerfont following a single oral 50 mg dose in 16 healthy male
subjects. In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 50 mg crinecerfont was administered with a
moderate fat breakfast following a 10 hour overnight fast. Following a 22-day washout period,
treatment period 2 commenced with subjects receiving 400 mg ketoconazole once daily for 5
days with standardized breakfast. On Day 6 of treatment period 2, subjects received
ketoconazole 400 mg and 50 mg crinecerfont with a moderate fat breakfast. Ketoconazole dosing
continued from Day 7 to 14 of treatment period 2 with standardized breakfast. PK samples were
obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours for crinecerfont. GMRs with 90% CIs were
calculated and compared for AUC0-∞, AUC0-tlast, and Cmax for crinecerfont with ketoconazole
versus reference (crinecerfont alone). All subjects completed the study.
Results
The PK profile of 50 mg crinecerfont with and without ketoconazole 400 mg is presented in
Figure 39. Comparison of GMRs with the 90% CIs for AUC0-tlast, AUC0-∞, and Cmax for 50 mg
crinecerfont with ketoconazole and crinecerfont alone are presented in Table 148.

20.2.8. Extrinsic Factors: Midazolam Study, Study
INT6752
Study Design
This is a phase 1, open-label, two-treatment, single-sequence PK interaction study of 8-day
repeated oral 100 mg doses of crinecerfont on single oral doses of midazolam in 15 healthy male
subjects.
The primary objective of this study is to assess the impact of 8-day repeated oral 100 mg doses
of crinecerfont on the pharmacokinetics of midazolam, as a probe substrate for CYP3A activity,
and the reversibility of the inhibition of CYP3A activity by crinecerfont 1 and 2 weeks after
crinecerfont last administration.
In treatment period 1, a single oral dose of 2 mg midazolam solution was administered under
fasting conditions. Following a 48-hour washout period, crinecerfont 100 mg was administered
daily with a moderate fat breakfast for 8 days as part of period 2. On Day 8, 15, and 22 of period
2, midazolam 2 mg oral solution was administered. On Day 8 midazolam was administered 2
hours after crinecerfont. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours
for crinecerfont. Midazolam plasma concentrations were obtained for 24 hours
postadministration on Day 1 of Period 1, and Days 8, 15, and 22 of Period 2. GMRs with 90%
CIs were calculated and compared for AUC0-∞, AUC0-tlast, and Cmax for midazolam with or post
crinecerfont 100 mg dosing versus reference (midazolam alone). All subjects completed the
study.
Results
The PK profile of 2 mg midazolam with and without crinecerfont 100 mg is presented in
Figure 40. Comparison of GMRs with the 90% CIs for AUC0-tlast, AUC0-∞, and Cmax for 2 mg
midazolam with or post 100 mg crinecerfont versus midazolam 2 mg alone are presented in
Table 149.

Conclusions
•

Coadministration of midazolam with steady-state concentrations of crinecerfont (8 days)

inhibitor of CYP3A4.

•

Midazolam AUC and Cmax levels at 7 days post crinecerfont administration were 1.04- and
1.02-fold, respectively, compared to midazolam treatment alone, thus, indicating reversibility
of the CYP3A4 inhibition by crinecerfont.

•

While this study was conducted with an earlier formulation of crinecerfont, it is anticipated

•

The dose of crinecerfont tested was 100 mg once daily for 8 days prior to midazolam

adults (Trial CAH3003), which was 100 mg twice daily. The study results can still assess the
impact of crinecerfont inhibition of CYP3A4. Based on PK data from Trial NBI-74788CAH2001, crinecerfont exposure in this DDI study may be about 50% lower than that under
the maximal clinical dose. Nonetheless, a more than 2-fold increase in midazolam exposure
(a minimal effect to be classified as a moderate CYP3A inhibitor) is not expected even if the
DDI study had been conducted with 100 mg bid. Overall, crinecerfont is expected to be a
weak CYP3A inhibitor at the maximal proposed dose of 100 mg twice daily.

20.2.9. Extrinsic Factors: Oral Contraceptive Steroids
Study, Study INT11387
Study Design
This is a phase 1, open-label, non-randomized, single sequence, two-treatment crossover PK
interaction of 21-day repeated oral 100 mg doses of crinecerfont on oral contraceptive steroids in
healthy female subjects. The primary objective of this study is to assess the effect of 21-day
repeated oral doses of 100 mg crinecerfont on the pharmacokinetics of oral contraceptive
steroids (OCS) in 25 healthy female subjects. OCS are nonsensitive CYP3A4 substrates, and it is
anticipated that a certain portion of the patient population who may be on crinecerfont may also
be on OCS. Crinecerfont was shown to be an inhibitor of CYP3A4 in the in vitro studies and,
therefore, evaluation of crinecerfont as an inhibitor for CYP3A4 substrates is necessary.
In the run-in phase subjects received an oral Minidril (0.03 mg ethinyl estradiol and 0.15 mg
levonorgestrel) tablet alone for 21 days. In treatment period 1, subjects continued with the
Minidril oral tablet for an additional 21 days. Following a 7-day washout period, treatment period
2 commenced with subjects receiving Minidril oral tablet with crinecerfont 100 mg for an
additional 21 days. OCS were administered with food except during treatment period 2, where
both drugs were administered after a moderate fat breakfast. PK samples were obtained at
prespecified time points over 24 hours and sparsely for 21 days for crinecerfont and OCS. GMRs
with 90% CIs were calculated and compared for AUC0-∞, AUC0-tlast, and Cmax for ethinyl

have a clinically significant increase in COC exposures.

20.2.10. QTc Study, Study NBI-74788-1719
Study Design
This is a phase 1 single-dose, randomized, placebo- and active-controlled, four-way, cross-over
study that evaluated the effect of crinecerfont on the QT/QTc (corrected QT) interval in adult
healthy subjects. The primary objective of this study was to characterize the effect of a single
therapeutic (300 mg) and supratherapeutic (800 mg) dose of crinecerfont on the heart rate- QTc.
A total of 48 adult subjects were enrolled and 41 completed the study. Each subject received
single doses of crinecerfont 300 mg, crinecerfont 800 mg, placebo, or moxifloxacin 400 mg
(positive control).
All treatments were administered with 240 mL water after 30 minutes following the start of a
high-fat, high-calorie breakfast. There was a washout period of 21 days between each treatment
group. Electrocardiogram samples were collected at specified times for 24 hours postdose. PK
samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours for crinecerfont and placebo
groups, while samples were collected at prespecified times for 24 hours for the moxifloxacin
group. Crinecerfont and four of its metabolites (NBI-756179, M4, M9, and M11) were analyzed
by LC-MS/MS. GMRs were calculated at 300 mg and 800 mg for crinecerfont and its major
metabolite NBI-756179.
Results
PK Analysis
The 800 mg dose of crinecerfont had 2.4-fold high GMRs for AUC0-tlast and AUC0-∞ compared to
the 300 mg dose. The 800 mg dose of crinecerfont had a 2.3-fold higher value for Cmax compared
to the 300 mg dose. A similar trend was noted with the major metabolite NBI-756179.
QTc Analysis
The mean-placebo-corrected change in baseline in QT interval corrected for heart rate using
Fridericia’s correction (QTcF) and 90% CI following 300 mg crinecerfont, 800 mg

for AUC0-∞, AUC0-tlast, and Cmax in the test groups (regimens B, C, and D) to the reference

This is a phase 1, randomized, open-label study in healthy adult subjects to evaluate the effect of
food on the bioavailability of 100 mg crinecerfont oral solution and to estimate the
bioavailability of 25 mg and 50 mg crinecerfont oral solution relative to 100 mg crinecerfont oral
solution. A total of 16 healthy adult subjects between 19 and 55 years of age were enrolled and
15 completed the study. One subject dropped out due to COVID. Crinecerfont oral solution at
25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg under fed conditions and 100 mg under fasted conditions were

20.2.16. Phase 3 Hard Gel Capsule vs. Commercial
Soft Gel Capsule Bioavailability and Food Effect
for Commercial Soft Gel Capsule, Study NBI74788-1736
Study Design
This is a phase 1, randomized, open-label study in healthy adult subjects to evaluate the
bioequivalence of soft gel and hard gel crinecerfont capsules and the effect of food on
bioavailability. The primary objectives of this study are to determine the BE under fed
conditions, of 100 mg crinecerfont soft gel capsule (commercial formulation) relative to
2×crinecerfont 50 mg hard gel capsules (phase 3 capsules); additionally, this study also evaluated
the effect of food on the pharmacokinetics of 100 mg crinecerfont soft gel formulation
(commercial formulation). A total of 50 adult subjects were enrolled and 44 subjects completed
the study. A total of 49 subjects contributed to the BE study, while a subset of 19 subjects were
used for the food-effect evaluation of the commercial formulation. For the BE study, crinecerfont
2×50 mg hard gel capsules, or 1×100 mg soft gel capsule under fed conditions were administered
to the subjects in a cross-over design with a washout period of 21 days.
For the food-effect study for the commercial capsules, data were reviewed from the BE study
and 19 subjects were recruited for the study and received 1×100 mg soft gel capsule under fasted
conditions. All subjects fasted overnight for at least 10 hours. For subjects in the fed state, a
high-fat, high-calorie meal was consumed in 30 minutes and was followed by drug
administration. For subjects in the fasted state, drug was administered with 240 mL of water. PK
samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours. Statistical analysis for the BE
between the phase 3 capsule and the commercial capsule food effect for the commercial capsule
included calculation of GMRs with 90% CIs comparing AUC0-∞, AUC0-tlast, and Cmax.
Results
GMRs with the 90% CIs for AUC0-tlast, AUC0-∞, and Cmax for 100 mg crinecerfont hard gel and
soft gel capsules are presented in Table 159. Comparison of GMRs with the 90% CIs for
AUC0-tlast, AUC0-∞, and Cmax for 100 mg crinecerfont soft gel capsules under fasted and fed
conditions are presented in Table 160. These results were independently confirmed by reviewer
analysis.

20.2.17. Phase 2 Dose-Finding Study, Trial NBI74788-CAH2001
Study Design
This is a phase 2, open-label, multiple-dose, dose-escalation study to assess the safety,
tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of crinecerfont in adult female and male
subjects (18 to 50 years of age) with a documented medical diagnosis of classic CAH with a
serum 17‑OHP level of ≥1,000 ng/dL at screening. The primary objectives of this study are to
assess different dosing regimens of crinecerfont in adults with CAH, evaluate the effect of
repeated doses of crinecerfont and different dosing regimens on endogenous levels of
pharmacodynamic (PD) biomarkers in adults with CAH, and evaluate the plasma exposures
following repeated doses of crinecerfont.
Crinecerfont doses evaluated were:
•

Cohort 1: 50 mg once daily at bedtime (2200 hours) (n=8 enrolled/8 completed)

•

Cohort 2: 100 mg once daily at bedtime (2200 hours) (n=7 enrolled/6 completed)

•

Cohort 3: 100 mg once daily with evening meal (1900 hours) (n=8 enrolled/7 completed)

•

Cohort 4: 100 mg twice daily with breakfast (0700 hours) and evening meal (1900 hours)
(n=8 enrolled/8 completed)

Each dosing regimen was administered over 14 consecutive days. A total of 18 subjects were
enrolled in the study, of which 13 subjects were re-enrolled in cohorts 3 and 4. Cohorts 1 and 2
received the crinecerfont dose with 237 mL of vanilla-flavored Ensure Plus while subjects in
cohorts 3 and 4 were in outpatient settings for most of the study duration and ate meals at home.
On the last day of dosing, subjects took the drug in cohorts 3 and 4 following a moderate fat,
moderate calorie evening meal. All subjects took their usual morning dose of concurrent
steroidal treatments at approximately 1000 hours.

PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points over 504 hours and plasma PK parameters
were calculated for crinecerfont and metabolite NBI-756179. Primary PD samples (17-OHP)
were obtained at screening and postdose at prespecified times over 15 hours. Key secondary PD
samples were obtained over 24 hours to determine average 17-OHP, A4, and ACTH over 24

20.2.18. Phase 2 Dose Justification Study for Phase 3
Study in Pediatric Subjects With CAH, Trial NBI74788-CAH2008
Study Design
This is a phase 2, open-label, multiple-dose, dose-escalation study to assess the safety,
tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of crinecerfont in pediatric subjects (14 to
16 years of age) with a documented medical diagnosis of classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency
(CAH) with a serum 17-OHP level of ≥800 ng/dL at screening. The primary objectives of this
study are to assess the safety and tolerability of crinecerfont, evaluate the effect of repeated doses
of crinecerfont on endogenous levels of PD biomarkers, and evaluate the PK of crinecerfont and
its metabolite NBI-756179.
Crinecerfont was administered as 50 mg twice daily with breakfast (0700 hours) and evening
meals (1900 hours). Concurrent steroidal dose was administered in the morning at approximately
1000 hours. Each dosing regimen was administered over 14 consecutive days. A total of eight
subjects were enrolled and completed the study. PK samples were obtained at prespecified time
points over 504 hours and plasma PK parameters were calculated for crinecerfont and metabolite
NBI-756179. Primary PD samples (17-OHP) were obtained at screening and postdose at
prespecified times over 15 hours. Key secondary PD samples were obtained over 24 hours to
determine average 17-OHP, A4, and ACTH over 24 hours.

in Figure 48 and the summary of PK parameters for the four cohorts is presented in Table 162.

20.2.19. Phase 3 Study in Adults With CAH, Trial
CAH3003
This is a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy,
safety, and tolerability of crinecerfont versus placebo in 182 adult subjects with classic 21hydroxylase deficiency (CAH). The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of
crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily in reducing daily GC dosage while maintaining adrenal
androgen control. Subjects were randomized 2:1 in crinecerfont: placebo group (122:60). The
study design and the doses for each period are presented in Figure 52.
PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points during the study duration and plasma
concentrations (ng/mL) were calculated for crinecerfont and its metabolites (NBI-756179, NBI742939 (M4), NBI-1084059 (M9), and NBI-1084060 (M11)). The primary study endpoint was
percent change from baseline (CFB) in GC daily dose at Week 24 with A4 levels controlled at
≤120% of baseline or ≤upper limit of normal (ULN) for age and sex. A key secondary endpoint
was CFB in A4 levels at Week 4. Data are presented until the end of the open-label period (12
months) where 174 subjects entered the open-label period. Two subjects in the crinecerfont PK
subset were not included, one due to an adverse event and another lost to follow-up, while one
subject in the placebo group was not included in the analysis as they withdrew from the study.

The analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) analysis of least-squares (LS) mean (SEM) percentage of
CFB for serum A4 at Week 4 for the placebo and crinecerfont groups were 21.2 (11.4) and -45.2
(7.7), respectively. The % LS mean difference (95% CI) between the crinecerfont and placebo
group was -66.3% (-91.6, -41.1) with a p-value of <0.0001.31 The median percent change from
baseline (range) after 4 weeks of dosing at 100 mg twice daily, during the GC stable phase, for
ACTH was -65.8% (-98.6% to 7442.9%).
Conclusions
•

By Week 2, the plasma crinecerfont 100 mg twice daily dose achieved steady state and mean
plasma concentrations for crinecerfont, and its metabolites (data not shown) remained similar
for the 12 months of data reported.

•

The trough plasma concentration (Ctrough) mean (% coefficient of variation [CV])
concentrations for crinecerfont at Weeks 4 and 24 were 1843.73 (48.9) and 2029.57 (47.1)
ng/mL.

•

At Week 4, ~66% reduction in the 24-hour average concentrations from baseline for PD
marker A4 at 100 mg twice daily doses was observed.

We defer to clinical and statistical reviewers for the assessment of primary and secondary
efficacy endpoints.

20.2.20. Phase 3 Study in Pediatric Subjects With
CAH, Trial NBI-74788-CAH2006
This is a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study evaluating the efficacy,
safety, and tolerability of crinecerfont versus placebo in 103 pediatric subjects with classic CAH
due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the efficacy
of crinecerfont in reducing adrenal steroid levels during a glucocorticoid-stable period, and key
secondary objective is to evaluate the efficacy of crinecerfont in reducing daily GC dosage while
maintaining adrenal androgen control. Subjects were randomized 2:1 in crinecerfont: placebo
group (69:34). The study design and the doses for each period are presented in Figure 53.
PK samples were obtained at prespecified time points during the study duration and plasma
concentrations (ng/mL) were calculated for crinecerfont and its metabolites (NBI-756179, NBI742939 (M4), NBI-1084059 (M9), and NBI-1084060 (M11)). The primary study endpoint was
CFB in serum A4 at Week 4. The key secondary endpoint was Percent CFB in GC daily dose at
Week 28, while Week 28 serum androstenedione was ≤120% of the baseline value or ≤ULN,
according to sex and either age (for Tanner stage 1) or pubertal stage (for Tanner stages 2 to 5).
Data are presented until the end of the open-label period (12 months) where 97 subjects (66
crinecerfont: 31 placebo) entered the open-label period and all completed the study.

20.3. Bioanalytical Method Validation and
Performance
We reviewed the bioanalytical method validation reports and performance for the quantification
of crinecerfont (NBI-74788l, SAR125543) and its metabolites (NBI-756179 (M6), NBI-742939
(M4), NBI-1084059 (M9), NBI-1084060 (M11)). Three LC-MS/MS methods were developed
and validated for the quantitative determination of crinecerfont and its metabolite concentrations
in human serum in the completed clinical studies. Detailed methods and validation parameters
are described below (Table 167, Table 168, and Table 169). The linearity of standard curve,
selectivity/specificity, assay accuracy and precision, extraction efficiency and dilution fulfilled
the standard acceptance criteria. The established frozen storage stability and run storage stability
covered the corresponding study period and sample analysis period. We determined that these
method validation and sample analysis are acceptable.

20.5.2. Introduction
The primary objectives of the Applicant’s analysis were to:
•

Develop a popPK model to characterize crinecerfont pharmacokinetics in healthy subjects
and adult and pediatric subjects with CAH

•

Evaluate the covariate effects on crinecerfont pharmacokinetics

•

Generate individual crinecerfont PK exposure metrics for E-R analyses for safety and
efficacy

20.5.3. Model Development
Data
The popPK analysis was based on PK data from four phase 1 studies in healthy subjects, two
phase 2 studies, and two phase 3 studies in subjects with CAH. The study design, study
population, dose levels, drug formulation, and type of PK samples are summarized in Table 173.
For clinical studies that were excluded and the associated rationale, details can be found in
Section 3.1 in the Applicant’s popPK report.
The final nonlinear mixed-effects modeling (NONMEM) data file for analysis contained 6647
PK observations from 342 unique subjects (Table 174). Note that nine subjects were included in
both phase 2 and phase 3 studies, contributing to 351 subjects in the summary tables. Table 175
provides summary statistics of the baseline demographic covariates in the analysis dataset.

Base Model
The base model was a three-compartment popPK model with transit compartment absorption and
linear clearance. Interindividual variability (or random effects) was modeled assuming a lognormal distribution for patient level random effects. Residual variability was described using a
log-additive error model during model development and subsequent model runs. Model
evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of
goodness-of-fit, diagnostic plots, significant reductions in objective function value, accuracy of
parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval excluding 0), successful model convergence,
and diagnostic plots.
Figure 54. Scheme of Base PopPK Model Structure

Source: Applicant’s popPK report, Figure 5.1, page 37
Abbreviations: ktr, transit compartment rate constant; ka, absorption rate constant; NT, number of transit compartments; Vc/F,
apparent central volume of distribution; V2/F and V3/F, apparent peripheral volumes of distribution; Q1/F and Q2/F, apparent
intercompartmental clearance; CL/F, apparent drug clearance; popPK, population pharmacokinetic(s)

Covariate Analysis
Covariate-parameter relationships were investigated and identified using clinical and physiologic
relevance, exploratory analysis, prior knowledge, and mechanistic plausibility. Collinearity of
covariates was assessed to ensure that no collinear covariates were added to the model. An
assessment of any remaining trends was conducted by graphical inspection of covariate effects
(plots of maximum a posteriori Bayes estimates of individual random effects and/or normalized
prediction distribution error versus covariates). Continuous covariates were evaluated using a
power function, and categorical covariates were parameterized as a fractional change.
In addition to the covariates listed in Table 176, any remaining trends in random effects for
dexamethasone use and Tanner stage were examined in a post hoc exploratory graphical

analysis. Only a limited number of subjects in the dataset (n=17) received concomitant
dexamethasone at baseline (≤1 mg total daily dose) with crinecerfont.

20.5.4. Final Model
The final popPK model included fixed effects of body weight on clearance and volume of
distribution-related terms. For pediatric subjects under 18 years of age, time-varying body weight
was used. For adult subjects, time-varying body weight was used for adult volume of distribution
terms. Allometric scalers were fixed to 0.75 and 1, respectively, for clearance and volume of
distribution-related terms. Effects of food and formulation were evaluated on mean transit time,
absorption rate constant (Ka), and relative bioavailability (Frel). Effect of baseline estimated
glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was evaluated on clearance. Effect of baseline age was
evaluated on central volume of distribution.
The parameter estimates for the final covariate model are listed in Table 177. The diagnostic
plots (observed versus predicted, conditional weighted residuals, normalized prediction
distribution errors, and Q-Q plots), for the final covariate model for all data are shown in Figure
55. The visual predictive checks (VPCs) for the final covariate model stratified by phase 3 study,
formulation, and disease status are shown in Figure 56. Relationships of ETAs (i.e., random
effects) for apparent clearance and select covariates are shown in Figure 57. Forest plot for
steady-state AUC is shown in Figure 58.

The reviewer was able to reproduce and verify the Applicant’s final popPK model, and no
discordance was identified. The model parameters were estimated with reasonable precision
based on the relative standard errors (RSEs) and the 95% CIs (as shown above). The highest
RSEs for the key PK parameters were 51.2% and 29.4% for Ka and Q2, respectively, and all
other RSEs were below 5%. The shrinkages were generally acceptable in supporting simulation
for dose selection in another population (between 20.5% to 33.9% except for Ka at 43.5%).
Given the populations studied (adults and pediatric subjects), formulation differences, and food
effect (fed and fasted states), the relatively higher variabilities around Ka and associated
interindividual variability are expected. Based on the observed versus predicted data scatter
plots, the data points are randomly scattered around the line of unity with no significant trend
identified. The conditional weighted residuals (CWRES) and normalized prediction distribution
errors (NPDE) plots also demonstrate no bias or misspecification of the final model.
Additionally, the VPCs and select ETA plots also support that the popPK model adequately
captures the central tendency of crinecerfont pharmacokinetics. For additional model diagnostic
plots, such as random effects versus covariates, refer to the Applicant’s popPK report. Overall,
the popPK model is adequate in describing crinecerfont pharmacokinetics in the target adult and
pediatric patient populations, in simulation for dose selection in the 10 to <20 kg pediatric group,
and in deriving phase 3 individual PK exposure metrics for E-R safety and efficacy analyses.

20.5.5. Comparison of Adult and Pediatric Exposures
Based on clinical benefits achieved with crinecerfont exposures (i.e., AUC24) corresponding to
200 mg once daily (Study TDR10671) or 100 mg bid (Trial NBI-74788-CAH2001), the
Applicant selected the 100 mg bid dosing regimen because of the potential to produce sustained
CRF antagonist activity over the entire day (refer to Section 12.1.1). For selection of the dosing
regimen for pediatric patients by weight bands (10 to <20 kg, 20 to <55 kg, and ≥55 kg,
corresponding to regimens of 25 mg solution bid, 50 mg solution bid, and 100 mg capsule bid),
the Applicant used exposure matching to the adult subjects. To match to the adult exposures of
100 mg bid, simulations were performed incorporating allometry for pediatric subjects with
CAH using the final popPK model.
A total of 500 virtual subjects were simulated for each dose level and weight band. Ages and
weight were sampled from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)
dataset, and crinecerfont doses were simulated for the fed state. Simulated exposures of steadystate AUC24 were compared between pediatric subjects and adult subjects. For the simulation,
PK parameters were fixed to the final popPK model values. Of note, the clinical studies did not
include pediatric subjects under 20 kg. Covariates sampled from the NHANES dataset provided
virtual pediatric subjects of 10 to <20 kg. Simulated steady-state AUCs are summarized in Table
178 and Table 179 and are illustrated in Figure 59 by dosing groups and formulation.

The simulation results demonstrated that pediatric subjects weighing ≥55 kg and 20 to <55 kg
have overlapping exposures (i.e., AUC at steady state) when compared to the adult exposures,
resulting in 91.6% and 76.8% of pediatric subjects within the 90% prediction interval,
respectively. For pediatric subjects weighing 10 to <20 kg, the percentage of simulated subjects
falling within the 90% prediction interval of the adult exposure was numerically lower (68.4%)
than those of the other two pediatric subgroups. Additionally, the median AUCs of the two
lowest pediatric weight bands were lower than the 50th percentile of the adult AUC.
To further assess the appropriateness of the 25 mg bid dosing in the absence of studying the 10 to
<20 kg population (i.e., no PK or clinical outcomes data), the following key points were
considered:
•

Based on the disease state, pathophysiology, and current standard of care, pediatric patients
down to 4 years of age with CAH are likely to fall under the 20 to <55 kg group (see Section
12.3.1).

•

PK data and clinical outcomes data were available from pediatric subjects weighing 20 to
<55 kg in the phase 3 clinical trial (Table 175), and this pediatric subgroup is more
physiologically similar when compared to pediatric patients weighing 10 to <20 kg regarding
physiology, disease state, disease progression, and expected efficacy response for CAH
(based on the indicated age cut-off).

•

Efficacy outcomes of the pediatric subjects weighing 20 to <55 kg are considered acceptable
per the clinical review team assessment (see Section 12.3.1).

•

The relatively higher exposure in adult subjects serve as the safety exposure coverage.
280

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
Therefore, the pediatric subgroup of 20 to <55 kg is an acceptable efficacy reference group for
exposure matching for the 10 to <20 kg group.
Further simulations of alternative regimens were conducted by the reviewer to support the 25 mg
bid regimen. For the virtual population, a total of 9500 subjects were generated using the
NHANES database across all 4 groups as shown below. Specifically, 1000 and 3500 subjects
were allocated to the 10 to <20 kg group and 20 to <55 kg group, respectively, with 500 virtual
pediatric subjects allocated for each subgroup at 5-kg increments. In the reviewer’s analysis, two
adjustments were made to reflect the indication for crinecerfont in this NDA: (1) the minimum
age was raised to 4 years, and (2) the upper bound of the adult body weight was capped at
155 kg, which is approximately one standard deviation (of the body weight distribution of the
overall PK population) above the highest body weight studied in the PK population.
The 25 mg bid, 37.5 mg bid, and 50 mg bid dosages of the solution formulation were simulated
for the 10 to <20 kg group. The proposed dosage of 50 mg bid was simulated for the 20 to
<55 kg group.
As shown in Figure 60 and Figure 61, the simulated regimens of 37.5 mg bid and 50 mg bid for
the 10 to <20 kg group had improved AUC and Cmax relative to those of the reference population
of 20 to <55 kg; however, relatively higher proportions of the simulated subjects were also
projected to have exposures above the 95th percentile of the reference exposures. Therefore,
25 mg bid for the 10 to <20 kg subgroup is expected to produce similar exposures to those of
50 mg bid for the 20 to <55 kg subgroup, and because a high proportion of subjects weighing 10
to <20 kg is expected to have exposures within the adult exposure, the exposures of the proposed
25 mg bid in 10 to <25 kg subgroup is expected to be safe and effective.

20.5.6. E-R Analysis
Using data from the phase 3 studies in adult (CAH3003) and pediatric (CAH2006) subjects with
CAH, E-R analyses were conducted independently in each population to characterize the
relationship between plasma exposure and clinical endpoints and to support evidence of
effectiveness of the proposed doses for adult and pediatric patients with CAH. The Applicant’s
objectives of the E-R analyses were to:
•

Develop an exposure-efficacy model for percent CFB in daily GC dose while maintaining
adequate control of androgen levels at Week 24 (CAH3003) and Week 28 (CAH2006) in
adult and pediatric subjects with CAH, respectively

•

Develop an exposure-efficacy model for the achievement of reduction in GC daily dose to
physiologic levels (≤11 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalent adjusted for body surface area
[BSA]) while maintaining adequate control of androgen levels at Week 24 (CAH3003) and
Week 28 (CAH2006) in adult and pediatric subjects with CAH, respectively

•

Develop an exposure-efficacy model for change from baseline in serum A4 (i.e.,
androstenedione) prior to morning GC dose at Week 4 while subjects were on a stable
background GC daily dose in adult and pediatric subjects with CAH

•

Develop an exposure-safety model for a safety endpoint in adult and pediatric subjects with
CAH, if deemed necessary

•

Evaluate the effects of select covariates of interest on E-R relationships

•

Compare the E-R relationships between adult and pediatric subjects

In the Applicant’s E-R model for GC response at Week 24 from baseline, the parameter
precision of fixed effects appears reasonable based on the 95% CI. Null effect is contained
within the 95% CI of age, sex, body weight, and baseline GC dose effect on intercept, indicating

suggests that the probability of achieving a GC response (i.e., GC dose at physiologic levels)
increases as crinecerfont exposure increases (within the range of studied exposure); however, the
95% CIs of the beta slope are numerically small (0.0000191 to 0.0000385) and approaching
zero, suggesting that the odds ratio is close to 1 and that other factors may also be driving the
probability of GC response. Overall, the results of this E-R analysis should be interpreted with
caution.
20.5.6.1.4. Safety
In the adult study, TEAEs that occurred with at least 5% greater incidence in the crinecerfont
arm were fatigue (24.6% crinecerfont; 15.3% placebo), coronavirus infection (13.9%; 8.5%), and
arthralgia (7.4%; 0%). Fatigue had the highest reported frequency in the crinecerfont arm and
was, therefore, selected as the AE for exploratory E-R analysis.

alternative dosing approaches are needed.

CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
In the Applicant’s E-R model for GC response at Week 28 from baseline for pediatric patients,
the 95% CIs are relatively wide for all parameter estimates. Null effect is contained within the
95% CI of sex on intercept, indicating minimal impact. Based on the final model predictions, the
exposure-response relationship suggests that probability of achieving GC response (i.e., GC dose
at physiologic levels) increases as crinecerfont exposure increases (within the range of studied
exposure). However, the 95% CI of the slope contains zero, suggesting that other factors may be
driving the probability of GC response. Additionally, considering the VPC plot of the observed
data and the relatively narrow range of studied exposures reflective of the exposure matching
approach, the result suggests that the E-R relationship is relatively flat and maximal response
(within the studied exposure) may be achieved in the pediatric patient population.
20.5.6.2.4. Safety
In the pediatric study, TEAEs that occurred with at least 5% greater incidence in the crinecerfont
arm compared to placebo were headache (24.6% crinecerfont; 6.1% placebo), upper respiratory
tract infection (11.6%, 0%), abdominal pain (7.2%; 0%), fatigue (7.2%; 0%), and streptococcal
pharyngitis (5.8%, 0%). Headache had the highest reported frequency in the crinecerfont arm and
was, therefore, selected as the AE for exploratory E-R analysis.
Figure 70. E-R Relationship for Safety (Pediatric)

Source: Applicant’s E-R report, Figure B.40, page 215
Solid circles represent the data points; the solid blue line represents the LOESS smooth trend line through the data
Abbreviations: E-R, exposure-response; LOESS, locally weighted scatterplot smoothing

CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
While there is an increasing probability of headache at Week 28 amongst pediatric subjects as
crinecerfont exposure increases (within the studied exposure range), the interpretation of this
analysis result is limited by the number of subjects who experienced this AE. In total, 17 and 2
subjects had headache in the treatment and placebo arms, respectively. Of note, the incidence of
headache in the active arm remains numerically higher than that of the placebo arm (24.6%
versus 6.1%, respectively). Overall, the results from the exposure-efficacy and exploratory
exposure-safety analyses support the proposed doses for pediatric patients with CAH in
achieving clinical benefits and support that no alternative dosing approaches are needed in the
pediatric subgroups.

Not applicable.

a The screening period can be extended by up to 4 weeks after discussion with and approval of the medical monitor to allow for delayed screening laboratory results that are needed to determine eligibility
or to accommodate other extenuating logistical issues, such as scheduling. The Week 4 visit will have a visit window of ±5 days, and subsequent visits through Week 52 will have a visit window of ±7
days. The Week 56 visit (if applicable) visit has a visit window of +7 days. All Week 28 assessments should be completed before a subject begins open-label treatment. Not all assessments must be
conducted on the same day, but all assessments for a given visit must be completed within the visit window. If a subject’s GC regimen is adjusted due to stress dosing, the subject should resume their GC
dosing regimen for at least 3 days before their next scheduled lab test if the duration of stress dosing is 3 days or less, and for at least 7 days before their next scheduled lab test if the duration of stress
dosing is ≥4 days (this 3- or 7-day window supersedes all other visit windows).
b At home or the study site. At Week 16 and Week 40, at home is an option if height is not required. During the screening period, blood and urine collection may be arranged at home.
c Only if a preceding GC dose adjustment occurred.
d Subjects will have further GC adjustment starting at Week 32 only if their Week 32 GC dose is >11 mg/m2/day.
e For subjects who discontinue the study prior to Week 52, assessments will be performed at the ET visit and at the safety follow-up visit, consisting of the same procedures as shown for Week 56 in the
schedule of assessments. A safety follow-up visit is not required if the last dose of study drug was at least 4 weeks prior to the ET visit. Subjects who complete the Week 52 visit and elect to not enter the
OLE will undergo a safety follow-up visit approximately 4 weeks after last dose of study drug.
f Only for subjects age ≥12 years of age.
g Tanner stage at screening and Day 1. Historical assessment of Tanner staging is acceptable if Tanner stage 5 has been previously documented. Tanner staging at subsequent visits is required only if
baseline Tanner stage <5. In addition, subjects with Tanner stage 4 at baseline do not need to undergo Tanner staging at Week 16 or Week 40.
h Measure blood pressure 3 times, in up to 1-minute intervals, after the subject has been sitting quietly for at least 5 minutes. Measure weight with subjects not wearing shoes or outerwear (e.g., jackets or
coats). Measure height (in subjects not wearing shoes) as the average of 3 to 6 measurements using a stadiometer (or length board) (Section 9.3.3). Height not required at Week 4 or Week 56 (all
subjects) or at Week 16 and Week 40 if growth <2.5 cm in past year, complete fusion of epiphyses on hand/wrist radiograph, or more than 2 years past menarche (females).
i Only for females of childbearing potential. Serum pregnancy testing at screening, urine pregnancy tests at other visits. For subjects with body weight <55 kg, see modified blood sample collection
schedules in Appendix B.
j Blood samples for A4, 17-OHP, and ACTH will be collected: For subjects with body weight <55 kg, see modified blood sample collection schedules for subjects with a body weight <55 kg in Appendix B.
For subjects who are ≥6 years of age with a body weight ≥55 kg: On Day 1 and Week 4 approximately 15 minutes before and just prior to dosing with the morning GC and (Week 4) study drug between
approximately 0800 and 0830 hours and at 2, 3, 4, and 6 hours after dosing. Any midday GC dose the subject is receiving should be taken after blood is sampled 6 hours after dosing. All subjects should
take their glucocorticoid dose the night before prior to 2100 hours.
k For all subjects, a blood sample for PK prior to the morning study dose will be collected at Weeks 4, 16, 28, 40, and 52/ET, if ET occurs prior to Week 52. At Week 4: for subjects who are ≥6 years of age
with a body weight ≥35 kg, blood samples for PK will also be collected approximately 2, 3, 4, and 6 hours after dosing.

l Salivary samples for adrenal androgens and precursors will be collected:
–Day 1 and Weeks 4, 28, and 52/ET: at approximately 0600 hours, at approximately 0800 hours prior to dosing with morning GC and (after Day 1) study drug and at approximately 3 and 6 hours after
dosing, and within 30 minutes prior to the evening dose of GC; if subject is not on an evening GC dose, then prior to bedtime. Any midday GC dose that the subject is receiving should be taken after the
salivary sample collection 6 hours after dosing.
–Weeks 8, 12, 16, 20, 32, 36, 40, and 44: prior to morning GC dose at approximately the same time as the blood sample. If a blood sample is not obtained at a visit (e.g., because no GC dose
adjustment was required), a salivary sample does not need to be obtained.
m For subjects with body weight <55 kg, see modified blood sample collection schedules in Appendix B. Subjects should take their GC dose the night before prior to 2100 hours and hold their morning

include ACTH at Weeks 16, 28, 40, 52/ET, and 56. Morning dosing should occur between approximately 0800 and 0830 hours with breakfast. At Week 28 and Week 52/ET, another blood sample will be
collected at 3 hours after dosing for subjects ≥6 years of age with body weight ≥20 kg.
n Only in females with the most recent prior bone age <14 years and males with the most recent prior bone age <16 years. Bone age assessment is not required at the ET visit if the subject had a bone

p EQ-5D-Y for age 8 to 15 years, EQ-5D-5L for age 16 years and older.

s Only for subjects ≥6 years of age. Baseline/Screening version used at screening, and Since Last Visit version at subsequent visits.
t Hirsutism scale only for females.
u Menstrual Cycle Questionnaire only for females who have undergone menarche and are not on hormonal or intrauterine device contraceptives.
v Palatability will be assessed for subjects ≥6 years of age, and ease of administration will be assessed by caregivers of subjects <6 years of age. The palatability/ease of administration assessment
should be administered within approximately 15 minutes after study drug dosing.
w Subjects will return all unused study drug and packaging, and a compliance check will be performed.
x For subjects with body weight <55 kg, see modified blood sample collection in Appendix B.
z Glucocorticoid dose adjustment should be considered based on hormone results, expected to be available within 7 to 14 days of blood sample collection.

22. Efficacy
The efficacy assessment was based on the two phase 3 trials, CAH3003 in adults and CAH2006
in children. The efficacy findings are discussed in Section 12.2 of this document.
The two phase 2 dose-finding trials—Trial CAH2001 in adults with CAH and Trial CAH2008 in
pediatric subjects with CAH—informed dosing for the phase 3 trials and are discussed in
Section 12.1 of this document.
The review team conducted additional subgroup analyses of the primary efficacy endpoint for
trials CAH3003 in adults and CAH2006 in children.

Subgroup Analysis of Primary Endpoint
Trial CAH3003
Analyses of the primary endpoint by subgroup showed that the glucocorticoid total daily dose
decreased from baseline to Week 24 in the crinecerfont group, compared with the placebo group,
in all prespecified subgroups (Figure 72). Interpretation of 95% CIs in some subgroups was
limited by their small sample sizes and likely some random highs and random lows in sample
estimates of subgroup treatment effects. Therefore, we also derived shrinkage estimates of
subgroup treatment effects using a Bayesian hierarchical model based on summary sample
estimates.
The total variability in the sample estimates is the sum of the within-subgroup variability of the
sample estimator and the across-subgroups variability in underlying/true parameter values.
Shrinkage estimates of the subgroup treatment effect, which borrows information from the other
subgroups while estimating the treatment effect for a specific subgroup, is a “weighted” average
of the sample estimate and overall estimate. The weights are based on the ratio of the betweensubgroup variability to the within-subgroup variability. The greater that ratio, the smaller the
weight on the overall estimate (the less the shrinkage).
For i =1, 2…, n; Yi represents the observed sample estimate of treatment effect in a subgroup
level i, assume Yi~N(µi, σi2) where:
•

𝜎2𝑖 are the observed variance for sample estimates,

•

𝜇𝑖 ~ N(µ, τ2), and

•

µ ~ N(0, 400), 1/τ2 ~ Gamma(0.001, 0.001).

The variance of 400 for the hyper-prior 𝜇 ∼ 𝑁(0, 𝑣𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 = 400), was chosen as
4 × 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑖𝑑𝑢𝑎𝑙 𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 of the treatment effect.

23. Clinical Safety
23.1. Abuse Potential
The FDA controlled substance staff (CSS) reviewed the drug abuse liability assessment of
crinecerfont. In a memorandum to NDA 218808 and finalized in Document Archiving,
Reporting, and Regulatory Tracking System (DARRTS) on October 23, 2024, CSS concluded:
•

The receptor binding and activity data indicate that crinecerfont is a CRF1 receptor
antagonist. Receptor binding studies demonstrated that crinecerfont did not bind to any
receptors, transporters, or ion channels typically associated with drugs having a potential for
abuse.

•

Additional studies including nonclinical abuse potential assessments and a human abuse
potential study were not requested.

•

A review of TEAEs in clinical studies did not reveal any evidence to suggest that
crinecerfont has a potential for abuse or physical dependence. The most prevalent AEs
observed in clinical trials were fatigue, headache, and pyrexia.

317
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
•

The proposed drug product, if approved under this NDA, will not require a Drug Abuse and
Dependence section in its label.

CSS concluded that crinecerfont does not appear to have abuse potential and should not be
controlled under the Controlled Substances Act. Crinecerfont does not require a Section 9 (Drug
Abuse and Dependence section) in its label.

23.2. Laboratory Analyses, Trial CAH3003
23.2.1. Chemistry, Trial CAH3003
There were no meaningful differences between crinecerfont and placebo groups in mean change
from baseline in any chemistry parameter during the double-blind treatment period. Renal
function remained stable (see Figure 74 and Figure 75) and lipid parameters in both treatment
groups declined slightly during the double-blind treatment phase (Figure 76).
Outlier analysis tables for chemistry and renal function parameters are shown in Table 195 and
Table 196. Other than what was discussed in earlier sections of this review, there were no
clinically meaningful differences in incidences of laboratory parameters outside the normal range
between treatment groups. The higher incidence of low bicarbonate (<20 mEq/L) and low
calcium (<8.4 mg/dL) with crinecerfont vs. placebo in this trial was not observed in the pediatric
trial; this lack of consistency across trials reduces the likelihood that these findings are drugrelated.
Outlier analysis for lipid parameters is shown in Table 197. The greater frequency of outliers in
some of the lipid parameters in the crinecerfont group is not clinically meaningful because the
mean change from baseline was not significant and not significantly different from placebo
(figures included).

27. Other Drug Development Considerations
The Division of Medication Error Prevention and Analysis 1 (DMEPA 1) concluded that the
proposed proprietary name, CRENESSITY, is conditionally acceptable.33
DMEPA 1 also reviewed the proposed CRENESSITY prescribing information (PI), patient
prescribing information, and container labels for areas of vulnerability that may lead to
medication errors and provided recommendations to minimize the risk for medication error.34
Labeling changes are discussed in detail in Section 29.

30. Postmarketing Requirements and
Commitments
The review team is concerned about a serious risk of inhibition of ACTH secretion in the
developing fetus, which may lead to fetal growth restriction, preterm delivery, or demise, and to
an unexpected serious risk of infant exposure to crinecerfont during lactation. The Division of
Pediatrics and Maternal Health (DPMH) in a memorandum of consultation filed to NDA 218808
in DARRTS on September 13, 2024, recommends a postmarketing requirement (PMR) for a
descriptive pregnancy safety study (DPSS) for the following reasons:
•

Three pregnancies occurred during the drug development program, indicating that females of
reproductive potential with classic CAH may take crinecerfont. Although there were
pregnancies that occurred during drug development, there are no data from these pregnancies
to inform the use of crinecerfont during pregnancy. Thus, a DPSS would provide necessary
pregnancy safety data.

•

Given that classic CAH is a rare disease, the number of pregnant patients who use
crinecerfont is likely to be small. With a small number of pregnant patients using
crinecerfont, a pregnancy exposure registry would be unlikely to adequately enroll patients;
therefore, a DPSS is preferred.

•

Crinecerfont is systemically absorbed and will cross the placenta. Crinecerfont has the
potential to inhibit ACTH secretion in the developing fetus, thereby reducing cortisol levels
in the fetus, which may result in fetal growth restriction, preterm delivery, or demise.

DPMH also recommends a PMR for a clinical lactation study to determine the extent to which
crinecerfont is present in human milk. Their rationale is that crinecerfont is present in animal
milk, which presents a potential for adrenal insufficiency or crisis in healthy neonates and infants
exposed to crinecerfont via breast milk.
The following are postmarketing requirements to assess the effect of crinecerfont on developing
fetuses and lactation:
•

Conduct a worldwide descriptive study that collects prospective and retrospective data in
women exposed to crinecerfont during pregnancy and/or lactation to assess risk of pregnancy
and maternal complications, adverse effects on the developing fetus and neonate, and adverse
effects on the infant. Infant outcomes will be assessed through at least the first year of life.
The minimum number of patients will be specified in the protocol.

345
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5496134

NDA 218808 and NDA 218820
CRENESSITY (crinecerfont) oral capsule and oral solution
•

Perform a lactation study (milk only or mother-infant pair study) in lactating women who
have received crinecerfont to measure concentrations of crinecerfont and its major
metabolites in breast milk using a validated assay and to assess the effects on the breastfed
infant, if available, based on study population.

DGE discussed advice from the Division of Pharmacovigilance in the Office of Surveillance and
Epidemiology regarding further assessment of suicidality and neutropenia in the postmarket
setting. The Division of Pharmacovigilance recommends the Applicant commit to the following
enhanced pharmacovigilance plan:
•

Neutropenia
 Submit all serious and non-serious domestic and/or foreign cases of neutropenia as 15day “alert reports”) through the 5th year following initial U.S. approval.
 Include narrative summary analyses of events of neutropenia in the required periodic
safety reports through the 5th year following initial U.S. approval. Use the Medical
Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) high-level term (HLT) “neutropenias” to
retrieve reports.

•

Suicidality
 Submit all serious and non-serious domestic and/or foreign cases of suicidal behavior
and/or ideation as 15-day “alert reports” through the 5th year following initial U.S.
approval.
 Include narrative summary analyses of suicidal behavior and/or ideation in the required
periodic safety reports through the 5th year following initial U.S. approval. Use the
MedDRA preferred terms (PTs) of “completed suicide,” “suicide attempt,” “suicidal
behavior,” and “suicidal ideation” to retrieve reports.

Narrative summary analyses of neutropenia and suicidality in the periodic safety reports should
include interval and cumulative data relative to the date of approval of CRENESSITY
(crinecerfont) and should provide an assessment of causality, with documentation of indication,
temporal association, duration of therapy, associated signs and symptoms, confounders,
underlying risk factors (e.g., psychiatric history), treatment given for the event, outcome, and
drug disposition.

1. Summary
In this submission the sponsor included reports of two animal carcinogenicity studies, one in
CD[Crl:CD(SD)] rats and one in CByB6F1-Tg(HRAS)2Jic mice. These studies were intended to
assess the carcinogenic potential of Crinecerfont, when administered via oral gavage at
appropriate drug levels for 100 weeks in rats and 26 weeks in mice.
Rat Study:
Survival data analyses:
1. For male rats, the survival analyses didn’t show any statistically significant dose
response relationship in mortality across the water control group and treated groups.
However, p-value of the likelihood ratio test is 0.0152<0.05 but the p-value of log-rank
test is 0.0675>0.05. The pairwise comparisons did not show any statistically significant
differences in mortality between the water control group and treated groups.
2. For male rats, the survival analyses didn’t show any statistically significant dose
response relationship in mortality across the vehicle control group and treated groups.
However, p-value of the likelihood ratio test is 0.0120<0.05 but the p-value of log-rank
test is 0.0563>0.05. The pairwise comparisons showed statistically significant
differences in mortality between the vehicle control group and the high dose group. The
p-value of the likelihood ratio test is 0.0428<0.05 and the p-value of log-rank test is
0.0393<0.05.
3. For female rats, the survival analyses didn’t show any statistically significant dose
response relationship in mortality across the water control group and treated groups or
across the vehicle control group and the treated groups. The pairwise comparisons did
not show any statistically significant differences in mortality between the water control
group and treated groups or between the vehicle control group and the treated groups.
Tumor data analysis:
1.

For female rats, the tumor data analysis showed statistically significant positive
dose response relationships across the water control and the treated groups in the
incidences of adenoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value<0.001), carcinoma
follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0032<0.025), and combined
adenoma+carcinoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value<0.001). The pairwise
comparisons between the water control and the high dose group showed

Reference ID: 5419597

NDA218808

Page 7 of 59

statistically significant increases in the incidences of adenoma, follicular cell,
thyroid gland (P-value=0.0041<0.05), carcinoma follicular cell, thyroid gland (Pvalue=0.0332<0.05), and combined adenoma+carcinoma, follicular cell, thyroid
gland (P-value<0.001).
2.

For female rats, the tumor data analysis showed statistically significant positive
dose response relationships across the vehicle control and the treated groups in the
incidences of adenoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value<0.001), carcinoma
follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value=0.0032<0.025), combined
adenoma+carcinoma, follicular cell, thyroid gland (P-value<0.001) and
schwannoma, uterus with cervix (P-value=0.0205<0.025). The pairwise

2. Background
In this submission the sponsor included reports of two animal carcinogenicity studies, one in
CD[Crl:CD(SD)] rats and one in CByB6F1-Tg(HRAS)2Jic mice. These studies were intended to
assess the carcinogenic potential of Crinecerfont, when administered via administered by oral
gavage at appropriate drug levels for 100 weeks in rats and 26 weeks in mice.
In this review the phrase "dose response relationship" refers to the linear component of the
effect of treatment, and not necessarily to a strictly increasing or decreasing mortality or tumor
incidence rate as the dose increases.

3. Rat Study
Two separate experiments were conducted, one in males and one in females. In each of
these two experiments there were three treated groups, one water group and one vehicle
control group. Three hundred and fifty rats of each sex were randomly assigned to the five
groups in equal size of 70 rats per group. The dose levels for treated groups were 5, 15 and
100 mg/kg/day. The rats in the water control group received the De-ionized water. The
study for the rats was designed to continue for up to 100 weeks.

Sponsor's analyses

3.1.1. Survival analysis
Intercurrent mortality data was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier product-limit method. An
overall test comparing all groups was conducted using a log-rank test (Allison, PD, 1995). If
this overall test was significant (p<0.05) and there were more than two groups, then a follow
up analysis was done where each treatment group was compared to the control group using a
log-rank test.

Reference ID: 5419597

NDA218808

Page 10 of 59

Results of all pair-wise comparisons were reported at the 0.05 and 0.01 significance levels. All
endpoints were analyzed using two-tailed tests.
Sponsor’s findings: Sponsor’s analysis showed the numbers (percents) of survival were 20
(29%), 21 (30%), 20 (29%), 18 (26%), and 15 (21%) in water, vehicle, and low, mid, high
dose groups, respectively in males and 20 (29%), 22 (31%), 17 (24%), 23 (33%), and 23
(33%) in water, vehicle, and low, mid, high dose groups, respectively in females.
No NBI-74788-related unscheduled deaths or euthanasias occurred in either sex, and no
statistically significant survival differences were noted.

3.1.2. Tumor data analysis
Tumor incidence data was analyzed using both survival adjusted and unadjusted tests. The
unadjusted tests were based on the incidence and number of sites examined for each tumor
type. The Cochran-Armitage test (Agresti,A. 1999) was for trend test and Fisher’s exact test
(Zar JH, 1999) was used to compare each treatment group with the control group. Trend
test was applied for all control and treatment groups that were arranged in a strictly
increasing dose level. The survival adjusted test was conducted according to the
prevalence/mortality methods described by Peto et al (Peto et al, 1980). The Poly-3 method
(Bieler and Williams, 1993) (Bailer and Portier, 1988) was used to assess prevalence of
tumors. The survival-adjusted rates based on the risk weights was displayed. The tests of
significance included both an overall trend and pair-wise comparisons of each treatment
group with the control. All p-values were reported using upper-tailed tests, unless otherwise
indicated.
Sponsor’s findings: Test article-related neoplastic microscopic findings were limited to an
increased incidence of benign and malignant thyroid follicular cell tumors (adenomas and
carcinomas) in females at
100 mg/kg/day.

3.2.2. Tumor data analysis
The tumor data were analyzed for the positive dose response relationships and the positive
pairwise comparison increases between each of the treated groups with control group. Both
the dose response relationship tests and pairwise comparisons were performed using the
Poly-K method described in the paper of Bailer and Portier (1988) and Bieler and Williams
(1993). In this method an animal that lives the full study period ( wmax ) or dies before the
terminal sacrifice but develops the tumor type being tested gets a score of sh =1. An animal

 w 
that dies at week wh without a tumor before the end of the study gets a score of sh =  h 
 wmax 
< 1. The adjusted group size is defined as Σ sh . As an interpretation, an animal with score sh

k

=1 can be considered as a whole animal while an animal with score sh < 1 can be considered
as a partial animal. The adjusted group size Σ sh is equal to N (the original group size) if all
animals live up to the end of the study or if each animal that dies before the terminal sacrifice
develops at least one tumor, otherwise the adjusted group size is less than N. These adjusted
group sizes were then used for the dose response relationship (or the pairwise) tests using the
Cochran-Armitage test. One critical point for Poly-k test is the choice of the appropriate value
of k, which depends on the tumor incidence pattern with the increased dose. For long term 104
week standard rat and mouse studies, a value of k=3 is suggested in the literature. Hence, this
reviewer used k=3 for the analysis of this data. For the calculation of p-values the exact
permutation method was used. The tumor rates and the p-values for the positive dose
response relationship tests and pairwise comparisons are listed in Tables 17 to 20 in the
appendix for male and female rats, respectively.
Adjustment for multiple testing: For the chronic study in rats, the adjustment of multiple
testing of the dose response relationship for a submission with one chronic rat study and
one transgenic mouse study, the more recently revised draft (January, 2013) FDA guidance
for the carcinogenicity studies suggests the use of test levels α =0.005 for common tumors
and α=0.025 for rare tumors for the chronic rat study. For pairwise comparisonsfor the
chronic rat study in the above type of submission with one chronic rat study and one
transgenic mouse study, the same guidance document suggests the use of test levels α
=0.01 for common tumors and α =0.05 for rare tumors for the chronic rat study.

NDA218808

Page 13 of 59

It should be noted that the FDA guidance for multiple testing for dose response relationship
is based on a publication by Lin and Rahman (1998). In this work the authors investigated
the use of this rule for Peto analysis. However, in a later work Rahman and Lin (2008)
showed that this rule for multiple testing for dose response relationship is also suitable for
Poly-K tests.
Reviewer’s findings: The tumor types in Tables 2 to 5 below showed p-values less than or

4. Mouse Study

these two experiments there were four treated groups, one water group, one vehicle control
